News.title: Terrifying ‘giraffe’s head’ sinkhole stunt unravels as rescuers believed live animal was trapped in ‘fake emergency’
News.content:
A CRAZY stunt has backfired after wildlife officials mounted a rescue operation believing a giraffe was trapped in a sinkhole.

South Africa‘s main opposition party, the Democratic Alliance, faced backlash after placing a stuffed giraffe’s head in a pothole at Mogale City, north-west of Johannesburg.



The stunt aimed to highlight dangerous road conditions, but backfired when wildlife rescuers abandoned an active mission to respond to the fake emergency.

The video posted by the party and led by Evert Du Plessis, the shadow member roads and logistics, and was captioned: “A sinkhole so deep a giraffe can stand in it.”



The incident has led to widespread public fury with animal lovers failing to see the funny side arguing the ploy wasted time and resources from wildlife services.

The Owl Rescue centre – who responded to the incident – received a number of panicked calls notifying them to the fake emergency.

read more world news TRAGIC STAR PROBE Police investigation launched into death of World Cup ace Jayden Adams



When they couldn’t verify if the incident was indeed an emergency, they decided to launch a rescue.

In a post to social media, they said: “Turns out, it was. The local branch of the DA thought sticking a stuffed giraffe head into a hole was a clever way to draw attention.

“I dunno… Maybe I just haven’t had enough coffee for today.

DA- You owe us a donation towards fuel please.”

The antic was intended to demonstrate how “deep and serious” the issue of potholes are, according to the DA.



They said: “Residents and small businesses in the area continue to live with the danger and disruption.

After receiving a great deal of support on social media, the Owl Centre said in a separate post: “We understand why you need to bring attention to the state of our roads and sinkholes, and we even get the joke.

“But using an animal to make a political point just crosses the line for us.

​”For us, seeing a stuffed giraffe head, a wild animal that was once wild and free, likely shot and mounted, stuck in a hole for political points just feels wrong.

“We probably have a different outlook on life than most because we work with these animals every day, but to us, using animal remains as a prop shows a real lack of respect and empathy for our wildlife and biodiversity.



“That was a few hours wasted that could have been spent saving real lives.”

Potholes have become a hot-topic issue as ancient infrastructure and overstretched services plague the state.

News.title: Teen football star & beloved great grandmother among six killed as ‘once in a lifetime’ floods rage through Indiana
News.content:
A TEENAGE football star and a beloved great-grandmother have been identified as the first victims of raging floods that swept through Indiana.

At least six people have been found dead and many are missing after storms lashed parts of the state creating a “once-in-a-lifetime” disaster.



Matthew Morey, 19, was pulled from the Mississinewa River on Saturday, the Delaware County Sheriff’s Office said, after he was reported missing near Muncie on Wednesday.

He and a group of friends had jumped into the swollen river for an unknown reason, officials said, and while his three pals were pulled to safety, Morey remained missing.



The search for him was suspended on Thursday due to dangerous weather conditions as his desperate mom begged for help.

“I’m hurt and I need som ehelp, and so we’re not there and I can’t get there,” she tearfully told NBC News on Friday as historic floods and strong currents hampered rescue efforts and blocked roads.

“I can’t get to him because there’s no – I can’t get in a boat. If I had a boat, I swear to God I’d be in that water…My hope is that he’s still alive.”

Morey was reportedly due to attend Purdue University on Monday to study engineering after he graduated from Delta High School this summer.



He played for the Delta Eagles football team, the Eagles basketball team, and the Delta Baseball Boosters.

“We are heartbroken for the Morey family and so deeply sorry for the loss of their son, Matthew,” the baseball team wrote in a statement on Facebook.

“Matthew chose basketball and football in high school, but we know he always loved playing baseball too.

“How lucky were these boys to get to share so much time in the dirt with him.

“Our thoughts, prayers, and love are with the entire Morey family and all who had the privilege of knowing Matthew during this incredibly difficult time. Once an Eagle, always an Eagle.”



The Delta Eagles football team praised Matthew for “being a great role model, teammate, and friend.”

“You will forever be in our hearts. With football season about to start, we know you will be looking down and cheering on your teammates.”

Great-grandmother Stephanie Jo Sallee, 58, has also been identified as one of those who died in the floods after she was found in a cornfield in Yorktown on Friday with her beloved dog.

“She had a heart for others. She never judged people. She persevered many trials in her life and remained a compassionate and loving person,” her family told WRTV.

Other victims include a four-year-old boy and two unidentified women.



Meanwhile, rescue teams have so far saved at least 95 people from surging floodwaters after a state of emergency was declared by the mayor on Friday when creeks and streams burst their banks.



The White River rose to a peak of 24ft in Anderson and Noblesville, marking a new record since 1913.

Residents across over a dozen counties were trapped in their homes, caught in floodwaters, and swept away as they tried to flee.

Footage shows some properties catching fire as power lines were downed.

Over 350 people were evacuated in Delaware County including a senior mobile home community.

Jacob Spence, director of Marion County Emergency Management, said it was a “once-in-a-lifetime” flood disaster in which over 11 inches of rain fell in 48 hours.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

An emergency declaration was granted for the battered state by President Donald Trump, triggering a federal disaster response.

Flood warnings are still in effect across parts of the state.

News.title: Infamous armed robber could be back on streets within weeks after parole hearing… even though £30m haul is still MISSING
News.content:
AN ARMED robber involved in Britain’s biggest ever cash heist could be released from prison within weeks — despite £30million still missing.

Stuart Royle, 67, has been granted a parole hearing on September 10 after he was jailed for his role in the infamous £53million Securitas robbery in Tonbridge, Kent, in 2006.



The former car salesman was jailed indefinitely in 2008 and ordered to serve at least 15 years after being convicted of conspiracy to kidnap, conspiracy to rob and possession of a firearm.

He was sentenced to a further six years in 2012 after he failed to comply with a £2million confiscation order.



Royle had his last parole bid denied in 2024 after the Parole Board deemed he was too dangerous to the public.

The board also did not recommend he be moved into an open prison.

He was reportedly the gang’s transport man and helped identify the home of Colin Dixon, whose kidnapping was central to the success of the raid.

The raid began on the evening of February 21, 2006 when two gang members posed as police officers and kidnapped the depot manager, Colin Dixon, on his way home from work.

The callous gang then abducted Dixon’s wife and eight-year-old son from their home and took all three to the cash depot where they were used as hostages to force staff to open up the facility.

The seven masked men held the family and 14 staff members at gunpoint, handcuffing them and making them lie on the floor while they stole almost £53million.



Royle and his six accomplices left behind £154million because their seven-and-a-half tonne lorry wasn’t big enough to transport it all.



Only £21million was ever recovered, with the remainder believed to have been moved through organised criminal groups.

Colin Dixon later called the raid “the worst night of my life”.

Earlier this year, Kent Police confirmed the robbery remains a live investigation with more than £30million still outstanding.

Royle’s last parole bid in 2024 was denied after the Parole Board was not satisfied that releasing him would be safe for the protection of the public.

The board also did not recommend him be released into an open prison.



Two men were charged last year for plotting the shooting of another of the Securitas gang, former cage fighter Paul Allen, who was hit twice and left paralysed from the chest down.

Chief Constable of Kent Police, Tim Smith, who was one of two senior investigating officers in charge of the Securitas investigation, said: “The robbery, including the kidnap of the depot manager, is one of the most elaborate in UK criminal history but it also stands as an example of Kent Police’s commitment to bringing offenders to justice and tackling organised crime.

“While the heist itself captured widespread attention, and understandably so, at the heart of this were terrified victims who were held and threatened at gunpoint.”

A Parole Board spokesperson said: “Parole Board decisions are solely focused on what risk a prisoner could represent to the public if released and whether that risk is manageable in the community.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“A panel will carefully examine a huge range of evidence, including details of the original crime, and any evidence of behaviour change, as well as explore the harm done and impact the crime has had on the victims.



“Parole reviews are undertaken thoroughly and with extreme care. Protecting the public is our number one priority.”

News.title: Salamina fires - live: Greek island filled with Brits in flames as evacuations ordered
News.content:
Two huge fires have broken out on the island of Salamina off the coast of Athens with evacuations ordered in multiple areas

Homes have burnt down and evacuation orders have been issued on the Greek island of Salamina after two massive wildfires erupted at the same time.

The separate blazes broke out in the Peristeria area, and Selinia areas, with the latter heading toward the popular tourist village of Kaki Vigla.

The mayor of Salamina, Giorgos Panagopoulos, told Greek news outlet ERT that "houses have burned down" in the Peristeria area. The mayor added: "The situation is difficult. There are two major fires, homes are under threat, and we have asked the police to bring us two ferry boats to Saterli Beach so that we can use them for people if we see that the situation becomes much more difficult."

Very strong winds blowing across Salamina are increasing the risk of the fire fronts spreading rapidly.

News.title: TV star Stephen Tompkinson talks about his 'greatest role' as he helps stars of the future
News.content:
Actor Stephen Tompkinson has every reason to blow his own trumpet, as Brassed Off celebrates its 30th birthday with a tribute concert at the Royal Albert Hall. The TV star, who played Phil Ormondroyd, the troubled trombone player and son of the band leader, who attempts to take his life, says it remains his proudest role. He tells the Mirror: “On October 2, they are holding a concert at the Royal Albert Hall to celebrate the 30th anniversary of Brassed Off. That is a very rare thing indeed. "It was a great film and it just shows its popularity when it sells out after all these years. It is probably the film that I am most proud of and I felt that at the time.” The soundtrack for the film, based on Grimethorpe's struggles against pit closures, was provided by the Grimethorpe Colliery Band. Stephen continues: "It was an amazing script and Pete Postlethwaite was an actor who had this way of making the most of what was written for him. "It was up for a load of awards, including a Peter Sellars award for comedy, an Evening Standard award, the Film César in France, and it was recognised in Spain, and Germany."

View 6 Images Actor Steve Tompkinson launches the first Tyneside Talent Unit at Tyneside Cinema, a pioneering new programme funded by Sir Graham Wylie Foundation.

As Amy Hunt strives to be fastest woman in the world ex teammate backs her for Olympic gold READ MORE :

This year means a double whammy of anniversaries for the actor, as the popular series Ballykissangel also turned 30 in February.

Stephen, 60, played Father Peter Clifford, a young English priest who transferred to a rural parish in Ireland. Pub landlady Assumpta Fitzgerald, played by Dervla Kirwan, was the first person he met in the village and they had a chemistry that reflected their romance off screen. Stephen, who is just back from working in Ireland again, continues: "I have just finished The Heights for Channel 5 with Anna Friel, which was set in Dublin. “I got to go back to Avoca in County Wicklow, where we filmed Ballykissangel, for the first time in 30 years, which was wonderful. "It has had a lick of paint and the church looked fabulous. The locals would come up to me and say ‘hello’ and ‘ah, it's yourself,’ like I had never been away. "I loved it. After that first series, it just really took off and we would get bus loads of tourists coming to see us film. "There would be 1,500 people there and we had to turn the cameras around to exclude them from the shot. It reminded me so much of John Wayne and The Quiet Man, which was filmed in Ireland and is one of my all-time favourite films.

‌



View 6 Images Actor Steve Tompkinson with the first talent unit students at the Tyneside Cinema in Newcastle

"It had an element of that, a sort of grandeur. But the tourism boost was just extraordinary. "We had to film there less and less, because so many people came to see it. The setting was so beautiful. It aired early in the year and it was filmed in the summer when the countryside really did look at its best. "I think viewers just wanted to see it for themselves. It was sunshine and picture postcard scenery. We knew that we had really made it big when Daniel O'Donnell came to visit."

View 6 Images Stephen Tompkinson attends the Pride of Britain awards 2019 Grosvenor House Hotel with Jess Johnson (Image: Andy Stenning/Daily Mirror)

Stephen’s diverse career, which has ranged from Drop the Dead Donkey to Eric, Ernie and Me, suffered in 2021 when he was accused of punching a drunken man making a noise outside his home in the early hours in Whitley Bay, North Tyneside, causing the man to fall and fracture his skull.

‌



The star admitted he missed out on parts and was unable to work while waiting two years for the case to come to court. He was found not guilty of causing the man grievous bodily harm at Newcastle Crown Court in May 2023. Afterwards Stephen paid tribute to his then partner, actress Jess Johnson, for standing by him.

Stephen, who starred as DCI John Thistletwaite in This Is Not A Murder Mystery (2025) has now put it firmly behind him.

View 6 Images Actor Steve Tompkinson at the first Tyneside Talent Unit at Tyneside Cinema. 30 young people were selected from over 300 for the first cohort.

The actor, who has been married twice and has a daughter, is now using his fame to help youngsters get into the film industry by promoting a new Tyneside Cinema film talent unit that provides career opportunities for many working-class young people in his native North East. More than 300 applicants were whittled down to 33 talented individuals for the cinema’s first intake.The Graham Wylie Foundation is funding the teaching of skills required to work in all aspects of film, from podcasting to camera operation, editing and production. Stephen says: "I want to dispel the myth that you have to go to London to succeed in our profession. Hopefully, with Andy Burnham, there will be more emphasis on the North and opportunities here. "They have a film studio coming to Sunderland; this new unit is so exciting. There are more than 30 like-minded young adults who will talk about their dreams and aspirations and feed off each other. That is absolutely priceless."

‌



New recruits Calum (c) McNair, 18, of South Shields, and Valerie Enriquez, 24, of Newcastle, told of their excitement at winning places on the new course

View 6 Images Tyneside Cinema Talent Unit students Calum McNair and Valerie Enriquez

Calum would like to be a director of photography or a cinematographer, while Valerie is interested in film production.

They are following in a fine tradition; Hollywood film maker Sir Ridley Scott has a unique connection to the Tyneside, which was founded by his great uncle Dixon Scott in 1937.

‌



The talent unit takes Stephen back to his days at the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama in London, where he studied from 1984-87.

He was one of the youngest there and the 'only Northerner' in his year when he travelled down from his home near Blackpool, Lancs., after moving there from Stockton-on-Tees when he was a child. He says: "The things you go through at that age make it nice to have the kindred spirits and friendships they are offering here. "I was there at the same time as James Nesbitt, James Purefoy, Jason Isaacs, Jared Harris, Graham Norton, and Christopher Eccleston. "Graham was younger and Chris was in the year above and helped me where he could. It really was a wonderful time to be there. "Looking back, the TV series Drop the Dead Donkey was my big break. I was 25 and it was such a great show to be a part of. The part of TV reporter Damien was great fun, he was just a psychopath.

"When they started showing it, people were very surprised that we were not made of latex, because it was the closest thing to Spitting Image at the time. "It was so nerve-wracking, because 20-25% of the show was written to reflect the big stories of that week, as you were going on air. You never knew what the topical subjects or your character's lines would be. “The show was filmed on the Wednesday in front of a live audience and on the Thursday they would do a voice-over to cover what the show was about. "We were always trying to make it seem spontaneous and unscripted, but there were postage notes all over the set with the lines on them. "We went back on the road with a stage version of it a couple of years ago. It was about how the TV station was going to be closed and felt like an Agatha Christie mystery, because you did not know who was going to take charge of it. "In the end, it was South Korea, but for a big part of it, people thought it would be Russia."

View 6 Images Actor Steve Tompkinson with students at the Talent Unit at Tyneside Cinema

‌



Stephen recalls learning valuable lessons in his early career making radio drama at the BBC, after winning the prestigious Carleton Hobbs award - a bursary for promising young actors. He recalls: "You were in a huge main studio in Broadcasting House with a single microphone, it was like a big goldfish bowl. "I forgot to speak into the mic the first time around and felt so stupid, because they could not hear what I was saying. I think that made me relax, because I won the award and performed in 54 plays in seven months. "It was an extraordinary turnover, but it was great experience. “The wonderful thing about radio is that it really makes you appreciate the writer, because without the writer, you were nothing. "You had to interpret the script, even if you only had one line with five words, how you emphasised them was key. “I had just left drama school and it was a real lesson for me."

News.title: Backlash as water firms say they should be able to hike prices during droughts
News.content:
Backlash as water firms say they should be able to hike prices during droughts

Water regulator Ofwat is weighing up proposals to introduce 'surge pricing' - meaning water scarcity can be taken into account when setting prices during dry summers

View 2 Images An aerial view of the Tittesworth Reservoir in the Staffordshire Moorlands as water levels fall (Image: Getty Images)

Water firms are pushing to be allowed to charge more during droughts amid growing anger about rising bills and shortages.

‌



Regulator Ofwat is considering 'surge pricing' - which would see the cost of water usage rise in the summer. Sector bosses say it would encourage Brits to save water - but critics warn it is punishing customers for years of failure.

‌



It comes just days after Andy Burnham warned water firms not to treat the public as "blank cheques". Under proposals being looked at by Ofwat, suppliers would be allowed to make water scarcity a factor in setting bills.

‌



An exceptionally dry summer has resulted in nearly 30 million people living with hosepipe bans, while wildfires tear through parts of the country. The government has not set out a position on surge pricing, but indicated it would not support anything that saw bills go up any further.

Water campaigner and former Undertones singer Feargal Sharkey said the measure would simply reward companies for failure. He said: “For 40 years, these companies have had legal obligations to help consumers to reduce their demand and they have failed at that comprehensively, just as they’ve failed to keep our rivers clean and failed to deal with our sewage. Now they’re going to penalise consumers for that failure.”

Rapists and child sex offenders to face pinpoint tagging in biggest ever monitoring expansion READ MORE :

Clacton by-election result as Nigel Farage beats Count Binface but refuses to attend READ MORE :

View 2 Images Feargal Sharkey hit out over the proposal (Image: (Image: Adam Gerrard/Daily Express))

‌



If given the go-ahead, water companies would be allowed to raise prices during droughts from next April. Other measures under consideration include making people pay a higher rate once their water use passes a certain threshold.

Ofwat last week gave a provisional go-ahead for firms to hike bills to fund an extra £3.4billion in spending to improve infrastructure. It has already allowed companies to increase prices by 36% between 2025 and 2030.

This comes despite mounting anger at raw sewage being dumped into rivers and seas and massive bonuses being lavished on executives. Debt-laden Thames Water is one of the firms provisionally allowed to increase customer bills between 2027 and 2030, alongside Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Wessex Water and South East Water.

‌



Mr Burnham responded last week: "I understand why people are angry - I am too. The truth is customers have been asked to pay more for years, yet serious pollution incidents are at record levels and the pipes are still leaking.

"None of which is the billpayer's fault, who should not be treated as a bottomless source of funding for other people's failures."

He said the water industry has been failing for "far too long" and said ministers are looking at ways to give the public more control and bring down bills. A petition on the Parliamentary website calling for a referendum on nationalising water companies has attracted over 172,000 signatures.

‌



Supporters of surge pricing argue it would incentivise saving water. The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) said any measures brought in must bring bills down.

A spokesman said: "We have already ring-fenced money earmarked for new infrastructure so it can only be spent on fixing the problems, and will go further by fundamentally reforming the water sector so that it works for the public, keeping bills as low as they can be.

“Water companies are trialling new charging structures which must, as promised, make bills fairer and more affordable while encouraging greater water efficiency.”

‌



In a statement Water UK - which represents firms in the sector - said: "To tackle drought water companies are upping their game on leakage, which has decreased to its lowest level on record. But we also need to consider whether we could help people save water by rewarding people through their water bill. This might include eliminating standing charges or expanding discounts for customers who save water. Government can also help new reservoirs be built faster by cutting the time needed for planning."

An Ofwat spokesperson said: "The efficient use of water is the is in the best interests of everyone, including businesses.

"The options we are progressing would support greater consideration of water scarcity and efficiency by water companies when setting their charges, and encourage more tariff innovation.

Article continues below

"We recently carried out a period of consultation on the proposals and will reach a final decision in the near future."

Last month analysis by Greenpeace found that water companies are wasting an enormous 2.87 billion litres of water every day through leaks. This is enough to fill 1,150 Olympic-sized swimming pools.

A nationwide hosepipe ban saves around 577 million litres per day, the charity estimates.

News.title: Essex aerodrome incident: Pilot rushed to hospital after plane crash horror at air show
News.content:
Essex aerodrome incident: Pilot rushed to hospital after plane crash horror at air show

The pilot is understood to have suffered 'serious' injuries following an 'air incident' at Stow Maries Great War Aerodrome near Woodham Ferrers, Chelmsford, Essex

View 2 Images Stow Maries Aerodrome in Essex (file image) (Image: Getty )

A pilot has been left with "serious injuries" after a plane crashed during an air show at an Essex aerodrome.

‌



Essex Police raced to Stow Maries Great War Aerodrome near Woodham Ferrers, Chelmsford, this afternoon, where it is understood there had been an "air incident" during the Stow Maries Air show.

‌



Officers were first called shortly before 2.25pm on Sunday, August 16. The sole occupant of the aircraft has been taken to hospital with serious injuries.

‌



Members of the public have been asked to avoid the area to allow responders to work, report Essex Live.

The aerodrome confirmed the incident and said the on site museum is now closed to the public.

‌



View 2 Images Stow Maries Aerodrome said the museum is closed to the public (Image: Google)

Police have meanwhile asked those attending to follow the instructions of organisers and the emergency services.

Stow Maries Great War Aerodrome said: "Stow Maries Great War Aerodrome can confirm that there has been an air incident during our Air Show.

Article continues below

"More information will follow shortly. In the meantime, the Museum is closed to the public"

An Essex Police spokesperson said: "Those attending the event are urged to follow the instructions of organisers and emergency service personnel.

"The public are asked to please avoid the area to allow responders the space to work at the scene."

News.title: Huge blaze in Greenfield forces Tesco to close as firefighters warn 'stay away'
News.content:
Multiple fire crews tackled a huge fire on an industrial site in Greenfield, Greater Manchester, with flames and smoke visible for miles around

Huge blaze in Greenfield forces Tesco to close as firefighters warn 'stay away'

Firefighters are tackling a huge blaze at an industrial site in Saddleworth

A huge fire broke out on an industrial estate in Greater Manchester with multiple crews racing to the scene and a Tesco supermarket forced to close.

The blaze on an industrial estate in Greenfield sent huge plumes of smoke into the sky above the town. Tesco has now reopened its store in nearby Wellington Road.

Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service said at the time the fire broke out: "Firefighters are tackling a large fire at an industrial building on Chew Valley Road in Greenfield.

"Due to the amount of smoke, residents are advised to keep their windows and doors closed. A cordon is in place and people should avoid the area if possible."

News.title: New Lidl £8 'atmospheric' lamp similar to £55 John Lewis offer out Thursday
News.content:
New Lidl £8 'atmospheric' lamp similar to £55 John Lewis offer out Thursday

Shoppers who like the look of John Lewis' versions could save £47 by opting for Lidl's budget-friendly alternative

View 2 Images The supermarket is updating its Special Buy deals on Thursday (Image: Getty)

Lidl is bringing out a new "atmospheric" lamp on Thursday, August 20, that looks similar to a version on sale at John Lewis. The supermarket regularly updates its Special Buy deals every Thursday and Sunday, and the next batch of items to land in stores includes various homeware items.

‌



The supermarket's new LED Table Lamp with Touch Function costs £7.99 and will be coming to stores across the UK in a few days. For those who like the look of John Lewis' Cara Glass Touch Lamp, but would prefer to stick to a budget, Lidl's version may be a more wallet-friendly option.

‌



John Lewis' version looks similar in shape and design to Lidl's £7.99 lamp, with both featuring a silver base, frosted glass and cylindrical appearance. However, by opting for Lidl's £7.99 version, John Lewis shoppers could save around £47.

‌



The John Lewis lamp comes in a pack of two for £55, meaning each lamp is worth £27.50. However, this would still be around £19.50 more than buying from the supermarket.

In the product description on Lidl's website, the supermarket says its £7.99 lamp has a touch-sensitive lamp base for switching it on and off. It comes with three brightness levels and a metal base with a matt-nickel finish.

View 2 Images Lidl's LED Table Lamp with Touch Function (L) and John Lewis' Cara Glass Touch Lamps (R) (Image: Lidl / John Lewis)

‌



Lidl adds: "Frosted glass shade for atmospheric, warm light. Includes LED light bulb with an integrated step dim function. Power cable: 1.6m. For indoor use only. Size: W10 x H25.5cm. Three-year warranty."

As for John Lewis, the product description reads: "We like how the opal glass shades on these petite table lamps diffuse the light and create a warm glow. Their chrome base is designed with touch functionality to offer three light levels. Tap it once to turn on the light, again to make it brighter and a final time to turn it off. Perfect for setting the right ambience in your space and conveniently supplied as a pair."

In the reviews on John Lewis' website, one shopper said: "Look expensive and are very unobtrusive on the bedside tables." A second said: "Very chic looking." A third said: "Love the different atmospheres one can create." However, a fourth wrote: "The lamps worked well for about three weeks until one of them just stopped working."

‌



What other Special Buys are coming to Lidl on Thursday?

Lidl will be bringing out a Livarno White Storage Stool for £14.99. Lidl describes it as a "comfortable and space-saving seating option". It comes with a padded, removable seat and it provides storage space inside.

There is also a "supersoft" Throw in Purple, Beige and White Shades for £7.99. As well as a White Luxury Renforcé Duvet Cover Set with a blue watercolour floral pattern for £11.99.

Article continues below

Some items will be available for less for shoppers with the Lidl Plus App. As with all Lidl Special Buys, once stock is gone, it is gone.

News.title: Lone tenant refuses to move from council estate facing demolition
News.content:
Lone tenant refuses to move from council estate facing demolition

Andy Roche has lived in the flat for almost 30 years and isn't winning to give up his home despite the council earmarking marking the entire estate in estate in Rochdale for demolition

View 6 Images Andy Roche is digging his heels in and refuses to leave his home in Rochdale (Image: / SWNS)

A lone tenant is halting the bulldozers by refusing to move from a deserted corner of a doomed council estate which is earmarked for demolition.

‌



Andy Roche, 51, is the last person living in Zedburgh, one of seven 1960s apartment blocks facing the wrecking ball at the Lower Falinge estate in Rochdale, Greater Manchester. He is digging his heels in despite six of the seven blocks already completely empty, leaving his one-bed flat as the sole occupied home among 126 properties earmarked for demolition. Rochdale Boroughwide Housing wants to flatten them and build up to 270 new homes.

‌



He insists he still loves living there despite the deserted walkways and plywood-covered windows around him. He says the appeal is the green space, lack of traffic and familiarity of a home he has known for nearly three decades - and he told the council he doesn't want to go. He pays £95 a week for the flat. Andy lives there with his partner, and they are both autistic.

‌



View 6 Images He's fighting a lone battle - but won't give up his home without a fight (Image: / SWNS)

New build nightmare with indoor temperatures topping 31C and homeowners 'overheating' READ MORE :

Andy, who is unemployed and has lived in the flat for 28 years, said: "We don't want to leave this area - it's where I've lived all my life since leaving my parents' home. "There's never any trouble, and we like all of the green space.

"Because we're both autistic, we have very specific needs when it comes to things like noise, smells and lights. We've given RBH a list of our housing needs - but they seem to be ignoring it."

‌



He said suggested alternatives included one property next to a pub and another near a metalworks. Work on Lower Falinge began in early 1968, with its deck-access blocks completed in stages into the early 1970s.

Today, Zedburgh is surrounded by six empty blocks - Ollerton, Newstead, Romsey, Quinton, Ullesthorpe and Vaynor. There are 126 homes across the seven blocks, leaving Andy's as the only occupied flat. Across the communal grassland, once-busy homes stand lifeless behind plywood.

View 6 Images New homes are planned on the Lower Falinge Estate with all-but one resident gone (Image: / SWNS)

‌



Andy said it has created an "eerie" atmosphere, adding: "We feel isolated. We worry about people breaking in when we're out of the flat."

He said people have begun hanging around the deserted estate since residents moved out and suspects some may be dealing drugs. With nobody heating neighbouring flats, his home is also colder and more expensive to keep warm.

Andy added: "When I hear someone outside, I think - have they come with machines to knock us down?

‌



"When I hear the letterbox, my heart sinks because I think there's going to be a letter saying that they're taking us to court. This has been going on for so long that I've almost forgotten what it was like to live here before."

The pair were served with a notice seeking possession in January and Andy said: "It's so distressing - I can't understate that. It's almost a matter of life and death with how distressing it is."

6 View 6 Images The man and his partner are the last left standing in a doomed block of flats (Image: / SWNS) 6 View 6 Images Andy maintains he is refusing to move from the doomed council estate (Image: / SWNS)

‌



The latest plans come less than a year after campaigners successfully challenged an earlier bid to demolish six blocks. RBH sought prior approval, but residents took the decision to judicial review and won.

The housing association has now returned with a wider proposal which also puts Zedburgh in the firing line. RBH says the blocks are at the end of their life and no longer provide safe, warm homes.

But Andy has questioned why other blocks from the same era have instead been refurbished to tackle damp and mould.

‌



Regeneration began in 2012 and RBH says three completed phases have delivered 100 new homes The result is a stark split between modern housing and boarded-up blocks waiting for the bulldozers.

In 2016, then-prime minister David Cameron referred to Lower Falinge as a "sink estate". RBH has not published a specific price tag for this phase. But in January it secured £55m in new bank funding to invest in existing homes and support regeneration projects across Rochdale.

View 6 Images Gemma Lucas has her own battle and lives on the Lower Falinge Estate (Image: / SWNS)

‌



The plans also promise improved public spaces and better walking and cycling links with the town centre. Elsewhere, several blocks not earmarked for demolition remain occupied.

Mum-of-six Gemma Lucas, 32, has spent three years in temporary accommodation there while waiting for a permanent council house.

She said: "We're in a housing crisis - but those blocks are just sitting there empty waiting to get knocked down. Why can't people move into them?"

‌



RBH intends to submit an outline application for the plans to Rochdale Council.

If approved, a further detailed application would still be needed before demolition or building work could begin.

A spokesperson for RBH said: "We understand this is a very difficult situation for the customers involved, and we have been and will continue to work with them and their representatives to support them with finding a new home that meets their needs.

‌



"The regeneration of Lower Falinge has been in progress over several years, in consultation with residents throughout.

"The seven blocks identified for demolition have been empty for several years and have reached the end of their life and can no longer provide the safe, warm homes our customers want and need to life healthy lives.

"We remain absolutely committed to supporting the one remaining household to move into suitable alternative accommodation.

Article continues below

"Since June 2025, we have made five offers of new homes, including properties within Lower Falinge and nearby. We will continue to provide tailored practical and financial support throughout the move alongside our partners."

News.title: Mounjaro 'four weeks' advice for women taking contraception at same time
News.content:
Mounjaro 'four weeks' advice for women taking contraception at same time

Women may need to use different methods for weeks after starting the jabs

View 3 Images Women may need to change their contraceptive methods when starting the jabs (Image: GETTY)

According to official guidance, women taking popular weight loss medications are urged to change their method of contraception after starting the medication, as it could “reduce the effectiveness”. Particularly if they are planning to start taking the weight loss drug tirzepatide, more commonly known as Mounjaro.

‌



Mounjaro has been found to potentially interfere with oral contraceptives. As a result, women starting the jabs are advised to add other contraceptive methods to their regimen for at least the first four weeks, and for four weeks after any dose increase, because the medicine slows stomach emptying and can reduce pill absorption.

‌



Official guidance recommends barrier methods, such as condoms, in addition to still taking the oral pill or moving to a completely different, non-oral contraception for the entire time you are using Mounjaro. Women who are changing their weight-loss medication or dose may also need to take similar precautions for four weeks after the switch.

‌



View 3 Images Weight loss injections can cause vomiting and diarrhoea as side effects (Image: GETTY)

There’s currently no evidence that other types of weight loss jabs, like semaglutide, which is the main ingredient in Wegovy, interfere with oral contraceptives in the same way. However, one common side effect of almost all weight loss medications could still impact it. For official safety details, read the MHRA Guidance on GLP-1 Medicines or consult the Superdrug Online Doctor Mounjaro Guide.

Faculty of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare guidance states: “Diarrhoea and vomiting are common side effects of the GLP-1 agonists and can reduce the effectiveness of the pill.”

‌



Women who are taking weight loss medications and oral contraceptives should be aware of when they experience these side effects, if at all. If vomiting occurs within three hours of taking your birth control, it could mean your body didn’t have time to absorb the pill properly and should be treated as a ‘missed pill’.

Similarly, if you experience severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, guidance states you should also treat your last oral contraceptive as a ‘missed pill’. And if the side effects are persistent, it might be worth moving to a different contraceptive entirely.

View 3 Images Vomiting and diarrhoea can reduce the effectiveness of contraceptive pills (Image: GETTY)

Article continues below

Missing just one contraceptive pill can reduce its effectiveness. However, the exact procedure you need to follow will depend on the type of pill you take and where you are in the pack cycle.

The information leaflet that comes with the box of contraceptive pills will have instructions on what to do if you have missed a pill, or you can talk to your pharmacist for guidance. Other types of non-oral contraceptives, like the coil, implant, injection or patches, won’t need extra precautions when mixed with weight loss medications. Speak to your doctor if you have any questions or concerns.

As the official guidance notes: “There is no reason to believe that GLP-1 agonists affect methods of contraception that are not taken by mouth, so it is okay to use any of these options.”

News.title: Watch: BBC visits smouldering market in Ukraine after strikes
News.content:
Six people have been injured at a market in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv, as the country was hit by a series of Russian strikes.

Five people were reportedly killed across Ukraine, while Russian officials said seven people were killed there, in strikes by Ukraine.

The BBC's Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson visited the market, known for selling items like books and posters, as firefighters worked to extinguish hot spots.

Follow live coverage.

News.title: Emergency phone alert put domestic abuse victims at risk, campaigners say
News.content:
Most people received the blaring alert at 19:00 BST on Friday - and it came as a surprise given the government had not told people it was coming, as it has done for tests of the system.

The notification, which cautioned against the use of disposable barbecues, naked flames or fireworks, was the biggest use yet of the emergency alert system and Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged the public to take it "seriously".

A Cabinet Office press release, posted to their website at about 18:45 on Friday, was missed by many in the media, which meant there was little warning to the public.

This potentially jeopardised domestic abuse victims trying to hide secret phones they use to seek support and try to escape abusers, some campaigners have said.

Women's Aid, the national charity aiming to end domestic abuse, is calling for more forewarning of alerts wherever possible.

Veronica Oakeshott, the charity's head of external affairs, told BBC News: "Survivors of domestic abuse frequently turn to second phones to help them access lifesaving support or flee from abuse."

It is vital the devices stay hidden, she said, before adding: "We would urge the government to forewarn the public that alerts might be issued, when possible."

It has been reported that senior government figures were discussing whether or not to send the alert hours before, on Friday morning.

The alert came after a spate of wildfires including one that destroyed 19 homes in Stourbridge, West Midlands, on Thursday.

News.title: Murder inquiry after man bitten by dog dies
News.content:
A murder inquiry has begun after the death of a man who was bitten by a dog on a footpath in West Yorkshire.

The 55-year-old was injured in an altercation on a disused railway line off Blacker Lane in Calder Grove, Wakefield, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday. He was taken to hospital in a critical condition but died just after 19:00.

West Yorkshire Police has appealed for two people, one of whom is called Sophie, who stopped to help the injured man to come forward.

A force spokesperson said a 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and of being the owner of a dog dangerously out of control in a public place, causing injury. He remains in custody.

Police said a German Shepherd dog believed to have been involved in the incident has been seized by officers.

Det Ch Insp Michael Cox said: "Sadly, a man has died and it is really important that we understand the circumstances of what has taken place.

"We know that two people, one named Sophie, stopped to assist the injured man and direct officers."

He added: "We would urge these two people to come forward to help us with our ongoing inquiries into this tragic incident.

"The initial altercation happened in an area used by walkers and we are urging anyone who has seen or heard any part of the exchange between these two men to please make contact."

News.title: Calls for public inquiry into Jason Arday 'witch hunt'
News.content:
Green Party leader Zack Polanski, and Labour MPs Bell Ribiero-Addy, Clive Lewis and Nadia Whittome are among the politicians to have signed the statement, alongside former England footballer Eni Aluko, National Education Union general secretary Daniel Kebede, and broadcaster Carol Vorderman.

It calls for an "immediate public inquiry into how to ensure a responsible press".

Arday, 41, was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday. He had resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education on 5 August after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.

Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.

The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work. Cofnas's post had been terminated amid a backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

Lord Woolley told BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House programme on Sunday he and a number of close friends had met Arday four days before he was found dead at a south London address.

He said Abbott and social activist Misan Harriman were among those who gathered to offer support as they had also experienced "horrible media attention".

He said Arday felt "hounded" and the relentless media coverage had been "a bloodsport".

"Diane said to him, she held his hand, and said we will help you get through this," he added.

"But on that day, we saw a man half his body weight and desperate beyond belief."

Lord Woolley said issues of plagiarism were constant in academia and that a number of individuals, who had been accused of plagiarism had not been subjected to the attention Arday had received.

"We have to ask this question, we have to talk about - which a lot of people don't want to talk about, is racism. You have to look at negatively differential treatment."

On 6 August Cambridge announced an independent investigation into Arday's appointment.

It is understood the university does not feel it right to decide on whether to proceed with its investigation.

But one of the academic's friends, Sir Simon Baron-Cohen, told Times Radio on Sunday it should go ahead to "see what we learn from it" because "this is the whole purpose of investigations".

A University of Cambridge spokesperson told the BBC that during his time at the university, Arday had received a range of support in relation to his physical and mental well-being, including counselling and support and advice.

"Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation," they added.

Cambridge celebrated Arday's appointment as a young black professor, one of a tiny and visible minority in academia. Only one per cent of professors in UK universities are black, making each appointment hugely significant.

More than Â£90,000 has now been raised for Arday's family, after Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon, who is also among the signatories to the petition, launched a fundraiser.

A vigil organised by group Stand Up To Racism is set to take place on Monday evening in Trafalgar Square.

News.title: Changing pubs into homes to be made harder under new rules
News.content:
The Campaign for Real Ale has previously said that pubs are being "lost forever to conversion or demolition as developers look to cash in on the desirable locations and unique architecture of pubs and social clubs".

The British Beer and Pub Association and UKHospitality have also campaigned against pub closures, with both largely blaming tax rises and other costs.

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said: "The biggest issue facing hospitality businesses is costs like VAT and business rates pushing pubs out of business in the first place.

"Anything that makes it harder to take these important assets away from their communities has to be welcomed, but the government should focus on continuing its strong start on fixing the harm done to hospitality over the past two years."

In July, the Labour government said pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England will be given a 20% cut to business rates on top of rates relief announced in January.

The NPPF update being published Monday also includes default approval for homes being built around railway stations in England in an attempt to increase housebuilding numbers.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said: "By unlocking thousands of homes around well-connected transport hubs, we're helping people live closer to work, school and the services they rely on, while backing local businesses and driving growth in our communities."

The update also means that some groups will no longer need to be consulted on housing development plans as part of the process of getting permission.

The Gardens Trust, a parks and gardens heritage and conversion charity, called the decision to remove its role as a statutory consultee "devastating".

It said it devalued parks and gardens and "makes them vulnerable to poorly informed development".

Under the changes, the Gardens Trust and Theatres Trust will still be notified of relevant applications and Sport England will continue to advise on significant cases.

Labour has set a target to build 1.5 million homes by 2029. According to official data, external, it has so far built 392,000 homes in England since coming into power in July 2024.

Shadow housing secretary Sir James Cleverly said Labour is "failing abysmally" to meet their target because of taxes and red tape.

"To try to fix their own mess, Labour are planning a power grab, seizing control from local communities and forcing them to accept development in the wrong areas because Labour won't build in the right areas," he added.

News.title: Watch moment police arrest wanted man while he slept on roof
News.content:
A stand-off involving a wanted man was brought to an end when police arrested him while he slept on a roof.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said emergency services had responded to an incident at a property on Reservoir Street in Salford, spending two days at the scene.

Footage shows officers from the force's tactical unit gently resting a ladder against the roof of a back porch, with an officer then grabbing the man while he was sleeping.

A struggle ensues and the man is pulled down, with his trousers appearing to fall down, before he is arrested by officers in the garden of the property.

Two police officers suffered minor injuries during the incident on Saturday.

GMP said it was asked by another force to arrest the man who was wanted on recall to prison for other matters.

The force said a 37-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of causing public nuisance, criminal damage, public order offences, burglary and assaulting two police officers.

He remains in police custody.

Det Ch Insp Helen Bagnall said: "During two days of disruption to the local community, we worked continuously with our partners to bring this matter to a safe conclusion.

"This was an extensive use of vital policing resources and clearly demonstrates the dangers our officers face on a daily basis in order to protect the people of Greater Manchester."

She thanked the people of Salford for their "patience and understanding" while emergency services dealt with the incident, adding some properties had been damaged as a result of the man's actions.

She said the force would work with partners to ensure affected residents would be supported.

News.title: People who fled Stourbridge fires start to return home
News.content:
People who had to flee their houses during the devastating Stourbridge fires are starting to return home, as a firefighter said it was "a miracle no one has died".

Many families are only just discovering the extent of damage to their homes as West Midlands Fire Service allowed some behind the cordon after three days.

Nineteen properties across five streets have been fully destroyed. Eight households have been able to view the shells of their former homes.

Aerial images of the scene appear to show some houses have remained entirely intact while those next to them have been burnt to the ground.

Residents of Brunswick Gate, Landsgate, Ounty John Lane, Quarry Park Road and Racecourse Lane were asked to gather to speak to fire chiefs one by one.

They then learned if it was safe to return or if their home needed significant repairs or had been lost entirely.

Earlier, Dudley Council's chief executive Balvinder Heran said 96 evacuated houses had escaped damage with 85 families able to return.

Thirteen households whose properties were damaged by fire have also been able to go back home.

News.title: Four 'extraordinary' Renaissance paintings stolen from Italian museum
News.content:
Four Renaissance paintings of "extraordinary value" have been stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy's culture minister has said.

Alessandro Giuli confirmed that three panels of the Polyptych of San Gregorio and a double-sided panel of the Madonna with Child and Christ in PietÃ , all attributed to Antonello da Messina, were taken from the Regional Interdisciplinary Museum of Messina on Saturday night.

Police are now probing how the thieves were able to enter the museum without triggering its alarms and who may have been responsible.

The incident is the latest in a string of museum heists across Europe that have led to a growing number of priceless works disappearing from public view.

Investigators are working on the initial suspicion that the paintings were stolen to order by black market art thieves, according to Italian news agency Ansa.

It reported that the Madonna and Christ in PietÃ was removed directly from inside a secure display case, while all the paintings taken were on wooden panels, preventing them from easily being rolled up.

The museum's director Marisa Mercurio said the theft was thought to have occurred around 21:50 local time (19:50 GMT) on Saturday.

"We are shocked by what happened," she told Ansa, describing it as "a great loss for the museum, for the city, the community and the art world".

Antonello da Messina was a 15th Century painter born and raised on Sicily, who would go on to become one of the early Renaissance period's master painters.

His San Gregorio Polyptych, painted in 1473, depicts the Virgin Mary holding an infant Jesus Christ, flanked by St Gregory and St Benedict as well as several angels.

The artwork, of which five panels survive, was commissioned for the monastery of Santa Maria.

News.title: UK-made drones strike targets inside Russia
News.content:
British-made drones are being used to strike targets in Russia for the first time.

The drones, built by two separate British companies, have been used in mainland Russia in widespread and successful targeting of military and industrial targets, including refineries and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries.

The strikes, first reported by the Sunday Times, external, are said to have caused more than Â£35bn in economic damage. A well-placed military source confirmed to the BBC the UK drones had been used.

British manufactured Storm Shadow missiles had earlier been used in the conflict, although this new phase is having a far more decisive impact.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has previously said drones using UK components and configurations have been used to attack Russian territory, including a fuel depot in the Kamensky District of the Rostov Region.

In April, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) announced it would supply Ukraine tens of thousands of drones, including long-range strike devices, in its biggest ever package.

The MoD said its support for Ukraine is "unwavering" and would stand by its ally "until it wins".

A spokesperson said: "We are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin's illegal invasion.

"This includes over 150,000 drones this year, cutting-edge Stone Cloak devices that hinder Russian air defences and innovative low-cost cruise missiles."

On Sunday, Moscow's mayor said about 600 Ukrainian drones were launched towards the city overnight, with roughly a third of the drones being destroyed, and three people were injured.

A warehouse belonging to Russian online retailer Wildberries was hit.

Wildberries, known as Russia's version of Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted since July.

Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.

News.title: Soldiers praised for 'phenomenal job' helping crews tackle wildfires
News.content:
In south Wales, about 14 separate fires were being tackled by crews on Sunday.

Mid and West Wales Fire Rescue and Service said crews were dealing with blazes at Rhandirmwyn and Ammanford in Carmarthenshire and Hay-on-Wye and Brecon in Powys on Sunday.

They have also attended fires in Gorseinon, Swansea, and Tenby, Pembrokeshire, as well as an incident involving smoke in Llanelli, Carmarthenshire.

Fire service manager, Geraint Thomas, described tree-height flames spreading in a pine forest in the Rhandirmwyn area of Carmarthenshire.

He said the perimeter of the fire expanded to 480 hectares with areas of broadleaved woodland, mountain moorland as well as pine forest burning within it.

"It's really challenging terrain in places," he said.

"The majority of the fire is quite deep-seated in the pine forest. We were limited in what we could see."

The Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service area manager said the flames are now under control thanks largely to much cooler conditions on Friday.

Chris Bryant, MP for Rhondda and Ogmore, said a fire in Treherbert, Rhondda Cynon Taf, had been "appalling" and he thanked crews from London who had provided assistance.

"Thankfully, there are fire engines from all over the UK and two helicopters have been in place all afternoon.

"I'm immensely impressed by the fire workers. But this can't be our new normal," he said, in a post on X, external on Saturday.

Monahan praised the Royal Logistics Corps and Royal Engineers in ensuring crews had water to tackle the fires.

"The Welsh water system is under pressure, so they're moving vast quantities of water from areas that we have it into areas where we're fighting the fire, so that we don't put too much pressure on the water system," he said.

"That's something people probably aren't aware of."

He also said the national emergency fire alert issued by the UK government to people's mobile phones in England and Wales on Friday was "absolutely necessary".

But he expressed disappointment that some people still did not appreciate the dangers.

"Even after that transmission, I stopped and found someone who was burning tyres underneath a tree.

"This is irresponsible behaviour," he said.

News.title: Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions
News.content:
Reform UK says it would aim to cut about Â£50bn from the benefits bill and replace the disability payments system, Pip, if it comes in to government.

Robert Jenrick, the party's treasury spokesperson, said the plans, to be set out in full on Monday, would be the most comprehensive overhaul to the welfare system in a generation and affect nearly three million people.

In an article for the Sunday Telegraph, external he said the current system is "suicidal empathy" and "a strange perversion of compassion".

Labour said it was "fantasy economics, built on stripping support from disabled people", while the Conservatives called it a "half-baked policy" and another "attempt to distract from" questions about the Â£5m gift party leader Nigel Farage received.

Reform's plans include making companies pay for any employees off sick for the first two years. Businesses with more than five employees would have to take out insurance to cover the cost.

Reform says this is modelled on the Dutch system and would incentivise employers to make adaptions and encourage people back to work to reduce their insurance premiums.

The party says they would cut the National Insurance contributions (NICs) paid by employers to offset the cost of this measure, insisting the change would be cost neutral for businesses.

In a policy document to be published next week, which the BBC has seen an extract of, the party estimates 2.89 million people would have their disability payments' removed, or modified, under plans to abolish Personal Independent Payments (Pip) for working age people.

The party would also remove the extra health-related payments on Universal Credit.

A new system, called a Health Security Allowance, would replace both Pip and the Universal Credit health element but only the most "severe, enduring and high-risk cases" would receive cash support, the document says.

Other claimants would be supported through a council-run programme to cover what Reform said would be the "verifiable additional costs" as a result of their disability.

To boost available support for people out of work, the party says it would spend an extra Â£1.85bn a year on interventions such as cognitive behavioural therapy, physiotherapy, and employment support.

Reform also wants to reform children's benefits, and is promising to align the system for anxiety, depression and ADHD in young people with its changes to the adult system. But this would only apply to new claimants.

News.title: 'Number of fatalities' and four injured after car drives on wrong side of motorway
News.content:
A number of people have died and four people have been taken to hospital following a two-vehicle crash in County Kildare.

The collision occurred on on the M9 Northbound at Junction 3 at about 03:00 local time on Sunday.

GardaÃ­ (Irish police) said a vehicle had been travelling on the wrong side of the carriageway when a head on collision occurred with a second car. They said there were a "number of fatalities".

The driver and front passenger, both female and aged in their 30s, of the second car have been removed from the scene to Tallaght University Hospital and both remain in critical condition.

A female rear seat passenger, aged in her 20s, was taken to St. Luke's General Hospital and is in a serious condition.

The third passenger, who is a child, has been removed to Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin and is in a serious condition.

The section of the M9 from Junction 3 to Junction 4 northbound and southbound remains closed with local diversions in place.

Irish broadcaster RTÃ have reported that gardaÃ­ said there was no pursuit taking place when the collision occurred.

GardaÃ­ said FiosrÃº (the Office of the Police Ombudsman) has been notified of the incident.

FiosrÃº's on-call team of investigators attended the scene and an independent investigation is ongoing.

The watchdog said a FiosrÃº investigation relates to incidents involving contact with gardaÃ­ where a member of the public has died or been seriously injured.

It said a referral does not necessarily mean a garda or gardaÃ­ have been accused of wrongdoing.

"Instead, it means that FiosrÃº should independently investigate the incident to ascertain whether or not the act or omission of a garda or gardaÃ­ may have resulted in the death of, or serious harm to, a person," it added.

News.title: Sinn Féin condemn burning of images of first minister on Derry bonfire
News.content:
Sinn FÃ©in has condemned the burning of images of First Minister Michelle O'Neill on a bonfire in Londonderry as "anti-democratic" and "sectarian".

On Saturday, a bonfire, from which almost 500 pallets were removed during the week, was set on fire beside a road in the Bogside area.

Photos of O'Neill, as well as union jacks, Israeli flags, Parachute Regiment, Somme Remembrance and Northern Ireland flags were attached to the bonfire.

Police are treating the burning of the effigies and materials as sectarian-motivated hate crimes.

In a post on social media, O'Neill said she would "not be deterred, distracted or intimidated".

"I will continue to call out sectarianism, anti-community activity and destruction wherever it comes from.

"These bonfires are a blight on our community," she said.

North Belfast MP John Finucane said these bonfires were "hate filled sectarianism" and "the very antithesis of Irish republicanism".

Youths placed pallets near the bottom of the Lecky Road flyover and set fire to it just before 23:00 BST.

Two other bonfires in the Creggan and Top of the Hill areas of the city also had flags and effigies placed on them before being set slight.

News.title: Man with dementia given days to leave Sweden
News.content:
Torossian said the situation had been "awful" and "traumatic" for the family.

"I'm just worried that if the police go in and try and take him, how is that going to affect my dad. We just want him to have some dignity," she said.

"We want him to be treated like someone - he's very vulnerable, and I just feel that this is really ruthless and harsh."

Torossian said doctors had advised the Swedish authorities the process of moving Mason to the UK would pose a "danger to his life".

When the UK left the European Union (EU) on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.

During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under a withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.

Torossian explained due to Mason's health conditions, a 'god man' - a legally appointed trustee - was given power of attorney to look after her dad's affairs.

Documents from the Swedish Migration Agency, seen by the BBC, state an application for permanent residency for Mason was made on 21 December 2021.

However, it was refused on the grounds documents showing he met the grounds for residency were not submitted.

News.title: Belgian Pocognoli confirmed as Scotland boss
News.content:
The Scottish FA say they have appointed "one of Europe's brightest emerging coaching talents" by securing Sebastien Pocognoli as Scotland men's new head coach on a two-year deal.

The 39-year-old Belgian, who replaces Steve Clarke, left Monaco at the end of last season and previously led Union Saint-Gilloise to a first league title in 90 years in 2024-25.

He becomes just the second foreign boss of the Scotland men's team, after German Berti Vogts.

"When I first heard of the interest, I was immediately excited about the opportunity," said former Belgium international Pocognoli.

"Scotland's supporters are famous for their passion - most recently at the World Cup in the USA - and I have experienced it myself as a player for Belgium when we played in 2013.

"Along with my coaching staff, I will do everything I can to give them a team to be proud of and build on the success that has been achieved already by my predecessor.

"Since negotiations began, I have been doing a lot of research, asking a lot of questions and looking at areas that we can build on."

News.title: Parents 'watering down baby milk' over high costs
News.content:
A baby bank says parents are turning to "unsafe" practices such as watering down baby formula milk to save money.

Megan Sinden, founder of Moorside Baby Bank in Consett, County Durham, said a couple of families spoke of putting less powder in to get another week's worth out of it, "which to me is quite dangerous".

She called for a cap on rising costs of formula, saying: "It's not a luxury item, it's a basic need for a baby."

Charity National Childbirth Trust (NCT) said its recent study found nearly half of parents (48%) were struggling more financially after having a baby, and added infant formula should always be prepared according to the manufacturer's instructions.

Infant formula is designed to provide the correct balance of nutrients for babies when mothers cannot or choose not to breastfeed, and adding extra water alters that balance.

The lower concentration can cause nutrient deficiency, coupled with the reduced ability of the baby's body to absorb the nutrients, NCT said.

"In turn, this can lead to poor weight gain, growth problems, and developmental delays," the spokesperson said.

"In serious cases, too much water in the formula may lead to more immediate health problems because a baby's body is not able to safely process the excess water."

The latest report, external by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) found the average retail price of some infant formula had increased by more than 25% in recent years.

Moorside Baby Bank opened in February 2025 and has so far helped 226 families with goods like clothes, nappies and baby wipes, which were mainly donated by the community.

Sinden, who is a community worker from nearby Stanley, said the bank struggled to get donations of baby milk "because it is so expensive" and instead relied on grants to buy the formula in.

Americans broadly believe that the economy is growing worse under Donald Trump’s stewardship and say that they are personally worse off after a year and a half of his second presidency.

The findings are part of a poll conducted by Focaldata for the Financial Times and gauged Americans’ mood about Republican control of Washington as the midterms rapidly approach.

Overall, Americans of all political stripes say that they are in a financially worse position than they were on January 19, 2025, when Joe Biden concluded his presidency and prepared to hand over the keys. 53 percent of all registered voters including nearly 25 percent of Republicans said they were in a worse position now, as the war with Iran and other issues continue to drive up consumer costs, including the price of fuel.

The poll also found a clear advantage for Democrats on a midterm generic ballot, with 51 percent of Americans saying they’d vote for a Democrat over a Republican in November’s midterm elections. 45 percent preferred the Republican.

It’s a plethora of warning signs for Donald Trump and his party as they seek to hold on to majorities in both chambers of Congress this fall. On the issue of jobs and the economy, more voters said they trusted Democrats over Republicans — possibly the worst sign in the poll for the GOP, which credited support on those issues for Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024.

open image in gallery Donald Trump's support is dropping among all voters, including Republicans ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

The president’s approval rating remains grim. 55 percent of Americans disapprove of the job he’s doing, and the poll once again shows his support among Republicans slowly beginning to crack. One in five now disapprove of his performance so far through his second term. His approval rating among Republicans dropped eight points between this latest poll, released Sunday, and FT’s previous survey in July.

Democrats need to pick up four seats in the Senate and the same number in the House to win double majorities in Congress next year. Doing so in either chamber would effectively put a stop to any partisan legislation for the next two years, effectively neutering the GOP’s agenda apart from what the president and his Cabinet secretaries can achieve at the executive level.

open image in gallery Democratic leaders Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries need just four seats in their respective chambers to win control of Congress in November ( Getty )

The retaking of both chambers even theoretically opens the door to the possibility of a third round of impeachment proceedings, but Democratic leaders have backed away from such inclinations in public statements and interviews as the midterms approach.

More likely is the prospect of Democrats seeking to expose the administration to political damage through congressional investigations if they retake the House or Senate. Democrats have already pledged to go investigate the Trump family’s financial dealings, which have included record-setting profits under his second presidency. Several committees are also eyeing the use of congressional subpoena power to investigate the firings and insitutional changes wrought by Elon Musk’s DOGE initiative before it was winded down last year.

open image in gallery Polling in July found that just one in three Americans support war with Iran ( AFP/Getty )

Republicans have endured the narrowest of margins in the House for more than a year, which has left the chamber constantly at war with itself and made passage of the “One Big, Beautiful Bill” last year an arduous task. The president, his team, and the GOP’s united refusal to negotiate with Democrats on its policy objectives has also forced the party to achieve the vast majority of its policy gains via the budget reconciliation package, which is limited to budget-related issues but allows for the 60-vote filibuster threshold to be avoided.

Trump has pushed Republicans to scrap the filibuster and hurriedly pass other legislation, to no avail.

This latest FT survey comes on the heels of a Reuters/Ipsos survey that found support for the U.S. war with Iran to be extremely low, with a wide majority of Americans believing that Trump had failed to lay out his goals or his strategy.

FT’s poll was conducted between August 7 to August 10 with a survey pool of 1,913 registered voters. The margin of error was 2.9 percentage points.

The four main cast members of Sam Mendes’ upcoming Beatles biopics have been spotted recreating one of the band’s most famous album covers.

The much-imitated image on the front of the 1969 record Abbey Road shows John Lennon, Ringo Starr, Paul McCartney and George Harrison using a pedestrian crossing outside the studio where the album was recorded.

It seems the moment will be included in one or more of Mendes’ four films, which will each focus on the lives of one of the band members.

Fan-shot footage apparently filmed from an apartment overlooking the crossing and shared on social media shows Harris Dickinson, Barry Keoghan, Paul Mescal and Joseph Quinn dressed identically to how the band appeared on the cover.

A member of the production crew can be heard counting to keep the four actors in time as they cross the road.

open image in gallery The iconic cover of The Beatles’ 1969 album ‘Abbey Road’ shows the four band members crossing the street outside the titular recording studio ( Apple Records )

The four films are set to be released simultaneously on April 7, 2028.

The surviving members of the Beatles, McCartney and Starr, have both given their approval to the new film series.

Paul Mescal revealed he had met McCartney as part of his preparations to play the musician, describing him as an "extraordinary man”, while drummer Starr has stopped by the set and spent time with Barry Keoghan.

The Saltburn actor revealed last year: “When I was talking to him, I couldn’t look at him. I was nervous, like right now. But he’s like, ‘You can look at me’. My job is to observe and kinda take in mannerisms and study him. I want to humanize him and bring feelings to it and not just sort of imitate.”

Babygirl actor Harris Dickinson will play John Lennon, with Stranger Things star Joseph Quinn as George Harrison. The films will also star Saoirse Ronan as Linda McCartney, Mia McKenna-Bruce (How to Have Sex) as Starr’s former wife Maureen Starkey Tigrett, Anna Sawai (Shogun) as Yoko Ono, and Sex Education’s Aimee Lou Wood as former model and photographer Pattie Boyd.

open image in gallery Paul Mescal, Barry Keoghan, Harris Dickinson and Joseph Quinn (clockwise from top left) in promotional images for the upcoming Beatles films ( Instagram/@lipaliverpool )

The real-life Boyd hit out at not being kept abreast of the production, telling a podcast: “I would have thought it would be polite to mention it to me or let me know that they got someone who’s going to be playing me.

“Don’t you think they’d let me know? Well, I haven’t been contacted by anyone. I could have really told them great stories. But I don’t think they want to know.”
