Sports.title: Arsenal thump Man City to send statement with Community Shield win
Sports.content:
Title-holders Arsenal delivered a statement performance in the Community Shield, thumping Man City 3-0 in Cardiff to send out a warning to all of their Premier League rivals.

The Gunners shocked City and their new boss Enzo Maresca with just 23 seconds on the clock when Myles Lewis-Skelly's sublime pass teed up Riccardo Calafiori to coolly convert the opener. The post-Pep Guardiola era couldn't have got off to a worse start for City.

Image: Arsenal's Riccardo Calafiori celebrates scoring their first goal

Arsenal's £34m summer signing Christos Tzolis then made the next two, heading across goal for Kai Havertz to force the second through Gianluigi Donnarumma before finding captain Martin Odegaard to tuck in a third just three minutes after half-time at the Principality Stadium.

Image: Kai Havertz doubled Arsenal's lead before half-time

Donnarumma was sat down by Odegaard for that goal and it summed up his poor performance behind a City defence which looked all over the place. They had needed Josko Gvardiol to clear Odegaard's effort off the line just before half-time when Donnarumma spilt the ball and the returning Bukayo Saka passed up two good chances to add more goals.

In contrast, Arsenal's backline, which had been questioned in pre-season after shipping eight goals in four matches, was robust. Their determination to shut City out was summed up when David Raya saved from Erling Haaland, Lewis-Skelly reached the rebound and then Ben White threw himself in front of a Jeremy Doku shot.

Tzolis off to a flyer Christos Tzolis is the first Arsenal player to assist two or more goals on his debut for the club since Willian in September 2020.

Haaland and £116m Elliot Anderson were withdrawn after underwhelming and the absence of Barcelona target Rodri was impossible to ignore. Yet, as Maresca searches for the right formula after City's decade of success under Guardiola, Mikel Arteta's Arsenal are primed to capitalise on their position of strength.

Transfer hints in team news Arsenal started Myles Lewis-Skelly, with the midfielder seemingly part of Mikel Arteta's plans after links away, but Gabriel Martinelli and Ethan Nwaneri weren't involved.



Man City left Savinho out of their squad, amid interest from Spurs in the winger, while Barcelona target Rodri was also absent after just returning from his World Cup break and a back treatment. Jack Grealish came on as a second half sub for his first City appearance since May 2025.

The last team to win the Community Shield and then win the Premier League title was Man City in 2018/19 when they landed a domestic treble. Subsequent success from winning this curtain-raiser is no guarantee but Sunday's victory looks like a launchpad for Arsenal as they go in search of back-to-back top-flight crowns for the first time in 91 years.

The key moments

1: GOAL! Arsenal score inside 30 seconds, with Myles Lewis-Skelly jabbing the ball through for Riccardo Calafiori to coolly finish.

20: SAVE! David Raya gets down to keep out Phil Foden's shot from the edge of the box.

28: GOAL! Martin Odegaard clips the ball to the back post where Christos Tzolis nods it across goal for Kai Havertz to head through Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Image: Arsenal's Kai Havertz (left) scores their second goal against Manchester City in the Community Shield

36: MISS! Jeremy Doku threads a pass for Erling Haaland but he skews his right-foot shot well off target.

38: YELLOW! Calafiori goes down in the box looking for a penalty from Abdukodir Khusanov's challenge but is booked for simulation.

40: SAVE! Raya parries Haaland's shot and Lewis-Skelly scrambles away the loose ball - but then Ben White has to block Doku's shot when Antoine Semenyo crosses.

43: CLOSE! White crosses for Calafiori to hit a volley but his effort goes wide.

Arsenal show their open-play threat On Sunday 100 per cent of Arsenal's xG against Manchester City came from open play (2.19).

45+1: OFF THE LINE! Josko Gvardiol scrambles the ball out of the City goalmouth after Martin Odegaard flicked the ball towards the net from a Donnarumma spill.

Half-Time: SUBS! Jack Grealish came on for his first Man City appearance since May 2025. Declan Rice also made his return to action for Arsenal.

48: GOAL! Martin Odegaard sits down Donnarumma and then prods in an Arsenal third from Tzolis' pass.

Arsenal land big win in curtain-raiser The past three Community Shields have been decided on penalties - Arsenal’s 3-0 win over Manchester City is the biggest margin of victory in a Community Shield game since 2014, when the Gunners beat the same opponent by the exact same scoreline.

63: CHANCE! Great play from Odegaard and then Declan Rice as they work the ball to Bukayo Saka but his shot is wide of the near post.

80: OVER! Saka skies another good chance from Piero Hincapie's low ball.

81: SAVE! Raya is sharp to push away Semenyo's drive.

Arteta impressed with Arsenal after Community Shield win

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta to TNT Sports:

"A really good performance so early in the season. To play at that level and to show the desire that we showed and their reaction. I was really impressed and I said to them that I really enjoyed watching them play.

"I'm a bit surprised because in pre-season, we had three different groups. Eight or nine arrived just five days ago to get tested, they trained two days and to play in that manner is extremely impressive. It tells you how much those players want it, the level of desire we have an the quality we have."

Odegaard: We wanted everyone to see our level

Arsenal captain Martin Odegaard to TNT Sports:

"We wanted to start here with the first trophy. We played some brilliant football so it was a great performance, a great way to start the season so let's keep it going. It was good for everyone to see our level. We showed that we're ready, we're serious, we want to do it again and there's more trophies to go. We're well prepared and ready to go."

Maresca: This is just the beginning

Man City boss Enzo Maresca:

"A big part of the game is in the first goal we concede. After the reaction is good. Before they score the second goal we had three or four chances to score. Then with the second goal it became more difficult.

"In general I'm always concerned - even when we win games! We just started. This is the beginning. We have many things to do better. Now we try to reset, analyse the game and think from Tuesday about the next game.

"The first goal we concede I didn't like. Then the second one there was no pressure on the ball. I don't know if it's for physical condition. We had many players - probably the club with more players at the World Cup."

Your views on Arsenal's big win

Jack: "It's only the Community Shield but great to see the dominance in the performance from Arsenal and great to see them get at City. Thought Odegaard and Tzolis looked great and Mosquera was a rock. Hopefully a title-retaining season to come!"

Maz: "If I was a City fan I'd be worried. Really worried. Was dreadful. Like the first game of preseason after two months off."

Scoth: "The Pep factor is gone, and so is the fear factor."

Owen: "Well, congrats to Arsenal from a City fan but I'm not worried in the slightest. Players getting used to a new manager that havent played a game with him yet. However, I will be worried if we put in that same performance against Bornemouth."

Danie: "Was not expecting that! I know it's only the Community Shield but Maresca said they'll be looking to win it and we destroyed them. Is Odegaard finally back? He was class today. That wasn't even our strongest team either had few missing, feeling rather confident for the coming season."

Bud: "Could Tzolis be the signing of the season?"

What's next?

Sports.title: Rayif roars back to his best to land Prix Jacques le Marois
Sports.content:
French 2000 Guineas hero Rayif bounced back to form to repel a strong raiding party in the Aga Khan Studs Prix Jacques le Marois at Deauville.

Francis-Henri Graffard's colt struck Classic gold on what was his seasonal debut in the Poule d'Essai des Poulains in early May, but his summer campaign has been interrupted, with a planned visit to Royal Ascot scuppered by a minor setback after which he ran a little below par when fifth in the Prix Jean Prat.

He had plenty on his plate stepping back up to a mile, with Aidan O'Brien's Irish 1,000 Guineas and Coronation Stakes winner Precise the hot favourite after bumping into top-class older filly Blue Bolt on her last couple of starts.

Fozzy Stack's Prix Jean Prat victor Thesecretadversary took the field along for much of the way, closely pursued by Karl Burke's Zeus Olympios, who looked the likely winner after quickening to the lead inside the final furlong.

But Mickael Barzalona delivered Rayif with a withering late run and he got up to deny Zeus Olympios an elusive first Group One success, with Precise close up behind in third.

"I'm very happy, it's a wonderful race to win, a very hard race to win," said Graffard.

"I kept my confidence in the horse. He ran pretty well the other day with excuses and he was in top form (today). Over that course you need the perfect trip and we had the perfect trip today.

"He travelled really well and picked up really nicely, he's very tough and game.

"He won the Poule d'Essai on very soft ground so everyone was saying he's a soft ground horse, but you need to keep trying and if these horses are to find their place at stud they need to be performing at this level.

"The Jacques le Marois is a very famous race - probably the second most famous race in France after the Arc - so it's a wonderful race to win. It means so much."

Rayif has a range of options for the second half of the season, including the Queen Elizabeth II Stakes at Ascot on Champions Day, for which he was cut to 4-1 second-favourite from 14-1 by Coral.

Graffard added: "It depends if we decide to go for the Prix du Moulin (September 6) or give him more time and the Prix de la Foret (October 4) could be an option - I wouldn't be afraid to drop him back in distance.

"There is the QEII at the back-end and we know he can handle soft ground."

Of the gallant runner-up, Burke said: "We always thought and hoped he would produce that sort of performance in a Group One. I think physically he's improving and he showed that today.

"He quickened twice there - first time I thought we'd got it, then he got challenged and then he quickened again and I thought we'd got it and so did Cliff (Lee, jockey).

"The winner, fair play to him, has come and cut us down. Francis can do no wrong, can he?

"We'll get him home and see how he is. It's got to be discussed, but as a trainer I'm very hopeful he'll stay in training next year and I think he'll just continue improving physically and strengthening, so hopefully if he doesn't win his Group One this year he'll certainly get it next year.

"I'd say the race at Longchamp (Moulin) will probably come a bit quick for him, maybe we'll wait for the QEII at Ascot."

Sports.title: Winther pips fellow Dane Højgaard in thrilling finish
Sports.content:
Jeff Winther ended a four-year wait to claim his second DP World Tour title on Sunday at the Danish Golf Championship, pipping compatriot Rasmus Højgaard in a thrilling finish.

Højgaard had been two shots behind the leader heading into the 17th hole, but sensationally chipped in for eagle from over a bunker to tie Winther at Great Northern Golf Club.

His stay at the top of the leaderboard was short-lived, with Winther immediately responding on the 16th with an eagle of his own, putting out after landing his drive on the green of the 304-yard par four.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rasmus Højgaard chipped in for an eagle before Winther putted out for an eagle of his own in the final four holes

The 38-year-old made par on the 17th and 18th to end his final round with a five-under-par 67, and took a two-shot clubhouse lead over China's Yanhan Zhou.

Zhou needed a hole-in-one on the par-three 18th hole to force a play-off with the Dane, but when he three-putted to make a bogey on the last, Winther's three-shot victory at his home event was officially confirmed.

Zhou would finish his week tied for second at 12 under par alongside a group of five other players that included Højgaard, England's Matthew Jordan, Finland's Oliver Lindell and Italian Filippo Celli.

Winther, who had worked as a greenskeeper 15 years ago, had never thought he would become a professional golfer, let alone become only the second winner of the Danish Golf Championship.

"[It's] impossible to rank this," the 38-year-old said after his round. "Just after my kids' birth. It was amazing.

"I don't think it's sunk in yet. I'm overly happy; we've been clapped off on every single green. Even when we hit poor shots. Still getting clapped off! The crowds carried me all week. It's been unbelievable."

Image: Winther came into his final round four shots off the lead

"I was never going to be a golfer. This is just insane, I'm in shock," he added.

Winther, whose last DP World Tour victory came at the 2021 Mallorca Golf Open, began his final round four shots behind overnight leader Romain Langasque, who endured a nightmare Sunday, posting five bogeys in his opening six holes to shoot a three-over-par 75 and end his week tied for seventh.

The Dane endured a mixed start, making two birdies on the fourth and fifth holes before bogeying the sixth and eighth.

A brilliant approach to the island green on the ninth set him up for another birdie before the turn, and Winther made more gains on the 10th and 13th.

But it was only after sinking his dramatic 31ft eagle putt on the 16th that he began to believe he had a chance of outlasting Zhou and Højgaard, who had just tied him at the top of the leaderboard.

"Rasmus chips in and I'm like: 'He just wants some attention, doesn't he?'" Winther said. "Then I sunk my own eagle putt, and I was over the moon. When that putt went in, that was the first time today I thought I had a chance."

Højgaard: It's not a great feeling coming up short

Image: Højgaard surged late on but ended his round on a sour note with a bogey on the 18th

Højgaard began his final round five strokes off the lead, but it was a tricky day for the European Ryder Cup star, who would combine two bogeys and two birdies to make the turn at level par.

After a birdie on the 11th and another bogey on the 12th, Højgaard would surge late, making back-to-back birdies on 15 and 16 before his eagle on the 17th.

His round would end on a sour note, with the Dane bogeying the last hole to shoot a three-under 69 and finish tied for second.

"I didn't expect to be in the position I was in coming down the last hole," Højgaard said. "To be honest, I struggled with my game all day. I made a few birdies and holed out, and then you're in the mix again.

"But I finished with a bogey, and that put more pressure on.

"I'd say when I made birdie on the 16th, I felt I could put up a good chance on 17, and then I'd be 12 under and potentially 13 under would have a chance.

"It was great to put myself in positions where I had a chance. But it's not a great feeling right now."

Sports.title: Calafiori’s fast start inspires Arsenal to big Community Shield win over Manchester City
Sports.content:
For Enzo Maresca, a miserable first meaningful game in charge of Manchester City that began with Arsenal seizing the lead after 24 seconds ended with Mikel Arteta’s side ­lifting the Community Shield. Arsenal eviscerated City, Riccardo Calafiori’s smart early opener after Myles Lewis-­Skelly’s brilliant pass ­seemingly leaving their opponents with irrecoverable damage. Kai Havertz doubled Arsenal’s lead on 28 ­minutes and Martin Ødegaard in effect sealed the win three minutes into the ­second half, taking great ­pleasure in ­fooling ­Gianluigi ­Donnarumma in the City goal before finishing. On this evidence, the post-Pep ­Guardiola era could be trickier than widely envisaged.

Christos Tzolis shone on the left, playing the whole game in Cardiff. He was involved in all three goals, assisting two. No Arsenal player played more passes into the final third. It was Tzolis’s cross to switch play to Noni Madueke, one of 10 passes before Calafiori rippled the City net. Between Lewis-Skelly rolling the ball to Martin Ødegaard at kick-off and Calafiori peeling off Abdukodir Khusanov to finish, City had a single touch of the ball; Elliot Anderson intercepted Calafiori’s pass aimed at Ødegaard in the City 18-yard box. But then Madueke cushioned a header for Ben White, who tucked into midfield, and Lewis-Skelly rolled Phil Foden before releasing Calafiori goal-side of Rúben Dias with a sumptuous reverse ball.

Just like that, Arsenal were away. Calafiori was mobbed by his teammates but wagged his finger in the direction of Lewis-Skelly, high­lighting the teenager’s part in the goal. Lewis-Skelly has been offered to clubs this summer but played a central role before being replaced by Martín Zubimendi.

Bruno ­Guimarães, wearing the No 39 shirt, a nod to his father’s taxi number in Rio de Janeiro while growing up, but this time in Arsenal red, was busy on his debut before being replaced by Declan Rice in a planned half-time departure. Tzolis, though, was the undoubted pick of the new faces on show. Anderson was unusually overwhelmed on his first appearance since the World Cup.

Arsenal were game but City seemed to treat the contest as an inconvenience. Maresca felt the ­reaction to Calafiori’s goal was encouraging and they did carve out a couple of chances. David Raya got a strong right palm to an Erling Haaland shot from distance and then White made a magnificent block to prevent Haaland a simple finish after Antoine Semenyo’s cross took a kind deflection. Gabriel Magalhães celebrated wildly after a clean tackle on Jérémy Doku. As Arsenal cavorted around the pitch presenting their latest ­trophy to their supporters, squiggles of confetti in the sky, Haaland trudged down the tunnel, hands clasped behind his back.

Calafiori’s early strike provided the perfect tonic for Arsenal to continue the party atmosphere that electrified their Premier League title parade across north London at the end of May. The importance of this victory will be debated, but by winning this competition, back at the ­Principality Stadium for the first time since 2006 owing to The Weeknd’s gig at ­Wembley, they put down an impressive marker as they look to build on last season’s success. City, without Rodri amid doubts over his future, with Barcelona pushing to sign the midfielder, lacked any ­semblance of control.

View image in fullscreen Martin Ødegaard (left) celebrates with Kai Havertz after scoring Arsenal’s third goal early in the second half. Photograph: Godfrey Pitt/Action Plus/Shutterstock

City had been lightly raced in comparison to their opponents – they played the first of their three pre-season matches this month in Hong Kong, while this represented ­Arsenal’s sixth outing since the World Cup – and how it showed. Arsenal were crisp in possession, clever in the way they pulled an ominously open City apart. Maresca’s side were exposed across the pitch but Donnarumma was ­particularly unconvincing in goal, at fault for Arsenal’s second, making a hash of his attempt to keep out Havertz’s header, and embarrassed for the third. ­Ødegaard delighted in feinting to shoot, sending Donna­rumma seesawing to his left, and then promptly firing in a simple finish. “Can we play you every week?” came the chant from the Arsenal support.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

For Arsenal, who begin their ­Premier League title defence at home to Coventry in Friday’s ­curtain-raiser, this impressive display will only heighten hopes of another ­blockbuster season. They seem well-equipped to fight on several fronts, though remain in the market for a centre-back, with Jarell Quansah and Ezri Konsa of interest. For City, who host Bournemouth next Sunday, there was little to whet the appetite. Semenyo was muted. Haaland’s only real sight of goal, towards the end of the first half, ended with the Norway striker sending a wayward shot wide of Raya’s net after the ball bobbled.

It was not supposed to be this easy for Arsenal. The previous three Community Shield matches had gone the distance, penalties ­deciding the ­winners. That was never on the agenda this time. Instead, ­Arsenal cruised to the biggest win in the ­competition since they beat City in 2014, when Arteta captained the side from midfield. “We want to build on what we achieved and continue to have the ambition to win major trophies,” Arteta said before the game. “That starts today.”

Sports.title: Flemming’s dramatic Burnley double pegs back West Ham on Championship return
Sports.content:
More games, less money but plenty of entertainment will make it a compelling Championship season for Burnley and West Ham. Zian Flemming’s two late goals secured a much-deserved point for the hosts as the Hammers cracked under pressure in this Premier League tribute act.

Maximilian Kilman and Manor Solomon pounced in the box to seemingly set West Ham on their way to victory but Flemming ensured the points were shared, scoring first from the spot and then from a corner. Burnley had missed numerous chances but found his golden touch at the right time.

Burnley started the game with plenty of question marks above their heads after the belated appointment of Nicky Hayen as head coach and a relatively quiet summer in the transfer market. The Belgian, whose previous experience of coaching in the UK came in the Cymru Premier at Haverfordwest, was celebrating his 46th birthday on Sunday and sent his team out intent on marking the occasion. Released from the desperately defensive football of the Scott Parker era, Burnley were aggressive and progressive in equal measure but were undone by a failure to carry out the basics.

Like Burnley, relegation had forced the sale of key players, but keeping Nuno Espírito Santo and Jarrod Bowen felt like significant moments. Having Kilman stay on was less exciting for Hammers fans, with the centre-back highly criticised since his £40m transfer from Wolves two years ago and unable to get in the team for much of last season. Thankfully for him, through a mix of Aaron Ramsey’s inept attempt at marking and Bowen’s delivery, he nodded West Ham into an early lead.

West Ham enjoyed more of the ball, as they can expect throughout the campaign, but Burnley were the more threatening. They countered at speed and in numbers but lacked a cutting edge as final balls and clinical finishing were absent, as the two teams mustered a solitary shot on target from seven attempts before the break. At the very least, the Clarets suggested they would be watchable after two seasons of Parker-ball.

View image in fullscreen Maximilian Kilman gives West Ham the lead as he heads home Jarrod Bowen’s cross. Photograph: COLORSPORT/Alan Martin/Shutterstock

While Burnley were frenetic, West Ham were more composed, looking to pick their moments. Nuno decided to end another anonymous Pablo Felipe display as he tries to find his level in England, sending on James Ward-Prowse, who spent a forgettable six months on loan at Turf Moor in the second half of last season. The plan was to add an extra body into midfield to stop the Burnley counterattacks but the hosts continued to look dangerous as Flemming went close with three headers, the last hitting the inside of the post.

There was little ambition to seek a second for West Ham as they sought to protect the lead rather than add to it, failing to have a shot in the first 25 minutes of the second half. Whether it was the most sensible strategy was debatable as they only maintained their advantage through a mix of good luck and poor decision-making from Burnley. Ollie Scarles was in the perfect position on the line to head clear another Flemming effort as the Burnley pressure and frustration grew with equal measure.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

After few glimpses of quality, West Ham showed some class through Mohamadou Kanté, who made light work of Marcus Edwards on the wing before finding Solomon to smash home from close range, undoing all of Burnley’s good work in one strike of the ball.

Scarles opened up the chance for Burnley to get back into the game, scything down Edwards crudely in the area. Flemming, finally, made no mistake, setting up a tense finish that concluded with an eruption when he netted the equaliser.

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo says this year is ‘probably’ his last as a footballer
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo believes this year is “probably” his last as a professional footballer, the 41-year-old Portugal captain said in an interview with Vogue magazine published on Sunday.

Ronaldo, who has established his place among football’s all-time greats with more than 950 goals for club and country, had previously spoken of retiring “soon” or within “one or two years”.

“This is probably my last year of football, and I want to leave a spectacular legacy,” the Al-Nassr forward told Vogue, saying his future after football was “all mapped out”.

“I have so many things to keep me busy that to tell you just one thing is hard,” he said, listing travel and padel among his favourite activities. “Because football could leave a big hole, you have to fill your time in various ways, not just one.”

Ronaldo married his partner, Georgina Rodríguez, in an intimate ceremony in the Portuguese resort of Cascais on Tuesday. The former Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus player told Vogue he wanted to “continue to enjoy what I’ve earned – what we’ve earned. Because after all it’s been 25 years with a lot of sacrifice.”

After being part of the Portugal side which reached the last 16 of the World Cup this summer, Ronaldo is due to link up with Al-Nassr for the new Saudi Pro League season.

Sports.title: Nabizada stunner edges Watford past Southampton as ‘Spygate’ still looms large
Sports.content:
Southampton will have to get used to being barracked as they travel the Championship this autumn, the “Spygate” team set to be everyone’s favourite boo boys in the second tier. Certainly that was the case in Hertfordshire, with Watford fans and players alike beside themselves after a hard-fought victory, decided by two memorable first-half goals.

Tonda Eckert, the Southampton head coach, remains under investigation for his part in the Spygate affair and presented a subdued figure both during and after this contest. He insisted that his team were more united than ever after suffering the indignity of being removed from last season’s playoffs, “but it would be easier to say that after a victory”, Eckert acknowledged.

Watford paid tribute to Kenny Jackett before the match, the one-club legend and local boy hailed with two minutes of applause. This celebration of longevity and connection, with a Panini-inspired tifo tumbling down the stands, cut a contrast with the current operation, where Alessio Dionisi has become Watford’s 12th full-time manager in just the past five years.

“I am very tired and my team was too by the end,” said the Italian who was coaching Empoli in Serie B last season. Dionisi praised the attitude of his team – “I liked the mentality of my players, in every moment I saw one team working together,” he said. He also benefited from the Pozzo family’s multi-club network and the local academy in digging out a victory.

The Spain under-21 attacker Iker Bravo was one of several signings to make the familiar trek from “sister” club Udinese this summer, and he made his mark quickly, opening the scoring with a quite stunning solo goal in the 12th minute. It was all his own work and Bravo had to deploy a combination of skills to turn an innocuous situation into real danger. Looking to latch on to a long ball some 40 yards from goal, the 6ftplaymaker won the first header then, crucially, got a second touch with an outstretched toe to get the ball under control. Bravo then span immediately and drove at goal, pushing his way into the box before chopping right and getting off a low shot that Daniel Peretz got a hand to, butcould not keep out.

View image in fullscreen Watford’s Amin Nabizada jumps for joy after scoring their second goal against Southampton. Photograph: Peter Tarry/PA

A great way to start any season, the energy among the Vicarage Road crowd grew immediately and the home side went on to dominate the first half. They doubled their lead in the 29th minute with a moment to remember for 19-year-old academy graduate Amin Nabizada who exploited the same gaps on the left of the Southampton defence to run with the ball from his own half before finishing precisely from a tight angle. “Nabizada was emotional but after the first 10 minutes he played well,” Dionisi said. “When there is one mentality amongst the team, then it’s better for him too.”

Southampton had the better of the second half, taking advantage of a drop in tempo from the hosts to assert their interests. A spell of concerted possession in the 56th minute ended with Kuryu Matsuki pulling out wide, the young midfielder Cam Bragg moving unmarked into the half space and his shift left finding the Canada World Cup star Cyle Larin to poke home from 10 yards out.

Larin had a chance to equalise just two minutes later with a shot on the turn but Federico Ravaglia – another new signing to impress for the Hornets – turned the ball round the post. When Finn Azaz came on as a second-half substitute for the Saints he bought an inch to fire off a low drive that went just beyond the left hand post. As a succession of dangerous set pieces were sent over by Ryan Manning, Southampton fans were singing “we’ll score when we want”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But as the game passed through a flurry of substitutions Eckert’s team were unable to generate enough momentum to truly unsettle Dionisi’s men. Their only further chance came in added time and was scuffed wide by Taylor Harwood-Bellis.

Eckert said he had been happy enough with his team’s performance beyond “two errors in possession”. He insisted his squad are “very close and united” as a group. “We had a different expectation for the result but the group looks united and we now need to turn that into results.”

Opening matches rarely offer much insight into how a season will pan out. But Watford fans were able to enjoy both temperate weather and a decent performance. If Southampton want to transform the negative energy of Spygate into something positive, meanwhile, they will have to start again next week.

Sports.title: Premier League fans’ previews: our club-by-club guide to 2026-27
Sports.content:
Arsenal

Having finally got the title monkey off our back, and with much of the competition in a state of flux, there’s plenty of optimism. Obviously the target is for Arteta to sustain the same appetite and intensity to mount a credible defence. The big questions are whether we can reproduce the same resilience at the back with Saliba on the long-term missing list, and will the introduction of Guimarães be the catalyst for the sort of midfield chemistry we’ll need to carve open opponents who plan to park the bus?

Key players/weak links On the evidence of our pre-season outings we urgently need the return of our remaining World Cup stars – Rice, Zubimendi and Saka should provide a renewed sense of purpose, both to counter any defensive fragility and to increase our goal threat. We’re all hoping for a breakthrough season for a beefed-up Max Dowman, and are anxious to discover if Tzolis is an upgrade on Trossard.

We still need to sign … Our friendly outings have shown the need for alternative attacking options, such as Atlético’s Julián Alvarez, and cover for Saliba – Quansah and Konsa are linked. But presumably any further arrivals will be dependent on some astute pruning of those who’ve failed to cut the mustard, such as Vieira and Nelson.

Our cult hero is … Benny Blanco’s off-the-ball shenanigans ensure that he’s enshrined as a firm terrace favourite, but it’s the demeanour of Declan Rice that will invariably set the tone for whether or not we’re destined for more success.

If we could sign two players from our past … Who wouldn’t want to add the artistry of Thierry Henry and Dennis Bergkamp to any team?

Aston Villa

It would be daft to not be optimistic when each year under Emery we’ve created great memories, regardless of the previous summer’s transfer merry-go-round. Top six and a cup run of any flavour would count as a good season, and it may be that our best moments are back-end weighted as we integrate some exciting new talent. I understand that Manzambi is the best thing to come out of Switzerland since the cuckoo clock, and any 22-year-old with 187 senior appearances (Garnacho) must be all right. Perversely, the financial regulations that are holding us back should prevent too much moaning if we don’t get off to a flyer, and having a ground with only three sides might even help us make VP a fortress. In all, I’m fired up for the new season.

Key players/weak links The senior pros all need to keep drinking the Emery Kool Aid, but why wouldn’t they? Konsa remains a colossus and the purple prose around McGinn is fully deserved. If Kamara plays 40 senior games and not his usual 25 it will improve our finishing spot by two. Normally naming a young player to watch in these pages guarantees them a loan move to Lincoln, but Brian Madjo has looked immense up front in pre-season.

We still need to sign … Marcus Rashford.

Our cult hero is … McGinn must already have done enough to have a hospitality suite named after him. Another two years and it could be a stand. He will be aware that Emery doesn’t deal in sentimentality so I expect yet another year in which SJM pushes for player of the season while being a key figure in the dressing room.

If we could sign two players from our past … Dwight Yorke, from 1995-96 when he switched to an out-and-out striker. And Gareth Barry: the complete midfielder.

We will finish 6th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Manchester United; 4. Chelsea. Bottom three: 18. Fulham; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Roberto De Zerbi.

Bournemouth

We’re so looking forward to this: our first ever season in a European club competition. It’s going to be monumental. Key players/weak links António Silva has big Senesi-sized shoes to fill at centre-half but we expect big things from him. I’m very optimistic. Twelve months ago we had Yoane Wissa refusing to train to force a move and the footballing world was convinced that our free-kick coach turned manager would get us relegated. Key players/weak links There’s a lot of excitement around new signing Mamadou Sangaré – so much so that he’s already got his own song. Callum Wilson is a shrewd signing too, and, at this stage of his career, seems happy to sit on the bench and knock a few in when called upon. Our explosive front three of Ouattara, Thiago and Schade have now had time to gel, and should cause plenty of problems. As for youngsters, 11 players aged 21 or under are vying for a place in the final 25-man squad. 19-year-old striker – and rapper – Kaye Furo is highly rated, as is 20-year-old centre-back Jannik Schuster. It’s a good sign that we’re getting to the point where our youngsters aren’t just making up the numbers.

We still need to sign … If there’s one position we could strengthen, left-back would be a good option. El Hadji Malick Diouf from West Ham has been rumoured.

Our cult hero is … Michael Kayode. Cemented his status by singing his own terrace chant on camera: “He eats spaghetti, he drinks Moretti, he hates Queens Park Rangers.”

If we could sign two players from our past … We’re probably a bit too “nice”. Whenever we need a short injection of old-school fire, fight and chaos, Terry Evans from our 1992 Division One-winning side and Terry Hurlock from that incredible 80s “Kamara, Bowles, Hurlock” midfield would be great to call upon.

Brighton

Having seen West Ham, Chelsea and even Crystal Palace go all the way in the Conference League, the main target is doing well in that and winning a first cup final since the 1910 Charity Shield. Am I optimistic about it happening? Not really. The competition looks tougher this year. Freiburg, Atalanta and Monaco all have proper European experience. Even the playoff round against Tromsø is a banana skin. I’m old enough to remember some pretty horrible trips to Carlisle when Brighton could never win north of Lake Windermere. Let alone inside the actual Arctic Circle.

Key players/weak links The key player will be whoever Fabian Hürzeler uses to fill the void left by selling Danny Welbeck: Georginio Rutter, Charalampos Kostoulas or Stefanos Tzimas. Not only did Welbeck score 13 goals last season, but most were vital equalisers or important winners worth 13 points. Allowing him to join Chelsea is a huge risk. If none of those younger alternatives who the club want playing more this season step up and replace Welbeck, there’s the weak link. And there are big question marks over all three.

We still need to sign … Danny Welbeck from Chelsea would be a good signing for his goals record and the experience he would bring to a young squad.

Our cult hero is … Rutter. Nothing says cult hero quite like having one Instagram account about your football career and another about the racehorses you own. With the racing one being more interesting.

If we could sign two players from our past … I’ll spare you another Welbeck answer and say Glenn Murray and Bobby Zamora instead. Hopefully, I’ll be able to revisit this on 3 June 2027 after we’ve just won the Conference League and Kostoulas has hit 46 goals in all competitions. Danny who?

We will finish 13th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester United; 3. Manchester City; 4. Chelsea; Bottom three: 18. Sunderland; 19. Ipswich; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Oliver Glasner.

Chelsea

A new top manager, some decent new signings and a feelgood factor within the squad – it’s hard not to be optimistic. We’ve finally brought some experienced players who should complement our younger players and take them to the next level. With no Champions League football, the target has to be top four and a good run in the domestic cups.

If we could sign two players from our past … John Terry to marshal the defence and Frank Lampard to bang the goals in. Both players gave 100% every time they stepped on the pitch and were also fantastic motivators. Two absolute legends who would grace any team in any era.

Coventry

There’s no downside to choosing optimism, so yes, we’re optimistic. I don’t expect a top-half finish but I do enjoy how the club’s being run and believe in our ability to compete. Clearly the target is to survive, but within that, if we can showcase what’s good about us and provide a challenge, that would be a very acceptable return.

Key players/weak links The money we’ve spent is basically unfathomable, but my focus has been on those who were so critical to our promotion. Matt Grimes connects everyone in the team so we’re relying on him doing that again, else we’ll have to develop a completely new way to function. Signing keeper Carl Rushworth also gives assurance at the back that we hope will translate into points. There are questions about our strikers (which feels barmy for a team that scored 99 goals last season). It’s not complicated – we simply don’t know if Wright and Simms have what it takes to score at the highest level. Aside from signing Aurèle Amenda, we haven’t touched our defence either. It’s a bold strategy. Liam Kitching and Jay Dasilva have improved significantly, but it’s hard to ignore the notion that we’re relying on players like this finding another uptick. However, new signing Caleb Yirenkyi looks very special.

We still need to sign … We saw how vital Brian Brobbey was for Sunderland last season. A dynamic, high-status striker would go a long way towards calming the nerves about our forward line. Is Taiwo Awoniyi able to be that guy? Let’s hope so. The rumours about Fikayo Tomori are exciting. If we could bring him in, good lord.

Our cult hero is … While the returning Gus Hamer is clearly our cult hero, Milan van Ewijk is the joker of the team. You’ll find him front and centre of every celebration. But don’t let the daftness fool you; he’s a serious, serious player.

If we could sign two players from our past … The original version of James Maddison was unlike anything I’ve ever seen. His game has adapted with age, which is a shame, but I’d love some of that early ingenuity. I’d also welcome back Viktor Gyökeres. He functions far better when he believes he’s the star man. Come home Vik and bash your way to upwards of nine Premier League goals for Coventry.

What are we expecting? Right now, it’s really difficult to say. The only key player to have exited (so far) is Maxence Lacroix, on whom we made a massive profit, but we still have to strengthen the squad so that it can cope with the rigours of going deep in the Europa League without risking our Premier League campaign – a lesson learned from last season. Our cult hero is … A few contenders. Mateta, obviously, chant-leader Dean Henderson and, potentially, our Brazilian attacker Matheus França. If we could sign two players from our past … Michael Olise without a doubt; he was clearly a world-class player at Palace and has continued to progress spectacularly. Fulham

I’m always optimistic at this stage of the summer – but there’s a bit of trepidation mixed in this time round. How on earth do you make an informed judgment on our chances when so much has changed? Hull

I’m very optimistic. Sure, chances are that we’ll get relegated but we’ll certainly not be the pushovers people are expecting us to be. We thrive when we’re being written off, as last season showed, and have a pragmatic manager who has us playing brilliant, transitional football which suits the Premier League. Key players/weak links As the squad currently stands, Oli McBurnie, Mohamed Belloumi and Charlie Hughes will be the key faces. Full-back is still a problem position for us: there’s only Ryan Giles on the left and questions over Lewie Coyle and Cody Drameh at this level on the right. Thanks to a late flurry in the window we’ve now got a healthy plethora of young talent hoping to break through. 18-year-old Australian Lucas Herrington comes as a fully fledged international and had the likes of Barcelona sniffing around before signing for us.

We still need to sign … We still really need depth in the full-back areas and desperately need a forward or two to compete with McBurnie. We could do with some more Premier League experience across the back line, too, as well as another back-up goalkeeper thanks to Jack Butland’s lengthy injury.

Our cult hero is … Definitely McBurnie. He’s a handful for every defender and a constant wind-up merchant. The kind of player you hate to be against but love to have in your team.

If we could sign two players from our past … I would have Jarrod Bowen on the wing and Andy Robertson in at left-back. Strangely, they were two transfers I thought might actually happen this summer following West Ham’s relegation and Robertson leaving Liverpool on a free. Alas, it wasn’t to be.

Carrick is getting the best out of a group who were spectacularly mismanaged for a couple of years. The difference he made in six months was ridiculous. After the longest goodbye in recent history, Casemiro has gone, replaced by midfielders who can actually run – but we could still be reliant on keeping injury-prone Mount fit. I hope it’s not a case of Glazernomics repeating itself, where we spend to qualify for the Champions League, then go shopping in the bargain bin once we’ve qualified. Give Carrick another couple of decent signings and I genuinely think we can challenge: Arsenal fell over the line, City have lost their greatest-ever manager, Liverpool’s defence already looks shot through and Chelsea have 35 first-team players, which should present its own problems. Realistically, I think we will finish third.

Key players/weak links We are looking forward to the link-up play between Tielemans and Bruno. Tielemans’s eye for a pass will be a boon for our forwards. I can see Sesko building on a decent first season but if we’re competing on four fronts we need to sign another striker. The weak spot is still left-back. Luke Shaw being fit was almost a miracle last season, but we can’t build a season around hoping his body holds together.

We still need to sign … A left-back, Lewis Hall would be my choice. We need another striker, we will probably get last-resort Watkins on the last day of the window, hopefully a straight swap for Rashford.

Our cult hero is … Carrick. He went from being the quiet bloke in the background to dragging United into the Champions League. There’s something very satisfying about a former United player coming back and actually understanding what the club is supposed to be.

If we could sign two players from our past … Robson and Rooney. Captain Marvel in midfield for the leadership, aggression and sheer refusal to accept defeat. Rooney because he was everything you want from a modern forward: technically brilliant, ferocious, selfless and capable of playing anywhere on the pitch.

We will finish 3rd. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Manchester United; 4. Liverpool. Bottom three: 18. Sunderland; 19. Leeds; 20. Ipswich. First manager sacked Oliver Glasner: gone before Halloween.

Shaun O’Donnell

View image in fullscreen Michael Carrick: cult hero. Photograph: Niall Carson/PA

Newcastle

We’re hurting. We’ve lost our most successful manager in decades, plus his talismanic captain. A-listers have departed and we’ve been humiliated in the transfer market, for the second summer running. Yes, a reset was needed, but we weren’t expecting it to be like this. At least, in Matthias Jaissle, we have a hungry, passionate young manager whose intensity will be welcomed. He certainly looks up for the fight and, despite our outgoings, the German has some exciting talent to work with. According to CEO David Hopkinson, this is “Newcastle United 2.0”. We guess we’ll know what that means in a few months’ time.

Key players/weak links Lewis Miley is “one of our own” and, with Tonali gone, can fulfil his potential. We’ll also be expecting improvements between the posts, with Lukas Hornicek and Ewen Jaouen competing for the keeper’s jersey. And if Yoane Wissa and Anthony Elanga can replicate their World Cup form, we might have a strike force on our hands. The weak links? Joe Willock, who contributed very little to the cause last season and, sadly, Sven Botman, whose form has never recovered from his anterior cruciate ligament injury in 2024.

We still need to sign … A replacement for Bruno Guimarães, leaders on and off the field, high-grade cover at both full-back positions, a centre-half … so not too much to ask … Benfica’s versatile full-back Amar Dedić and Milan’s centre-half Fikayo Tomori would certainly be a good start. Crucially, we need to blend more experience into our youthful side, but any deals will have to be done in stealth mode, given Liverpool’s recent behaviour …

Our cult hero is … Big Dan Burn. A giant of a man, with a heart to match.

If we could sign two players from our past … Alan Shearer for his leadership and goals, and of course, the much-loved, and much-missed, Kevin Keegan. Both knew what it meant to wear the black-and-white shirt.

We will finish 10th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Liverpool; 4. Chelsea. Bottom three: 18. Ipswich; 19. Coventry; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Álvaro Arbeloa.

David and Richard Holmes

View image in fullscreen Matthias Jaissle: welcome intensity. Photograph: Jamie Johnston/Focus Images Ltd/Shutterstock

Nottingham Forest

If nothing else, it can’t be as chaotic as last season. We survived fairly comfortably in the end – thanks Vítor! – then sacked him in favour of Glasner, with the rationale being that the Austrian has won silverware. So the target this time isn’t only a decent league finish, but also something in the cabinet.

Key players/weak links The key, like last season, will be Morgan Gibbs-White: the talisman, the on-pitch leader, and the guy who makes things happen for the Reds. After being overlooked for Tommy T’s England squad, he will be keen to continue to show his worth.

We still need to sign … Getting Ousmane Diomande feels important; Murillo and Milenkovic make a great pair but we were still vulnerable in defence last season, and the new guy should balance with the attributes of the established duo. For all that we have loads of wingers, we do desperately need a reliable striker: we can’t continue to rely on a 35-year-old with a chronic knee problem.

Our cult hero is … Fans of other clubs love to take a swipe at our owner, and Reds supporters are frequently quick to jump to his defence. For all the controversies, I genuinely think Marinakis has been great for Forest and for English football: ruthlessly ambitious, aware that decision-making carries risk as well as reward, and unwilling to shrink in the face of so-called “big clubs” or the authorities. He has made some high-profile mistakes but does not shy away from making big calls (sorry Vítor!). And, of course, as Palace fans are aware (along with most of Greece), the Big Guy will also stand up for what he thinks is right and proper, and doesn’t care what other people think.

If we could sign two players from our past … Stan Collymore and Des Walker: pace, power, brilliance.

We will finish 12th. Top four 1. Chelsea; 2. Arsenal; 3. Liverpool; 4. Man United. Bottom three 18. Crystal Palace; 19. Coventry; 20. Hull. First manager sacked De Zerbi.

Rich Ferraro, 1865: The Nottingham Forest Podcast

View image in fullscreen Ousmane Diomande: important arrival. Photograph: Lee Keuneke/Every Second Media/Shutterstock

Sunderland

I’m optimistic – but definitely cautiously optimistic. Last season completely exceeded our expectations and finishing seventh with Europa League football on the horizon was incredible. However, Europe changes things. The biggest challenge will be managing the extra games without losing the spark that made us so enjoyable to watch. I’d be very happy with a comfortable mid-table finish and a decent European run. Consolidating ourselves in the league has to be the priority.

Key players/weak links Xhaka is still absolutely pivotal – he brings so much leadership and control – while Le Fée is probably the player I most enjoy watching. I’m also really excited to see what Talbi does this year. He was managed really well last season without too much pressure being put on him, but this feels like his season to really kick on. I don’t think there’s an obvious individual weak link; the concern is whether we have enough depth to compete on multiple fronts.

We still need to sign … I’d still like another attacking option, ideally someone who can play on the right and offer genuine end product. Geny Catamo is an interesting link, but I know the club won’t move unless the figures line up. More than anything, I want quality depth. We could play a ridiculous number of games this season, so we need options rather than simply another big name.

Our cult hero is … Wilson Isidor without question. His “football is life, Sunderland is life” clip probably summed it up perfectly. He gets the club and we genuinely love him. Add in the personality, the goals and his ability to do something brilliant or completely chaotic, and he feels destined to go viral several times this season.

If we could sign two players from our past … Kevin Phillips is the obvious first choice. Put peak Phillips alongside Brobbey and you’ve got a ruthless finisher playing off someone who can hold the ball up and occupy defenders. My second would be Amad. He’d give us quality, creativity and unpredictability out wide, and after how loved he was during his loan spell, bringing him back would feel like a proper homecoming. Put Amad on the wing with Phillips and Brobbey through the middle and I’d be getting dangerously carried away very quickly.

We will finish 12th. Top four: 1. Arsenal; 2. Manchester City; 3. Liverpool; 4. Manchester United. Bottom three: 18. Fulham; 19. Coventry; 20. Hull. First manager sacked Sergej Jakirovic.

View image in fullscreen Wilson Isidor: ‘Sunderland is life’. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images

Tottenham

Nothing screams more “Tottenham Hotspur” than stating we’re going to have an outstanding season having finished 17th twice in succession and narrowly avoided relegation. We probably should have gone down. Somehow West Ham managed to be a little bit more rubbish than a team that could barely win home games. Roberto De Zerbi and Enic’s personality change (spending money on end products) is why I’m flirting with the idea of a top-five finish. Absolute greed on my part, but it’s fun to believe. Top eight would be grand.

Key players/weak links Still work to do, but the backline has been rebooted and Micky van de Ven has signed a new contract. In midfield, with Tonali and Fernandes (two of the best mids available to sign) and with Kudus and Deki to return, we finally have depth and quality and strength. The aim will be to galvanise and rejuvenate our home form and regain that confidence and swagger. The key is De Zerbi. His appointment has changed everything. As for youngsters, Luca Williams-Barnett has all the potential to be something special.

We still need to sign … We’ll need plenty done over the next few windows, but ideally, we could do with a winger (we’ve been chasing Savinho for what feels forever) plus a No 10 and a forward. Maddison getting injured again is a concern. We need more than just Solanke up top, with Richy likely to leave.

Our cult hero is … Djed Spence for his World Cup heroics – but we are selling him to Inter. So it has to be the Spurs social media team, the togetherness vibe is the feelgood cleansing we need.

If we could sign two players from our past … It’s a cheat code, but let’s add Harry Kane to the frontline and Gareth Bale to the wing (or any position he wants).

We will finish 17th/1st. Top four: 1. Tottenham; 2. Manchester City; 3. Liverpool; 4. Manchester United. Bottom three: 18. Nottingham Forest; 19. Newcastle; 20. Aston Villa. First manager sacked Mikel Arteta.

Sports.title: End of an era? South Korea’s sun sets in the Premier League but Japan rise
Sports.content:
It has been a cruel summer for South Korea. The national team crashed and burned at the World Cup, the police are investigating the football association, reports have emerged about bribes paid to foreign referees in 2011 and 2012 and there is a real prospect of the English Premier League being Korean-free for the first time since 2005.

That was when Park Ji-sung signed for Manchester United, to start a love affair between the Land of the Morning Calm and England’s top tier that has continued ever since. Park won four titles and his mantle was taken over in 2015 by Son Heung-min at Spurs.

Son ended his successful decade, during which he became a club captain, by lifting the Europa League in 2025. There are other Taegeuk Warriors who are fondly remembered such as Ki Sung-yueng, Lee Young-pyo and Lee Chung-yong, and then those that would be tougher quiz questions. Cho Won-hee, Yun Suk-young and Park Chu-young barely featured for Wigan, QPR and Arsenal respectively.

Others have cult hero status. Ji Dong-won’s last-minute winner against Manchester City will never be forgotten by Sunderland supporters while Lee Dong-gook, who had a long and successful career, could not hit a barn door with Middlesbrough. While there have inevitably hits and misses, overall, the exports have been a source of pride.

Now, though, those who stayed up late or got up early to watch their compatriots are going to have more free time. After Son left London for Los Angeles, Hwang Hee-chan was the sole participant, but the forward went down with Wolves. There are three Koreans on Premier League books, but Yang Min-hyeok of Spurs, Brentford’s Kim Ji-soo and Park Seung-soo of Newcastle are likely to be once again loaned out.

There was talk of Lee Kang-in leaving Paris Saint-Germain for England, but in July the 25-year-old attacker joined Atlético Madrid to take Antoine Griezmann’s No 7 shirt. The former child TV reality star, introduced to the nation at the age of six and at Valencia’s academy four years later, is now perhaps Asia’s biggest name, but is going to play in England only in Champions League games. At the moment, there are not many other Koreans who look capable of becoming established Premier League players.

That is not the case for Japan, with the Land of the Rising Sun taking the mantle from its eastern neighbour. Last season, Kaoru Mitoma shone with Brighton while there was also Daichi Kamada at Crystal Palace, joined at Selhurst by Takehiro Tomiyasu, Ao Tanaka at Leeds and Wataru Endo with Liverpool.

View image in fullscreen Hwang Hee-chan was relegated with Wolves last season. Photograph: Anna Gowthorpe/Shutterstock

The new season will see more. As Lee was signing for Madrid, Hull snapped up Hidemasa Morita, last seen in England playing for Sporting Lisbon in the Champions League quarter-final against Arsenal in March. Shortly after, Daizen Maeda became Ipswich’s first Japanese player. The forward, who joins after a successful Celtic spell with five league titles, was last in action for Japan against Brazil at the World Cup.

While that game, with the five-time champions coming from behind to win in the 96th minute, was a frustrating one for the Samurai Blue, the team at least did OK. Korea’s World Cup campaign was, however, a disaster with a 2-1 win against Czechia followed by a 1-0 loss by Mexico and a truly dismal defeat by the same scoreline to South Africa. The head coach of the national team and the president of the FA have resigned and Park Ji-sung has been roped in head a new “reform football committee”. It’s a mess.

Park has talked of the need to follow Japan’s long-term philosophy to close the gap with what is clearly Asia’s best team. Increasingly, Japanese players, who have historically headed to Germany first, want to play in England. It is perhaps not a coincidence that two of the promoted Premier League teams have recruited Samurai Blue as there are plenty who have impressed in the Championship in recent years.

It all leads to growing Japanese interest in the Premier League and the opposite in Korea. In 2022, AIA, Tottenham’s shirt sponsor, commissioned a report that claimed there were 12 million fans of the club in the country. Even given Son’s undoubted popularity, wild European claims of fan numbers in Asia have been a feature since before Park arrived at Old Trafford 21 years ago. There are certainly nowhere near 12 million now, with one Korean TV executive saying viewing figures for Spurs games are nowhere near what they were.

That is hardly surprising as widespread Premier League interest in Korea, like Japan, not a historic lover of English football, is still largely player driven. During his time in London, Son’s smiling face would appear in the top corner of the television screen when he was on the pitch to keep casual viewers from turning over. In Park’s time, Manchester United games were often the only one shown all weekend.

When City and the rest of the world were witnessing the Agüero moment in 2012, in Korea, fans had to watch the entirety of United at Sunderland. That was the final sighting of Park in a red shirt and it looks as if Hwang’s appearance against Burnley in May will be the last Korean representation in England’s top tier for some time.

Sports.title: Scotland appoint Pocognoli as successor to Clarke in fresh approach
Sports.content:
The Scottish Football Association has appointed the Belgian Sébastien Pocognoli as the successor to Steve Clarke as manager. The 39-year-old, who was sacked by Monaco in June, will become the country’s first non-Scottish manager since Berti Vogts, who was in charge from 2002 to 2004.

Clarke’s abrupt departure came after Scotland were knocked out of the World Cup at the group stage. He had signed a four-year contract extension immediately before the tournament. It quickly became clear the SFA would turn towards a foreign manager with the Danes Jon Dahl Tomasson and Kasper Hjulmand being linked with the position.

Pocognoli, a left-back who played for Brighton and West Brom, will probably be welcomed by Scotland fans seeking a fresh approach. Clarke was in position for a generally successful seven years, including appearances at three major tournaments, but was often criticised for a pragmatic style.

After a period in youth coaching, Pocognoli enjoyed a successful time in charge of Union Saint-Gilloise in his homeland. Under Pocognoli, Union won their first title in 90 years in 2025. A move to Monaco followed, but Pocognoli lasted eight months and 38 games in France. The former Everton and Belgum winger Kevin Mirallas is expected to join him in the dugout.
