World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Disaster diplomacy and a persistent peso
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum spent the weekend before this week began in Puebla, kicking off the 2026 National Reforestation Day from the mountain pass between the Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl volcanoes. There, marking the International Day of the World’s Indigenous Peoples, she declared that the Paso de Cortés — named for the conquistador who marched through it in 1519 — would be a great candidate for a new name.

On Monday morning, the president’s attention had shifted south: a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing hundreds. Sheinbaum immediately pledged Mexico would send Colombia everything it needed, but the country’s military rescue brigade quickly ran into a diplomatic hurdle, part of a tangle of certification disputes and friction that unfolded even as quietly extraordinary Mexican solidarity continued — not just with Colombia, but with wildfire-stricken Canada as well. Colombia’s quake also revived an old question for Mexico, one we explore in more depth here: with Venezuela and now Colombia both rattled by major temblors this year, does Mexico’s own position on the Pacific Ring of Fire mean its odds just went up?

Otherwise, the week of Aug. 10-14 in Mexico brought big economic headlines, athletic glory and advances in the Ayotzinapa criminal case.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Mexico extends a hand abroad

Mexico’s instinct to help its neighbors was on full display this week. More than 300 Mexican firefighters traveled to British Columbia to help battle over 100 active wildfires that have forced tens of thousands to evacuate, drawing an outpouring of gratitude on Canadian social media. Farther south, a 45-member team of Mexico’s famed “Topos” rescue brigade reached Cali, Colombia, on Wednesday to dig through earthquake rubble — but only after Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella initially rejected their help, citing sovereignty concerns.

On Thursday, Sheinbaum confirmed that an official Mexican Army rescue brigade had not been authorized to enter Colombia and therefore remained at home. According to the president, Colombia’s new government demanded a type of certification the Mexican team does not have. Mexico kept sending humanitarian aid regardless — more than 58 tonnes of food, water and medicine by week’s end.

Ex-governor bound over in Ayotzinapa case

In one of the week’s most significant justice developments, former Guerrero Governor Ángel Aguirre was ordered to stand trial over his alleged role in the 2014 disappearance of 43 Ayotzinapa students. Prosecutors allege Aguirre ordered the destruction of security footage from Iguala’s Palace of Justice on the night the students vanished, partly to protect a nephew with ties to a local criminal gang. Aguirre, who resigned as governor weeks after the disappearances, remains jailed at the Altiplano maximum-security prison as the case — one of Mexico’s most notorious unsolved human rights tragedies — grinds toward trial nearly 12 years later.

The super peso returns

Mexico’s currency briefly broke back below 17 to the US dollar on Friday morning for the first time since 2024, in what analysts are calling the return of the “super peso.”

The peso has now strengthened for four consecutive days and appreciated more than 5% this year, a move Citibanamex attributes largely to global dollar weakness rather than Mexican fundamentals. Still, by the MND Peso Index™, which compares a basket of goods in Mexico and Dallas, the currency looks overvalued by 2.4% — a smaller gap than June’s 2.9%, suggesting the exchange rate isn’t too far removed from what prices on the ground would imply.

Homicides fall, but Sinaloa gets reinforcements

Security officials reported on Wednesday that the daily homicide average has fallen 51% since Sheinbaum took office, with July recording the lowest monthly tally of her administration so far. Even so, nearly half of the country’s murders remain concentrated in just seven states, Sinaloa among them. That reality was underscored by the Navy’s deployment of over 1,700 personnel to Mazatlán after the port city logged its bloodiest month of the year in July, as fighting between rival Sinaloa Cartel factions Los Chapitos and Los Mayos continues to spill beyond Culiacán into the tourist-heavy coastal city.

Visa fights spill into the mañanera

Washington’s campaign against Mexican political figures widened this week.

Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, the son of former President López Obrador and a former Morena party organization secretary, said the United States had revoked his visa, accusing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his deputy of a politically motivated move. At Friday’s mañanera, Sheinbaum called the decision “essentially political in nature,” urging Washington to produce evidence against anyone it targets while insisting the dispute won’t spiral into a broader conflict with the United States.

Business indicators to know

Peso: Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued.

Trading just above 17 to the dollar, its strongest level since February, even as the MND Peso Index™ pegs it as 2.4% overvalued. Inflation: July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.”

July’s headline rate came in at 3.12%, its lowest since May 2020, though Banxico Governor Victoria Rodríguez says it’s too early to “claim victory.” Jobs: Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high.

Formal employment shed 19,550 positions in July, a seasonal dip IMSS attributes to the school year’s end, even as average wages hit a record daily high. Industry: Industrial activity grew 0.2% month-on-month in June, lifted by mining and construction, while manufacturing logged its 12th straight month of annual decline.

Cyclospora cleared in the Riviera Maya

After British health authorities flagged a spike in cyclosporiasis cases among travelers returning from Mexico, Cofepris tested food and water samples from 16 Riviera Maya hotels — and found no trace of the parasite. All 43 samples, drawn from Playa del Carmen, Puerto Morelos, Tulum and Isla Mujeres, tested negative, and no contamination indicators turned up elsewhere. Mexico’s Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cyclosporiasis cases nationwide this year, a tiny fraction of the population, though the source of the UK cases remains unidentified.

Tourism notes

June brought 4.11 million international tourists to Mexico, up just 1.1% year-on-year — a muted bump given that Mexico hosted 12 of its 13 World Cup matches that month.

Tulum’s airport will regain five international routes this winter to cities in Canada and the United States, part of a state push to reverse a steep decline in international traffic.

Sargassum accumulation, though still tracking toward the second-heaviest year on record, has begun easing across most monitored stretches of the Quintana Roo coast as collection efforts and shifting currents bring relative relief to hard-hit beaches like Tulum and Playa del Carmen.

Mexican athletes seize the moment

It was a banner week for Mexican sport. The under-20 men’s soccer team defended its Concacaf title, beating the United States 2-0 at Mexico City’s Estadio Banorte for a record 15th championship, with defender Cristóbal Alfaro scoring twice.

Meanwhile, Mexico delivered its best-ever medal haul at the Central American and Caribbean Games, where the delegation topped the table with a record 407 medals in Santo Domingo. The government announced every medal — not just an athlete’s best result — will now earn a cash prize, a change Conade chief Rommel Pacheco said was Sheinbaum’s own idea.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: How fragile is Chacahua’s lagoon ecosystem? A conversation with locals on the Oaxaca coast
World.content:
A bus from Puerto Escondido. A minibus, aka colectivo, from Rio Grande. Then a lancha, or small boat, across the water to Zapotalito. One more open-air truck and you’ve made it.

Laguna de Chacahua sits along the western coast of Oaxaca, part of the state’s more than 300 milePacific coastline – a lagoon ecosystem padded with jungle flora, where the network of mangroves roots the island in its gurgling brackish tides.

It is part of the municipality of Villa de Tututepec de Melchor Ocampo and around 100 miles down the coast from the popular beach city of Puerto Escondido. In the daytime, the high sun smelts the soft sand and rocks while hammocks loll idly in the low breeze. After sunset, bioluminescent plankton set the water aglow in a neon blue glacé.

Technically, Chacahua is a barrier island, meaning it is not entirely separate from the mainland but is only accessible by boat. The community is predominantly Black and Afro-Indigenous, partially linking back to the Spanish enslavement of Africans and their forced labor in Mexico in the 16th and 17th centuries. But many residents make their way over from the mainland to surf, fish and enjoy the more relaxed pulse of daily life.

“Here, you can be whatever you want to be,” Augusto, an architect living in Chacahua, tells me. “And nobody is going to look down on you; you’re living in a free place.”

‘The sea is starting to reclaim the land’

But it isn’t all peace in paradise. Coastal environments and their communities are facing increased exposure to natural hazards.

The rainy season from June to September brings storms and natural climate variations, but Oaxaca state’s geography, situated along Mexico’s southwest Pacific coast, leaves it particularly vulnerable to climate change. Pacific hurricanes and Atlantic basin tropical systems pose a dual threat, alongside the increasing reality of heavy rains, droughts, and rising temperatures and sea levels.

While it is difficult to find more localised data for the island, average yearly temperature in Oaxaca City rose by 1.1 degrees Celsius (2 degrees Fahrenheit) between 1994 and 2024. While this figure may seem small, it represents a rapid change over three decades, even at the local level.

Global sea level rise has been affecting the coast of Oaxaca, and Chacahua is no exception. Drawing from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) 6th Assessment Report, NASA’s Sea Level Projection projects extreme sea level rise along Oaxaca’s Pacific coast, and the lagoon’s low relief offers little defense.

Sitting in a cabana just 100 meters inland, Augusto points towards Playa Chacahua. “The sea is starting to reclaim (the) land. That’s why the houses over there are collapsing.”

It was Hurricane Pauline in 1997 that dramatically shifted the landscape of Chacahua, the lagoon rising to such a level that a new inlet was created and swathes of the beach were eaten away. Today, the beach faces an ever-greater risk due to the damaging erosion.

‘Everyone fishes sooner or later’

Fishing is integral to life in Chacahua, and the catch is diverse – shrimp, puffer fish, oysters, blue crabs, and red snapper by the Bajo Este. “There are all kinds of fish,” Antonio says. “There’s a bit of everything here.”

Antonio started fishing at the age of 8 with his grandfather. At 17, he began fishing for sharks; tiburoneros (shark fishermen) use a simbra, a 14-kilometre-long (9-mile) fishing line with around 300 hooks every 18 meters.

“We’d head out along the Guerrero coast, going out toward the horizon where the sun sets … to where you can’t see a thing anymore,” Antonio tells me. “Transatlantic ships pass through there. We’d stay one night and head back the next day.”

The population is no more than 800 and, according to Antonio, more than half of its residents are fishermen.

“Everyone fishes sooner or later,” he says. But security isn’t promised. “Later, some move onto other jobs because fishing is just a matter of luck.”

Santiago was born on the island and has been a fisherman for 20 years.

“Because of the rains and the storms that come, it’s more dangerous now. It’s more dangerous than compared to before. It used to be a good life.”

The ecocide of the Chacahua-Pastoría Lagoons is a key culprit, with toxic chemical influx from local oil-crop industries, as well as chemical waste from a lime-oil factory beyond Zapatalito. Shrimp and fish populations are declining. Locals have faced the consequences of diminishing catch and have even demanded government action.

In 2013, local fishermen’s collective, supported by the Human Rights Ombudsman of the People of Oaxaca (DDHPO), produced a report regarding violations against the inhabitants of Zapotalito, Chacahua, La Pastoría and El Corral details the public health risks, loss of livelihood and environmental degradation that communities have faced due to federal infrastructure projects, such as Irrigation District 110 and breakwaters in the Boca de Chacahua.

The resilience of mangroves

Part of a roughly 51-square-mile national park designated in 1937, Chacahua Lagoon is surrounded by a network of mangrove corridors, anchoring the island in verdant, woody tresses. Mangroves are trees or bushes that thrive in brackish tidal waters, often where a river meets the sea, offering nesting grounds for a diversity of wildlife.

The red mangrove (Rhizophora mangle), black mangrove (Avicennia germinans), white mangrove (Laguncularia racemosa), and buttonwood (Conocarpus erectus) are also essential to maintaining the health of the local ecosystem.

Their long, complex root systems are adapted to survive in low-lying waters, optimising oxygen absorption and filtering out saline contamination. They endure conditions that are virtually impossible for other plants, and their resilience is recognized by the locals.

Angél runs a grocery shop in the central square. His family has been living on the island for generations. The salinity of the sea is getting worse, he concedes, but “the mangroves are strong. We don’t have to cut them that much.”

“The mangroves are doing well,” Antonio agrees. “They’re tough. When they fall, they land upright,” due to their roots.

The resilience of locals

Perhaps Antonio and Angél aren’t giving themselves enough credit. In reality, mangroves are vulnerable to climate change, specifically increasing salinity, hurricane events, and worsening El Niño patterns. But it’s the locals who demonstrate climate resilience every day, in working as a community to restore the things that Angél says the government is neglecting financially and administratively.

“The effort is made every day; it’s part of life here on the island,” Augusto says. “People engage in what’s called tequio, voluntary community work to help the environment.”

In the same way, the fishermen are taking it upon themselves to try and mitigate the marine pollution, but there is a limit to what can be done without wider support.

Tequio “takes place because people love their land,” Augusto explains, but as Angél marks, the climate is getting hotter, the sea saltier, and the water warmer.

On top of this, the briny waves of gentrification are lapping at the island’s shores. Lavish cabanas with their polished wood walls and hiked-up rent are beginning to rear their haute heads.

Tourism has also been shown to worsen pollution. In Mexico’s Caribbean coast, the tourism sector accounts for one-third of the region’s total waste, and light pollution has been proven to pose threats to turtle populations, of which species such as the Leatherback are populous in Chacahua.

What’s in store for Chacahua?

Oaxaca has been strongly affected by hurricanes Otis, John, Erick, and Boris in the last four years.

While federal budgeting continues to be an issue for Natural Protected Areas across Mexico, local cooperatives, in tandem with the National Commission of Protected Natural Areas (CONANP), are taking measures to respond to growing tourism in the state of Oaxaca and have made major steps in wildlife protection and sustainable infrastructure, but the direct effects on Chacahua are yet to be comprehensively reported.

Looking into its climate future, Chacahua is standing at a delta. It goes without saying that the community has demonstrated its climate resilience through supporting mangroves, keeping the waters around the island clean, and reconstructing and relocating seafront buildings.

However, without sufficient government support, the effects of environmental jeopardy and injustice may ultimately uproot the mangrove system and local way of life to an irremediable degree.

Millie Deere is a freelance journalist.

World.title: How Múcara became one of Mexico’s best restaurants
World.content:
If you flip through the Guía México Gastronómico — an annual 200-page book that maps a flavorful constellation of Mexico’s most delicious restaurants, from the northernmost corner of Baja California to the southernmost point of Chiapas — you’ll find it: Múcara.

Off the page, the restaurant is located on a steep, narrow road in the historic center of Xalapa, Veracruz, tucked away — somewhat inconspicuously — between a comic shop, a tamalería, apartments, cafés and bars crammed with college students. It’s easy to miss. In fact, if you were to pass by for the first time, you’d likely skip right past it.

And yet, the intimate fonda, which seats a maximum of 20 diners at seven tables, has quietly risen to become among the most notable restaurants in the country — and is the first in Xalapa’s history to garner such prestigious national recognition, as designated by an editorial board of influential food critics, journalists, sommeliers and hospitality experts in Mexico.

How Múcara became a destination eatery

That is, Múcara is one of Mexico’s best places to eat. And they’ve earned it, despite not being in a buzzy or touristic hub of the nation.

Múcara’s objective is clear. Their menu is about retaining and expanding the overlooked culinary lineage of Veracruz through a delicious balance of elevated-yet-homely dishes — highlighting seasonal ingredients, refined cooking techniques and hyper-regional recipes. Strangely, it’s a radical concept in Veracruz’s capital city, where the dominant foods seem to be burgers, wings, pizza and pasta, and where if you were to ask a local where to find the best traditional Xalapeño bites, the list would be brief. That glaring absence is what inspired Múcara to open in 2016, when Lesterloon Sánchez Trinidad, a lifetime Xalapeño and the founding chef behind Múcara, first launched his vision.

“I wanted people to discover the regional foods from this area; Veracruz food is one of the oldest in the world,” says Sánchez Trinidad. “Veracruz includes the Olmec, and this region has been a historical crossing for Europeans, Asians, Arabs and the world. It’s the cradle of Mexican food. But at the national level, Veracruz is very forgotten. Modernity has caused us to spend our time differently and change our techniques in the kitchen. The previous generation is turning off their ovens, and things are rapidly changing. The history is being lost.”

A life-changing dining experience

At Múcara, that history is potent, and edible. And most of it is life-changingly delicious.

For lunch, that might taste like a courtesy apéritif of tepache de limón (a bold, citrusy shot of fermented lime juice) to go along with a glass of agua de acuyo (a refreshingly sweet and herbal dose of pepperleaf extract), anchored by a round of enchiladas encacahuatadas (a rich portion of four enchiladas, made with in-house tortillas that are rolled up and with filled shredded chicken, then bathed in a very mildly spiced peanut mole and blanched peanuts sprinkled atop).

There’s also envueltos de plátano (rolled tortillas, stuffed with mashed bananas and drenched in sweet, chocolatey mole); enmoladas de tlatonile (tortillas with chicken and regional tlatonile sauce, brought over from the nearby mountain town of Huasteco, and accompanied with epazote, a tea plant, and chile compeño, a rare pepper that is cultivated in Comapa, Veracruz).

Salads include a rich fig variety or a native peach criollo option. Another standout is the pasta with huitlacoche (house-made pappardelle pasta mixed with flavorful corn fungi, nata, garlic, onion, aged cheese and a touch of olive oil). The menu is relatively compact in its offerings, but at Múcara, it’s about quality and perfection, rather than empty spectacle. It’s about savoring the basics, rather than seeking the bombastic.

Mixing and matching the menu

Of course, aspects of the menu are constantly in flux, depending on the time of year and what ingredients are available from producers and local markets, making it an interactive dining experience where you can jigsaw yourself into nirvana with just about any combination of plates at your table.

Having studied the culinary arts in Mexico City with some of Mexico’s most prominent chefs as a young cook, Sánchez Trinidad — who is relatively young — has compiled and combined over a decade of experience in the kitchen through trial and error. Initially, he opened Nao as a café and pambassería (a small shop that only sold pambazos, the small sandwich of Xalapeño fame, of which he says were prominent in his upbringing but are no longer seen as commonly around Xalapa). Unfortunately, Nao closed during the pandemic, though its closure allowed him to shift his full attention to Múcara, the more ambitious of his projects. That focus has paid off, as Múcara has converted into a decade-long fixture in the city’s culinary scene.

If you go to Yucatán, you’ll easily find 20 or 30 places to eat Yucatán food,” Sánchez Trinidad tells Mexico News Daily. “Same in Puebla for Poblana food. Or in Oaxaca. But in Xalapa, there’s nothing like that. It’s an interesting case study. How is it possible that as a state capital we don’t even know our own cuisine that well? What are our dishes?”

Old-school Veracruz cuisine made modern

On a drizzly Xalapeño afternoon, you can discover the answer to Sánchez Trinidad’s rhetorical question. Múcara is a refuge for the state’s fading past — a slow-cooking, old-school type of joint in modern digs, where no one is rushing the process for the sake of instant gratification, but instead cherishing each bite and all that it offers and imparts about Veracruz’s diverse history. In many cases, Sánchez Trinidad has pulled recipes from his childhood memories of preparing food with his mother and grandmother. His restaurant isn’t just a love letter to his state; it’s an entire library’s worth.

Elegant yet elemental

As a result of his careful attention and thoughtful choices, the meals are orchestral: simple, yet highly calibrated and masterfully executed, highlighting the contradictory pleasures of Mexican cuisine as being elegantly refined while, simultaneously, retaining its most elemental essences.

“The origin of the name Múcara comes from a rock (fossilized coral and marine sediments) that was taken out of the sea,” Sánchez Trinidad explains. “They made buildings out of that. The oldest buildings in the Veracruz port are made from it. Churches, forts, everything. Those old buildings remain and haven’t fallen, and that’s what we strive to be for Veracruz cuisine.”

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Thank you, Harry Styles: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A few nights ago, my wife and I watched the movie “Three Amigos” with Steve Martin, Chevy Chase and Martin Short. Even though the movie was first released in 1986 — 40 years ago! — I recently saw a classic clip of them in my social media feed that inspired me to want to watch it again. The clip was of them ordering a beer in a Mexican bar. The bartender says, “We have no beer, only tequila.” They ask, “What is tequila?”, to which the bartender replies, “It’s like beer.” They proceed to do a shot and have a hilarious reaction. Not exactly Emmy award-winning lines and acting, but funny nonetheless.

I understand that the movie is meant to be a parody and not taken too seriously, but I will admit I was surprised at the overt stereotypical imagery used to portray Mexico. Nearly every man shown was dirty, poor and drunk. Nearly every woman shown was poor, sun-burned and disheveled — except, of course, for the few ladies who fell in love with the “three amigos.” The “bad guys” were also drunk and dirty, but also had lots of guns and made a living from robbing people. In addition to the characters, the images of Mexico and Mexican life were about as negatively stereotypical as you could imagine: poor, dusty, lawless, run-down and in the middle of the desert. People hanging around and drinking in the middle of the day, not hesitating to start shooting people. Of course, this is nothing new. Hollywood portrayals of Mexico in this way first began in Western movies in the 1910’s — over 100 years ago!

Again, I know some of you are thinking “lighten up Travis, it’s just a comedy film”. I get that, but the decades of stereotypes about Mexico portrayed in movies have had an impact on people’s perceptions about the country and its people. A few months ago, one of our writers wrote an in-depth article about it here: Stereotypes worth 1,000 words: Mexico’s visualization in the media.

And it’s not just Mexico — other countries suffer the same fate at the whims of Hollywood writers and producers.

In the decades after the “Three Amigos” movie, the Hollywood narrative of Mexico changed from the wild west version to the drug lord/narco version. Countless series were made of the cartel leaders, the cartel lifestyle, with “Narcos” from Netflix being the most popular one. In fact, “Narcos” has been one of the most-viewed series ever produced by Netflix. So, for over one hundred years, Hollywood has presented Mexico (not always, but very frequently) as a dirty, lawless location in a Western movie, and more recently as the home of cartels and the drug trade.

Which brings me to the point of my column today: Thankfully, that image is beginning to change. Not by Hollywood, but by musicians (most of them non-American). Over the past two weeks, I couldn’t help but notice in my social media feed all of the images of U.K. mega-star Harry Styles hanging out and enjoying Mexico City. He is in the city to do six concerts over nearly two weeks, and countless videos of him enjoying the city have been popping up. Jogging in Chapultepec Park, going for walks on the tree-lined streets with his girlfriend, eating tacos, standing in line for breakfast pastries — basically, looking and acting like a local and seemingly enjoying every minute of it.

Harry Styles continúa caminando muy relajado por las calles de la CDMX, a un día de su concierto. 🥹 Confiesen, ¿alguien ya se lo encontró? 👀😍 Video por: alexasaeenz pic.twitter.com/NPJqOXrX7r — EstiloDF (@EstiloDF) July 30, 2026

He is the latest artist to do this, but certainly is not the first. Earlier this year, Colombian-born Shakira did a total of 14 concerts (13 in stadiums + 1 free one in the zocalo) in Mexico City. She was seen for weeks hanging out and enjoying the capital city. Also in the past few months, Irish rock band U2 filmed a music video in the city and took time to visit with President Sheinbaum. And Korean mega-K-pop group BTS did a three-day concert series in the city and were seen hanging out and enjoying the sights, as well as visiting with Sheinbaum. Late last year, Dua Lipa — who is Albanian and grew up in the U.K. — spent a week in Mexico City performing three concerts as well. She was seen dancing in nightclubs, eating late-night tacos, and genuinely enjoying the city she calls “one of her favorites in the world.”

What an incredible change this has been in the portrayal of the country. After decades of Hollywood portrayals of Mexico as a lawless, unsafe, dirty place, you now have real stars genuinely hanging out and having a good time in Mexico. The images appear to be real, genuine, authentic and spontaneous — as different from Hollywood as you can get. It would be easy to have a cynical take on these musicians and simply say that what they are doing is good for their own business. Of course it is, but I would prefer someone making money by getting out, walking around, talking to locals and eating local food rather than presenting a stereotypical, outdated and false narrative.

The World Cup was a similar phenomenon. In the months leading up to the games, the media warned us of the dangers of cartel violence and protests. The reality that we saw was of the visiting fans from Colombia, the U.K., Japan, Korea and many other countries having an absolute blast with locals across the country. It truly felt authentic, which is precisely what made it so fascinating to watch.

So let’s hope that we are beginning to see a new trend of how Mexico is being presented to the rest of the world. If so, I think it will have a hugely positive impact on the country and hopefully finally do away with the negative stereotypes that were so common in past decades.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Fitch Rio de Janeiro AAA: City Hits Top National Rating
World.content:
Brazil · Credit Ratings

Key Facts Rating: Fitch raised Rio’s national long-term rating to AAA(bra) from AA+(bra).

Fitch raised Rio’s national long-term rating to AAA(bra) from AA+(bra). Short term: The city also holds the highest short-term national rating, F1+(bra).

The city also holds the highest short-term national rating, F1+(bra). Outlook: The outlook is Stable, both for the national long-term rating and the standalone credit profile.

The outlook is Stable, both for the national long-term rating and the standalone credit profile. Standalone: The PCI (Standalone Credit Profile) was upgraded to BB+ from BB, with a Stable outlook.

The PCI (Standalone Credit Profile) was upgraded to BB+ from BB, with a Stable outlook. Risk profile: Fitch assigned a ‘Medium to Low’ risk profile and an ‘a’ financial profile.

Fitch assigned a ‘Medium to Low’ risk profile and an ‘a’ financial profile. Peer comparison: Rio now shares the top national tier with São Paulo state, which also holds AAA(bra) and an international IDR of BB.

Rio now shares the top national tier with São Paulo state, which also holds AAA(bra) and an international IDR of BB. International: The city also carries an international rating of BB long-term and B short-term, Stable, held at Brazil’s sovereign ceiling; AAA(bra) is the national-scale mark.

Fitch’s upgrade puts Rio’s city finances in the elite tier of Brazilian subnationals.

Fitch Ratings has upgraded the city of Rio de Janeiro to AAA(bra)—the highest credit rating on Brazil’s national scale. The Fitch Rio de Janeiro AAA action, reported on August 15, 2026, lifts the city from its previous AA+(bra) and applies to the municipality’s long-term national-scale debt.

Rio de Janeiro just earned Fitch’s top national-scale credit rating. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Fitch Rio de Janeiro AAA rating means

In plain terms, AAA(bra) is Fitch’s top mark for Brazilian issuers on the domestic scale. It signals an extremely strong capacity to meet financial commitments, far above the risk of default.

The city also received F1+(bra), the highest short-term national rating, and a Stable outlook. This means Fitch expects the solid financial position to hold over the next 12 to 24 months.

You might wonder why the national scale matters. For Brazilian investors and institutions, it is the benchmark that directly influences borrowing costs and market confidence.

Think of it as the local gold standard — it measures Rio against other Brazilian issuers rather than against the world. On the global scale the city carries a separate BB rating, but AAA(bra) places it in the top tier of domestic creditworthiness, no small feat for a city with such a complex fiscal history.

Why Fitch raised Rio’s credit rating

According to O Globo’s report on the Fitch analysis, the upgrade stems from steady fiscal consolidation and disciplined budgeting. Rio has posted recurring improvements in its operating results, with current revenue—especially the ISS service tax and IPTU property tax—growing robustly.

Higher current savings, which Fitch calls ‘poupança corrente,’ mean the city has more money left after covering day-to-day expenses. That surplus can fund public investment without piling on debt, and it helped shrink the debt stock relative to net current revenue over time.

The Standalone Credit Profile (PCI) also rose from BB to BB+, reflecting stronger intrinsic credit quality. Fitch’s assessment highlights a ‘Medium to Low’ risk profile and an ‘a’ financial profile, which are key metrics for gauging long-term stability.

You might ask what drives this — it is the combination of own-source tax revenue growth and prudent spending. A city that collects more from its own taxpayers and keeps costs in check is inherently more resilient, especially in a volatile economy like Brazil’s.

How Rio compares to other Brazilian states and cities

On the national scale, Rio de Janeiro now sits in the same top tier as São Paulo state, which also holds AAA(bra) with a Stable outlook. Both share a ‘Medium to Low’ risk profile and an ‘a’ financial profile, per Fitch.

The two also line up on the international scale, where each carries a foreign-currency rating of BB. In one respect Rio actually edges ahead — Fitch places the city’s standalone credit profile at BB+, one notch above São Paulo state.

That comparison matters because São Paulo is Brazil’s largest subnational issuer. For investors and residents, it signals that Rio’s city finances are now viewed with the same confidence as the country’s most creditworthy state.

Here is a nuance worth understanding: the AAA(bra) is a domestic mark, while Rio’s international rating stays at BB. That BB is capped by Brazil’s sovereign ceiling — a city cannot be rated above its own country on the global scale, no matter how strong its books.

So a national AAA does not equal a global AAA — the two scales measure different things. The achievement is still notable, placing the city well ahead of the separate, more challenged credit profile of the STATE of Rio de Janeiro.

What the upgrade means for investors and residents

For Latin America-based investors, the Fitch Rio de Janeiro AAA rating is a clear signal of reduced credit risk on the city’s debt. The national-scale top mark makes its bonds more attractive to domestic institutional buyers and could lower future borrowing costs, while the city’s international rating sits at BB — capped by Brazil’s sovereign ceiling — for foreign investors weighing global-scale risk.

For residents, a stronger credit profile often translates into better terms for public infrastructure projects, from transit upgrades to sanitation works. It also reassures businesses that the city can honor contracts and payments, which supports local economic activity.

If you’re an investor looking at Brazilian fixed income, this upgrade is a positive signal. It suggests that Rio’s debt is now among the safest domestic options, potentially leading to tighter spreads and more stable returns.

For the city itself, the improved rating could open doors to more favorable financing from development banks and private lenders at home and abroad. That’s a tangible benefit for municipal projects that need upfront cash.

Of course, you should also watch for the state of Rio’s fiscal troubles, which can sometimes spill over to the city through shared budgets or political pressure. But the upgrade shows the city is carving its own path toward fiscal health.

What to watch next

The upgrade lands during Mayor Eduardo Paes’s administration, though no direct quote from him is available in the public reporting. The city hall has not issued a formal press release on the rating action as of this writing.

Keep an eye on the city’s quarterly fiscal disclosures to see if the AAA(bra) holds. If current revenue growth slows or debt metrics worsen, Fitch could revise the outlook, so the Stable outlook is not a permanent guarantee.

You should also watch for any changes in the ISS and IPTU tax collections, as they are the primary drivers of the city’s revenue strength. A dip in these would be a red flag for the rating.

Finally, watch Brazil’s sovereign rating, because the city’s international BB is pinned to that ceiling. If the country is upgraded, Rio would have room to rise on the global scale too — a lift the city cannot earn on its own.

In the meantime, the Fitch Rio de Janeiro AAA rating stands as a testament to the city’s fiscal discipline. It’s a story worth tracking, especially if you’re invested in Brazilian subnational debt or just curious about how cities rebrand their financial credibility.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does AAA(bra) rating mean for the city of Rio de Janeiro? AAA(bra) is Fitch’s highest national-scale credit rating in Brazil, indicating extremely strong capacity to meet financial obligations. It’s a domestic measure, not comparable to international ratings like BBB or AA. Did the state of Rio de Janeiro also get upgraded? No, the upgrade applies only to the municipality (city) of Rio de Janeiro. The state of Rio has its own separate credit rating, which is not part of this action. Does the city of Rio have an international credit rating too? Yes. Alongside the national-scale AAA(bra), Rio carries an international rating of BB (long-term) and B (short-term), Stable, held at Brazil’s sovereign ceiling. The AAA(bra) is a domestic mark, while a city cannot be rated above its own country on the global scale. What does a Stable outlook mean? A Stable outlook means Fitch expects the rating to remain unchanged over the next 12-24 months, barring unexpected fiscal deterioration. It’s a sign of confidence in the city’s current financial trajectory.

Sources: O Globo Economia – Fitch eleva nota de crédito do município do Rio de Janeiro a ‘AAA’; Fitch Ratings – International Public Finance; The Rio Times – Fitch national-scale AAA(bra) usage context; Valor Economico – Fitch subnational/corporate rating actions (context)

World.title: Ecopetrol Sirius Gas Field: Startup Could Slip to 2031 as Colombia’s Gas Crunch Looms
World.content:
Colombia · Energy

Key Facts First gas: Official target is 2030, but an August 2026 exclusive says Ecopetrol’s board already assumes a one-year slip to 2031.

Official target is 2030, but an August 2026 exclusive says Ecopetrol’s board already assumes a one-year slip to 2031. Resource size: More than 6 trillion cubic feet of gas in place (gas-in-place, not certified reserves); designed to produce ~13 million m³/day for about 10 years—roughly half of Colombia’s current gas demand.

More than 6 trillion cubic feet of gas in place (gas-in-place, not certified reserves); designed to produce ~13 million m³/day for about 10 years—roughly half of Colombia’s current gas demand. Partners: Petrobras operates with 44.44% and Ecopetrol holds 55.56%, in the deepwater GUA-OFF-0 block under contract with regulator ANH.

Petrobras operates with 44.44% and Ecopetrol holds 55.56%, in the deepwater GUA-OFF-0 block under contract with regulator ANH. Location: The Sirius-2 discovery well sits about 77 km off Santa Marta in ~803 meters of water; the newer Sandia-1 well is ~42 km offshore in ~1,285 meters.

The Sirius-2 discovery well sits about 77 km off Santa Marta in ~803 meters of water; the newer Sandia-1 well is ~42 km offshore in ~1,285 meters. Leadership: Ricardo Roa left on 30 July 2026; Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra is acting president, with board chairman Luis Felipe Henao behind the Permian comments.

Ricardo Roa left on 30 July 2026; Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra is acting president, with board chairman Luis Felipe Henao behind the Permian comments. Import squeeze: Gas imports hit a record 33% of consumption in early July 2026, and Moody’s sees the deficit reaching up to 39% of demand this year.

Ecopetrol’s Sirius gas field faces a potential one-year delay to 2031, while Colombia’s gas imports hit record highs.

If you are tracking Colombia’s energy future, the Ecopetrol Sirius gas field is a name you need to know—and its official 2030 start-up date may already be slipping. An August 2026 Valora Analitik exclusive, based on internal board documents, shows Ecopetrol’s own board assumes the project could enter operation a year later, in 2031.

Ecopetrol’s Sirius is a deepwater gas discovery in the Colombian Caribbean. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What is Sirius and why does it matter?

Sirius is a large offshore natural-gas project in the Colombian Caribbean, sitting in a deepwater block known as GUA-OFF-0. The Sirius-2 discovery well lies about 77 kilometers off the city of Santa Marta in roughly 803 meters of water, while the newer Sandia-1 well sits about 42 km offshore in around 1,285 meters.

The project is a joint venture between Brazil’s Petrobras, which operates it with a 44.44% stake, and Colombia’s state-controlled Ecopetrol, which holds 55.56%. The block is under contract with the National Hydrocarbons Agency, Colombia’s oil-and-gas regulator known as the ANH.

The partners cite “more than 6 trillion cubic feet” of gas in place—that is the total gas estimated in the reservoir, not a certified, proved-reserves figure. The field is designed to pump about 13 million cubic meters a day for roughly 10 years, which would cover close to half of Colombia’s current gas demand.

That scale is why Sirius is being called one of the most important gas finds in Colombia in years. For a country watching its fields decline, a single offshore project of this size can reshape the national supply picture.

A timeline that could stretch into 2031

The official start-up date is 2030, according to both Ecopetrol and Petrobras. But an August 2026 exclusive from Valora Analitik, citing internal board documents, reports that Ecopetrol’s own board already assumes the project could slip a full year to 2031.

Board chairman Luis Felipe Henao called that one-year extension risk “totalmente real”—totally real—while insisting the mission under Colombia’s new government is still to open in 2030. For you, the honest takeaway is to plan for a possible delay rather than bank on the earlier date.

The gap between the public target and the board’s working assumption is unusual to see in the open. It tells you that even the people closest to the project are hedging their bets on timing.

Ecopetrol says the current focus is on cutting the schedule wherever possible to protect the 2030 goal. Whether it succeeds depends on drilling results, permits, and the pace set by the incoming administration.

Leadership shake-up—and a key Permian quote

A big change hit the top of Ecopetrol on 30 July 2026, when Ricardo Roa stepped down as president and chief executive. Juan Carlos Hurtado Parra took over as acting president from 31 July, and as of mid-August no permanent CEO had been named.

In the same stretch, board chairman Luis Felipe Henao—not the CEO—drew attention with his comments on Ecopetrol’s US assets in the Permian Basin. He said selling the Permian right now would be “el peor error”—the worst mistake—”en este momento,” at this moment.

Henao called the Permian Ecopetrol’s best business, with the lowest cost per barrel and the largest share of profit, an asset the company simply cannot walk away from. That matters because Colombia’s government has long debated whether the state oil firm should exit fossil-fuel projects abroad.

Colombia’s gas crunch: why Sirius is urgent

Colombia is leaning harder on imported gas each month. In the first half of 2026, imports covered about 30% of national supply—around 300 million cubic feet per day.

Then, in the first week of July, imports jumped to a historic record of 33% of consumption, roughly 320 GBTU per day. Ratings agency Moody’s projects the gas deficit could reach up to 39% of national demand across 2026.

Those import records are not just statistics—they translate into higher costs that ripple through power plants, factories, and household bills. New domestic supply from a field like Sirius is exactly what could slow that trend.

**Why a LatAm reader should care:** If you live in or invest in Colombia, a widening gas gap can push up energy bills and rattle industries that depend on cheap, steady supply. Sirius, once flowing, could cover a meaningful slice of domestic demand—but if it slips to 2031, you may face a tighter, pricier market for a year longer.

Recent drilling progress

The Sirius area holds several wells, including Sirius-1, Sirius-2, and Copoazu-1, plus the newest exploratory well, Sandia-1. Drilling on Sandia-1 began on 12 June 2026 and reached its final depth on 29 July, with results still under evaluation.

Each additional well is part of the effort to confirm how much gas can actually be produced and to move the project toward development. For you, a successful appraisal strengthens the case that Sirius will eventually deliver—though the exact timing stays uncertain.

What to watch next

Keep an eye on Ecopetrol and Petrobras updates on the Sandia-1 evaluation and any revised project milestones. Watch, too, whether the incoming permanent CEO and the new government fight to hold the 2030 date or quietly accept 2031.

The board’s frank admission of a possible delay is a cue to manage your expectations. In the meantime, Colombia’s record gas imports are a steady reminder of what is riding on this one field.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Ecopetrol Sirius gas field? Sirius is an offshore natural-gas project in the Colombian Caribbean, operated by Petrobras with Ecopetrol as partner, containing more than 6 trillion cubic feet of gas in place. When is Sirius expected to start producing gas? The official target is 2030, but Ecopetrol’s board assumes it could slip to 2031, as reported by Valora Analitik in August 2026. Who made the ’worst mistake’ comment about the Permian? Ecopetrol’s board chairman Luis Felipe Henao, not the CEO, said selling the Permian assets now would be ’el peor error’ and the ’worst mistake’ at this moment. Why is Colombia importing more gas? Domestic production has not kept pace with demand; imports hit a record 33% of consumption in July 2026, and Moody’s projects a deficit up to 39% of demand in 2026.

World.title: Milei Economic Model Shows Signs of Strain in Argentina
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts BCRA slowdown: August daily dollar purchases average ~US$33 million, down from ~US$103 million in July.

August daily dollar purchases average ~US$33 million, down from ~US$103 million in July. Reserves plateau: Gross reserves hover near US$49.5 billion, per Infobae daily reports.

Gross reserves hover near US$49.5 billion, per Infobae daily reports. Poll pattern: About 6 in 10 Argentines disapprove of the economic course, across multiple pollsters.

About 6 in 10 Argentines disapprove of the economic course, across multiple pollsters. Opposition weak: No single leader or coalition is clearly benefiting from the dip in support.

No single leader or coalition is clearly benefiting from the dip in support. Country risk rise: JP Morgan’s EMBI for Argentina climbed to ~470 basis points, the highest in two months.

JP Morgan’s EMBI for Argentina climbed to ~470 basis points, the highest in two months. Melconian warning: Economist Carlos Melconian says the government ‘will have to change’ course.

Economist Carlos Melconian says the government ‘will have to change’ course. Investor caution: Infobae reports Wall Street is reducing Argentina exposure amid election worries.

The Milei economic model is showing signs of strain—from slower reserve buying to weaker poll numbers and investor caution. We break down what’s really happening.

You may have heard that Argentina’s Milei economic model is hitting a rough patch, but what’s actually straining—and how much is real versus media noise? Let’s break down the key signals.

President Javier Milei faces growing questions over his economic model. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Why the Milei economic model is under scrutiny

The Milei economic model—anchored on crushing inflation and building reserves—is showing visible friction this August. The central bank (BCRA) has cut its daily dollar purchases to the lowest level of the year, and a pile of polls shows approval sagging.

Yet the picture is nuanced. The government still projects monthly inflation below 2%, and the opposition is not clearly benefiting from the dip.

So what’s really going on here? Let’s look at the numbers.

Central bank slows dollar buying to defend the peso

In the first 10 business days of August, the BCRA netted just +US$330 million, averaging about US$33 million per day, per TN. That’s a sharp drop from July’s ~US$103 million daily average, as Ámbito reported.

Reuters noted that the peso is trading near its record low of ~1,500 per dollar, and the BCRA moderated reserve buying from over US$90 million a day in July to under US$24 million a day in the last week. Market sources, like Roberto Geretto of Adcap, see this as a deliberate shift.

So what’s the market read? Reporters say the BCRA is prioritizing defense of the exchange rate and nominal stability over faster reserve accumulation.

That’s a journalistic inference, not an official BCRA statement. Still, it fits the data.

Gross reserves remain around US$49.5 billion, per Infobae’s daily tracking, so there’s no collapse. But the slower buying pace is a clear sign the model’s priorities are being recalibrated.

Polling: ~6 in 10 reject the economic course, but no clear alternative

Multiple polls converge on the same pattern: roughly six in ten Argentines disapprove of the economic course. For instance, AtlasIntel for Bloomberg (fieldwork July 30–August 3, 1,120 cases) found 62.4% disapprove of Milei, with 54.7% rating the government’s performance ‘bad or very bad.’

Hugo Haime & Asociados (via Crónica, August 12) reported only 14% support the Milei economic model as-is, while 47% want to change it totally. ESPOP Universidad de San Andrés (August 5–11) found 69% dissatisfied with how things are going.

But here’s the balance: no single poll asks literally ‘do you support the Milei economic model’ and gets 60% ‘no.’ The ~6-in-10 figure is a consistent pattern across pollsters, not a single question.

And crucially, the opposition is not clearly benefiting. Analysts describe a ‘board without clear leaders,’ meaning voters are unhappy but haven’t flocked to an alternative.

That’s an interpretation from political observers, not hard voting-intention data.

Wall Street turns cautious, but not panicked

Investor sentiment has cooled. Infobae ran a headline on August 16 saying Wall Street was reducing its Argentina exposure, with alarm over falling government support.

The article, citing unnamed investor sources, says backing has stagnated near 35%, seen as insufficient to win in 2027. Investors, it adds, ‘don’t want to risk a complicated electoral scenario.’

That’s Infobae’s narrative—it names no specific U.S. banks or position sizes. Even so, the country risk index (JP Morgan’s EMBI) rose to 466–472 basis points in mid-August, the highest in about two months, per Infobae and La Nación.

That reading is a real market signal, and it tends to move in tandem with the political mood.

The S&P Merval stock index fell 3.2% on August 11, then slipped another 0.76% on August 13. Named analysts, like Gabriel Caamaño of Outlier consultancy, say Argentina is underperforming even a weak emerging-market backdrop.

Eric Ritondale, chief economist at Puente, points to firm U.S. interest rates pressuring emerging-market bonds broadly—so not all of this is Argentina-specific. Still, the University Torcuato Di Tella’s Government Confidence Index fell from 40% to 37%.

The government’s side: growth is the new focus

The government isn’t standing still. Bloomberg reported on August 12 that Milei is easing the cash crunch to reignite economic growth, shifting from a singular focus on crushing inflation toward supporting jobs and growth.

Milei’s approval, per Bloomberg, is ‘mired near the lowest levels of his Presidency,’ but the government still projects monthly inflation below 2%. That’s the official line, and it’s not fantasy—inflation has fallen dramatically under Milei.

Economist Carlos Melconian, however, warns that the government ‘will have to change.’ He describes a ‘complicated dead-end where it lacks reserves, must buy dollars, must reactivate the economy, and must collapse inflation.’ That’s a sharp critique from a respected voice.

The tension is real: the model that crushed inflation is now struggling to deliver growth without breaking the exchange rate. But Melconian’s warning is his opinion, not a market consensus.

Why you should care

If you’re investing in Argentina or watching Latin America, these signals matter because they suggest the Milei economic model is entering a delicate phase—one where reserve accumulation slows, confidence dips, and election jitters start to price in.

Yet the lack of a clear opposition leader means the situation isn’t a simple ‘regime change’ play. For expats, this could mean a steadier but slower path for the peso, and for investors, it’s a reminder to watch country risk, not just headlines.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Milei economic model failing? Not necessarily. The model has crushed inflation and stabilized the economy, but it’s showing strain—central bank dollar purchases are at a 2026 low, and approval polls are weak. Economists are divided, with some warning of a ’dead-end’ and others seeing a necessary adjustment. What does the central bank’s slower dollar buying mean? It suggests the BCRA is prioritizing defending the peso over building reserves quickly. Daily purchases dropped from ~US$103 million in July to ~US$33 million in August, per TN and Ámbito, as the peso trades near its record low. Are Argentines rejecting the economic model? Polls show roughly 6 in 10 disapprove of the economic course, but no single poll asks that exact question. The opposition is not clearly benefiting, so it’s a vote of no confidence in the current path, not a surge for an alternative. How are investors reacting? Cautiously. Country risk has risen to ~470 basis points, the Merval dipped, and Infobae reports Wall Street is reducing exposure. But analysts note that global factors, like U.S. rates, also play a role, so it’s not all Argentina-specific.

Wellington’s global fund adds Sabesp to top-10 holdings as it shifts away from US equities, citing attractive valuation and growth potential in Brazil’s privatized water giant.

Global asset manager Wellington Management—with US$1.3 trillion under management—has bought shares of Brazil’s Sabesp (SBSP3), making it one of the ten largest positions in its global fund. This strategic move—Wellington buys Sabesp—comes as the firm deliberately underweights the US market, signaling confidence in Latin America’s largest water utility.

Sabesp, Sao Paulo’s water utility, has drawn a major global investor. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Why Wellington is betting on Sabesp

Laura Howenstine, Investment Director of Wellington’s Global Quality Growth strategy, explains that the fund is positioned underweight the US, overweight Europe, healthcare, and real estate. Sabesp, now a top-10 holding, fits this cautious yet selective approach, offering steady cash flows and a defensive profile that appeals in uncertain markets.

The purchase reflects a broader trend of international investors seeking value outside overvalued US equities. Sabesp’s privatization in 2024, which reduced the state’s stake from 50.3% to 18.3%, unlocked operational efficiencies and attracted strategic investors like Equatorial (EQTL3), which bought 15% for R$6.9 billion (~US$1.32 billion).

This is not just a passive index bet. Wellington’s active choice highlights a conviction that Brazil’s utility sector offers better risk-adjusted returns than many developed-market peers.

For a fund of this scale, even a small position can move markets. The fact that Sabesp made it to the top-10 list suggests the team sees multi-year upside.

The Global Quality Growth strategy’s approach is to look for businesses with durable competitive advantages. Sabesp’s monopoly-like position in São Paulo state fits that profile perfectly.

Sabesp’s financial and market position

According to an independent valuation report from July 2026, Sabesp’s market-value equity stands at R$85.42 billion (~US$16.4 billion), implying R$24.36 (~US$4.68) per share. The ADR trades around US$4.60, suggesting the market sees room for appreciation.

As the water and sanitation utility for São Paulo state, Sabesp provides essential services with predictable demand. The company’s privatization has led to improved governance and investment capacity, making it an attractive long-term holding for global funds like Wellington.

Secondary market data indicates Wellington held roughly 10.5 million Sabesp-linked shares after increasing its stake in Q1 2026, valued at an estimated US$64 million—though these figures are approximate and not officially confirmed.

That implied value per share is about 5.9% above the current ADR price, a modest but positive signal. The discount may narrow as more foreign investors become familiar with the story.

The privatization process itself was a milestone: by cutting the state’s stake to 18.3%, the company gained more independence to pursue efficiency and expansion.

This newfound flexibility is key. Sabesp can now invest in infrastructure upgrades without as much political interference, which should improve service quality and financial returns.

Why this matters for LatAm investors

For investors focused on Latin America, Wellington’s move is a powerful endorsement: a US$1.3 trillion giant sees Brazil as a safer bet than the US. It underscores the growing appeal of privatized infrastructure assets in the region, which offer stable returns and inflation protection.

As global fund flows shift, Brazilian equities—especially utility plays like Sabesp—stand to benefit. This could lift valuations across the sector, creating opportunities for both local and foreign investors looking to tap into the country’s economic recovery.

The underweight US stance is a contrarian call in a market that has been led by tech giants. Wellington’s preference for value and defensive sectors implies a rotation that could favor Brazilian assets.

If more global managers follow suit, Sabesp could see increased liquidity and a potential rerating. That would be a positive tailwind for all Brazilian utilities.

For LatAm investors, this is a signal to pay attention to companies with strong fundamentals and strategic repositioning, not just headline growth.

Brazil retail sales show mixed signals

In separate data, Brazil’s retail sector showed resilience: official IBGE figures show June retail sales rose 0.5% month-on-month, beating forecasts. The private Stone retail index also climbed 0.9% in July—a second consecutive monthly gain, hinting at steady consumer demand.

However, Stone cautioned it’s ‘still too early to talk about an improvement,’ noting the recovery is fragile. For investors, this mixed picture suggests caution, but it also reflects a potential base for growth, especially if interest rates ease further.

The positive retail data supports the idea that Brazil’s domestic economy is not collapsing, which is important for utility demand. Even if growth is slow, steady consumption means steady water usage.

Yet the fragility Stone highlights reminds us that nothing is guaranteed. Political noise and fiscal concerns could still derail the recovery.

For Sabesp, though, this is less of a concern. Water demand is inelastic, so even a weak economy would not hurt its core business much.

What this means for your portfolio

If you’re considering Brazilian exposure, Wellington’s Sabesp purchase highlights the value in privatized utilities. These assets combine essential services with improving profitability, making them a defensive anchor in a diversified portfolio.

However, remember that global funds like Wellington also hedge by underweighting the US—a sign of broader market uncertainty. You should weigh the potential for Brazilian growth against geopolitical risks and currency volatility, ideally with professional advice.

Sabesp’s valuation per share (R$24.36 ~US$4.68) suggests a modest upside from current levels, but the real story is operational improvement. As the company invests in infrastructure, long-term returns could outperform the market, especially if Brazil’s economy accelerates.

The ~5% discount from the implied fair value is not huge, but it does offer a margin of safety for patient investors. If the company meets its targets, that gap could widen.

Diversification is key, so even with a signal like this you shouldn’t put all your eggs in one basket. Combine Sabesp with other sectors or regions to manage risk.

Also, keep an eye on currency movements. A stronger real would boost returns for foreign investors, but a weaker one could offset gains.

The global context: Why Wellington is cautious on the US

Wellington’s decision to underweight the US is based on a mix of high valuations and slower growth prospects. In contrast, emerging markets like Brazil offer higher potential returns with less crowding.

For Brazilian investors, this global trend could mean more foreign capital flowing into local assets. That could strengthen the real and boost the stock market as a whole.

Ultimately, Wellington’s move is a vote of confidence in Brazil’s long-term story. When a US$1.3 trillion manager decides to buy, it’s worth paying attention.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Wellington buy Sabesp shares? Wellington sees Sabesp as a defensive, high-quality utility with strong cash flows, especially after its privatization. The fund is underweighting the US market and sees better value in Brazil, making Sabesp a top-10 holding. Is Sabesp a good investment for foreign investors? Yes, especially for those seeking stable infrastructure exposure. The independent valuation suggests fair value around R$24.36 per share, and the ADR offers easy access. However, currency risk and political factors should be considered. What does it mean to be ’underweight’ the US? Underweight means Wellington’s fund holds a smaller percentage of US stocks than its benchmark index. This is a strategic bet that other regions, like Europe and Brazil, will perform better. How has Sabesp performed since privatization? Since the 2024 privatization, Sabesp has improved efficiency and governance. The state’s stake reduced from 50.3% to 18.3%, and the company has attracted strategic investors. The valuation report from July 2026 shows a solid equity value of R$85.42 billion (~US$16.4 billion).

World.title: Banco Master pension rule reshapes Brazil’s RPPS funds
World.content:
Brazil · Pensions

Key Facts New rule: CMN Resolution 5.272/2025, issued 18 December 2025 and effective 2 February 2026, limits uncertified RPPS to federal bonds and limited payroll loans.

CMN Resolution 5.272/2025, issued 18 December 2025 and effective 2 February 2026, limits uncertified RPPS to federal bonds and limited payroll loans. 85% affected: As of July 2026, 85% of Brazil’s 2,132 RPPS lacked Pro-Gestao certification, so they face the restriction.

As of July 2026, 85% of Brazil’s 2,132 RPPS lacked Pro-Gestao certification, so they face the restriction. Pro-Gestao: A governance certification (levels I-IV) from the Ministry of Social Security; higher levels allow more investment options.

A governance certification (levels I-IV) from the Ministry of Social Security; higher levels allow more investment options. Banco Master collapse: The Central Bank liquidated Banco Master in November 2025, causing losses for many RPPS that held its bonds.

The Central Bank liquidated Banco Master in November 2025, causing losses for many RPPS that held its bonds. Master exposure: Rioprevidencia had R$2.618 billion (~US$502 million) with Master as issuer or manager; federal prosecutors found ~R$1.87 billion (~US$359 million) in Master paper across various RPPS.

Rioprevidencia had R$2.618 billion (~US$502 million) with Master as issuer or manager; federal prosecutors found ~R$1.87 billion (~US$359 million) in Master paper across various RPPS. Big-name filter: The same resolution lets RPPS use funds only if a large-scale (S1/S2) provider — like Itaú, BB, Bradesco, BTG, Caixa or XP — runs them, closing the door on Master-type small banks.

The same resolution lets RPPS use funds only if a large-scale (S1/S2) provider — like Itaú, BB, Bradesco, BTG, Caixa or XP — runs them, closing the door on Master-type small banks. Private pensions safe: PGBL/VGBL open pensions supervised by Susep/CVM are not affected by this rule.

A new CMN rule curbs risky investments for most public-servant pension funds after Banco Master’s collapse, but your private PGBL/VGBL plan is safe.

You may have seen headlines saying that 85% of Brazil’s private pensions can now only hold government bonds — but that framing is not quite right. This new Banco Master pension rule targets public-servant pension funds, known as RPPS, not your personal PGBL or VGBL plan.

New rules push Brazil’s public pension funds toward government bonds. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What exactly is the Banco Master pension rule?

The rule is CMN Resolution 5.272, issued by Brazil’s National Monetary Council (CMN) and enforced through the Central Bank. It applies to RPPS—the pension funds for municipal and state public servants—not to private open pensions.

RPPS that lack the ‘Pro-Gestao’ governance certification can now make new investments only in federal government bonds (títulos públicos) or in payroll-deductible ‘consignado’ loans, capped at 5% of assets. They can’t add new money to other assets like stocks or private credit, though they can keep existing holdings.

This is a big shift — before the rule, these funds had far more freedom.

The 24-month adjustment window gives them time to align with the new limits.

The measure — CMN Resolution 5.272/2025, issued 18 December 2025 and effective 2 February 2026 — is enforced by the CMN, not by Susep or CVM, which regulate private pensions.

The 85% claim explained

The 85% figure is often misread as a portfolio percentage — it is not.

It refers to the share of funds without Pro-Gestao certification — as of July 2026, 85% of Brazil’s 2,132 RPPS lacked it.

Because the rule restricts exactly those uncertified funds, roughly 85% of RPPS are now effectively confined to federal bonds plus limited consignado loans. That’s 1,813 funds, not 85% of all pension assets or private pensions.

It’s crucial to understand: this does not apply to PGBL/VGBL private pension plans. If you hold one of those, your plan is supervised by Susep and CVM and remains untouched.

Why did this happen? The Banco Master collapse

The trigger was the Central Bank’s liquidation of Banco Master in November 2025. Many RPPS had invested heavily in Master’s subordinated ‘letras financeiras’ (bank bonds) and linked fund units, and those investments turned sour.

For example, São Roque Prev in São Paulo had R$113 million (~US$21.7 million) tied to the Master group — R$93 million (~US$17.9 million) in bank bonds plus R$20 million (~US$3.8 million) in a linked real-estate fund.

Rio de Janeiro’s Rioprevidencia had a court freeze of up to R$135.15 million (~US$25.9 million). The state audit court (TCE-RJ) found Master as issuer or manager across R$2.618 billion (~US$502 million) of Rioprevidencia money, including R$970 million (~US$186 million) in Master bank bonds.

Maceió’s IPREV in Alagoas had R$97 million (~US$18.6 million) under federal investigation. Federal prosecutors estimate roughly R$1.87 billion (~US$359 million) was placed in Master paper across various RPPS between October 2023 and December 2024.

Note: there is no single consolidated national loss figure. Cases are still being investigated, and numbers are preliminary.

What is Pro-Gestao and how does it help?

Pro-Gestao is a governance certification created in 2015 by the Ministry of Social Security. It has levels I to IV, with each level requiring stricter governance, risk management, and transparency practices.

RPPS with higher certification levels (I to IV) keep graduated access to private credit, bank bonds (up to 20%), stocks, multimarket funds, real-estate funds, and foreign assets. So the more certified a fund is, the more freedom it has to invest.

A recent portaria (SRPC/MPS 1.183, July 2026) created new criteria for levels II and III, making it easier for funds to climb the certification ladder if they meet the requirements.

The idea is to reward good governance — if a fund shows it can handle risk responsibly, it earns more investment options.

The 85% without certification tend to lack the resources or the will to meet these standards quickly.

The big-provider filter and extra guardrails

CMN Resolution 5.272/2025 adds another guardrail on top of the bond limits, and it took effect on 2 February 2026.

RPPS may now put money into an investment fund only if that fund has at least one large-scale service provider — an administrator or manager in the Central Bank’s top S1 or S2 tiers, such as Itaú, Banco do Brasil, Bradesco, BTG, Caixa or XP.

Banco Master sat in the smaller S3 tier — too small to clear this new bar.

In plain terms, a fund run only by a small institution like Master can no longer receive RPPS money — a direct response to the losses.

The filter is meant to keep public servants’ retirement savings away from thinly capitalized players. It is one more layer of protection layered onto the bond restriction.

Why this matters for LatAm investors and expats

If you hold a Brazilian private pension — a PGBL or VGBL — this rule does not restrict your plan at all.

Your plan stays flexible and is still overseen by Susep and CVM, not the CMN, so you can breathe easy.

However, if you are a public servant in a Brazilian municipality or state, your pension fund may be affected if it lacks certification. Check with your fund to see its Pro-Gestao status.

For investors in Brazilian markets, this rule signals a broader regulatory push toward safer, more conservative public pension investments. That could reduce demand for riskier assets like small-bank bonds, potentially affecting yields.

The Banco Master case is a cautionary tale about the importance of governance and due diligence. It highlights how concentrated bets on a single institution can go wrong.

For expats and LatAm investors, keeping an eye on regulatory changes like this helps understand the risk landscape in Brazil. It’s not about your private pension, but it shows how the government is tightening oversight to protect public funds.

In short: your PGBL/VGBL is safe. The rule is about public funds, and it’s a direct result of real losses—so it’s a positive step for financial stability.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the new rule affect my PGBL or VGBL private pension? No. The rule applies only to RPPS—public-servant pension funds. PGBL and VGBL open pensions supervised by Susep and CVM are not affected. What is Pro-Gestao certification? It’s a governance certification created in 2015 by Brazil’s Ministry of Social Security, with levels I to IV. Higher levels reflect stronger risk management and unlock more investment options. Why did the Central Bank liquidate Banco Master? Banco Master was liquidated in November 2025 after financial troubles. Many RPPS had invested heavily in its bonds, leading to losses and prompting the new rule. What are consignado loans? Consignado loans are payroll-deductible loans where payments come directly from the borrower’s salary or pension. The new rule allows RPPS to invest up to 5% of assets in these loans.

World.title: Casas Bahia Loss: Q2 Net Loss R$10.1bn, EY Doubts
World.content:
Brazil · Retail

Key Facts Net loss: R$10.117 billion (converted as of Aug 15, 2026, ~US$1.94 billion) in 2T26, up from R$555 million (~US$107 million) a year ago.

R$10.117 billion (converted as of Aug 15, 2026, ~US$1.94 billion) in 2T26, up from R$555 million (~US$107 million) a year ago. Non-cash items: R$9.1 billion (~US$1.75 billion) in write-offs, including R$5.7bn (~US$1.09bn) in deferred tax assets and R$971m (~US$186m) in goodwill.

R$9.1 billion (~US$1.75 billion) in write-offs, including R$5.7bn (~US$1.09bn) in deferred tax assets and R$971m (~US$186m) in goodwill. Adjusted loss: R$978 million (~US$188 million), excluding one-offs.

R$978 million (~US$188 million), excluding one-offs. Revenue: R$6.977 billion (~US$1.34 billion), up 1.6% YoY; adjusted EBITDA R$518M (~US$99M), down 9.4%.

R$6.977 billion (~US$1.34 billion), up 1.6% YoY; adjusted EBITDA R$518M (~US$99M), down 9.4%. Going concern: EY declined to conclude on financials, citing the R$11.2bn (~US$2.15bn) first-half loss and negative equity of R$8.27bn (~US$1.59bn).

EY declined to conclude on financials, citing the R$11.2bn (~US$2.15bn) first-half loss and negative equity of R$8.27bn (~US$1.59bn). Restructuring: Company evaluating new out-of-court or judicial restructuring; 298 stores closing.

Company evaluating new out-of-court or judicial restructuring; 298 stores closing. Share reaction: BHIA3 is down about 80% in 2026 to roughly R$0.65 (~US$0.12); markets were closed over the weekend, so the first reaction to these results comes when B3 opens Monday.

Brazilian retailer Casas Bahia reports a massive R$10.1bn (~US$1.94bn) quarterly loss, EY withholds its opinion, and the company considers another restructuring.

The Casas Bahia loss for the second quarter of 2026 was staggering — the retailer (BHIA3) posted a net loss of R$10.117 billion (~US$1.94 billion, converted at USD/BRL 5.21 as of Aug 15, 2026), a roughly 18-fold jump from the R$555 million (~US$107 million) loss a year earlier. The headline number was inflated by R$9.1 billion (~US$1.75 billion) in non-cash, one-off items tied to its transformation plan, so the adjusted loss came to R$978 million (~US$188 million).

Casas Bahia is closing nearly a third of its stores as part of its turnaround plan. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)
