Why the Casas Bahia loss is worse than it looks

Even after stripping out the one-offs, the adjusted loss of R$978 million (~US$188 million) is still a sharp deterioration from the R$555 million (~US$107 million) adjusted loss a year ago. Revenue inched up 1.6% to R$6.977 billion (~US$1.34 billion), but profitability slipped—adjusted EBITDA fell 9.4% to R$518 million (~US$99 million), and the margin dropped from 8.3% to 7.4%.

Gross profit actually improved, rising 10.9% to R$2.293 billion (~US$440 million) with a margin of 32.9% (+2.8 percentage points). The problem is not sales; it’s the weight of past debts and the cost of restructuring.

The company’s turnaround plan, dubbed the ‘Transformation Plan,’ began in 2023 when CEO Renato Horta Franklin and CFO Elcio Mitsuhiro Ito took the helm. That plan initially focused on operational fixes, but the second quarter of 2026 brought what the company calls ‘Phase 2,’ which involves more drastic measures like store closures and layoffs.

EY refuses to sign off: a red flag for investors

Auditor Ernst & Young (EY) declined to issue a conclusion on the quarterly financial statements, citing material uncertainty about Casas Bahia’s ability to continue as a going concern. EY pointed to the R$11.2 billion (~US$2.15 billion) first-half loss, negative net working capital, and negative shareholders’ equity of R$8.27 billion (~US$1.59 billion).

In its review report dated Aug 15, 2026, EY said it was “unable to perform sufficient review procedures to support a conclusion” and that the uncertainty “may cast significant doubt” on the company’s future. For investors, this is about as loud an alarm as an auditor can sound without saying “bankrupt.”

What does ‘going concern’ mean in plain terms? It is an accounting idea — a company is assumed to keep operating for the foreseeable future, usually at least a year.

When an auditor questions that assumption, it means they see a real risk the company might not survive. That does not necessarily mean bankruptcy is imminent, but it makes raising money or refinancing debt much harder.

What the R$9.1bn non-cash charges mean

The bulk of the loss comes from a R$5.7 billion (~US$1.09 billion) write-off of deferred tax assets—a paper move that doesn’t affect cash but wipes out future tax benefits. Add a R$971 million (~US$186 million) goodwill impairment and R$1.8 billion (~US$345 million) in provisions for store closures, contract revisions, and staff reorganization.

These charges are part of the company’s ‘Phase 2’ transformation plan, which includes closing 298 stores—about 28.7% of its network—and cutting 1,900 jobs, roughly 6.7% of the workforce.

The write-off of deferred tax assets is especially telling. It means the company no longer believes it will earn enough future profit to use those tax credits.

The charge does not drain cash today. But it signals management’s own doubt about the recovery.

Casas Bahia mulls another restructuring

The company says it is evaluating options to reorganize its capital structure, including a new out-of-court or judicial restructuring — though nothing has been formally filed yet. This would follow a previous out-of-court deal in 2024 that renegotiated about R$4 billion (~US$0.79 billion) in debt.

CEO Renato Horta Franklin and CFO Elcio Mitsuhiro Ito, both in place since 2023, are leading the turnaround effort. Net debt stood at R$1.2 billion (~US$230 million) at the end of June — small next to earnings, at just 0.5 times adjusted EBITDA over the last twelve months.

The trouble is the equity hole. With shareholders’ equity deep in the red, raising fresh money becomes very hard.

A judicial restructuring — known in Brazil as ‘recuperação judicial’ — would give the company court protection from creditors while it renegotiates debts. An out-of-court option is a private deal with creditors, but it needs their consent and offers less protection.

The fact that the company is even weighing these paths shows how serious things have become.

Delayed results: what took so long?

The second-quarter results were originally scheduled for Aug 12, but the release was pushed to Aug 14 and then to the weekend. The final report was published early Sunday, Aug 16, after markets closed, which is highly unusual for a major retailer.

Such delays often point to the need for more time to prepare disclosures. Here, the holdup likely reflects the sheer complexity of accounting for the huge write-offs and the auditor’s careful review.

Investors dislike surprises, and the wait added to the anxiety before the release.

When the numbers finally landed, markets were already closed for the weekend. So the first real reaction to these results will come only when B3 opens on Monday.

For long-term holders, it has been a brutal year.

What this means for you

If you live in or invest in Latin America, Casas Bahia is a bellwether for Brazilian retail and consumer confidence—and this result is a stark warning. The chain’s troubles show how quickly a household name can unravel under debt and operational stress, even when revenue holds up.

For shareholders, the stock has already lost about 80% of its value in 2026, sliding to roughly R$0.65 (~US$0.12). Because markets were closed over the weekend, the first reaction to these numbers will come when B3 opens on Monday.

If you are a supplier and Casas Bahia enters a court restructuring, you may have to renegotiate payment terms or even accept less than you are owed. If you are an employee, the 1,900 layoffs are a harsh reminder of how volatile retail can be.

And if you are just a shopper, watch for clearance sales as stores close — while knowing service may slip in the shuffle.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Casas Bahia’s net loss in Q2 2026? Casas Bahia reported a net loss of R$10.117 billion (~US$1.94 billion) for the second quarter of 2026, up from R$555 million (~US$107 million) a year earlier. Why did EY decline to issue a conclusion on Casas Bahia’s financials? EY cited material uncertainty about the company’s ability to continue as a going concern, pointing to the R$11.2 billion (~US$2.15 billion) first-half loss, negative net working capital, and negative shareholders’ equity of R$8.27 billion (~US$1.59 billion). How many stores is Casas Bahia closing? The company is closing 298 stores, representing about 28.7% of its total network, and cutting approximately 1,900 jobs, or 6.7% of its workforce. Is Casas Bahia considering a new restructuring? Yes, Casas Bahia says it is evaluating options to reorganize its capital structure, including a new out-of-court or judicial restructuring, but has not yet filed anything.

World.title: Brazil 2026 Election Campaign Kicks Off with Lula, Bolsonaro
World.content:
Brazil · Politics

Key Facts Campaign opens: Brazil’s 2026 election campaign officially began Sunday, August 16, after the August 15 registration deadline.

Brazil’s 2026 election campaign officially began Sunday, August 16, after the August 15 registration deadline. Lula’s launch: He held his first rally at Vila Euclides stadium, site of his 1970s union activities, and removed his hat citing cancer treatment.

He held his first rally at Vila Euclides stadium, site of his 1970s union activities, and removed his hat citing cancer treatment. Flavio’s focus: Bolsonaro opened at Copacabana wearing a bulletproof vest, citing over 1,800 death threats and a planned attack.

Bolsonaro opened at Copacabana wearing a bulletproof vest, citing over 1,800 death threats and a planned attack. Caiado’s start: Goias governor launched with a Mass and car caravan, positioning himself as opposition to Lula.

Goias governor launched with a Mass and car caravan, positioning himself as opposition to Lula. Zema’s bid: Minas Gerais governor also began his campaign on August 16, though details remain general.

Minas Gerais governor also began his campaign on August 16, though details remain general. Marcal’s status: Pablo Marcal registered despite ineligibility, with assets of R$7.4 billion (~US$1.42 billion), pending court ruling.

From São Bernardo to Copacabana, candidates hit the trail for the 2026 race, with Marcal’s sub judice bid adding intrigue.

Brazil’s 2026 election campaign officially kicked off on August 16, with the first day of vote-seeking after Saturday’s registration deadline. The Brazil 2026 election campaign features an emotional launch by President Lula and a security-focused rally by Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, setting the stage for a fierce race.

Lula at his campaign opening in Sao Bernardo do Campo. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Lula’s Emotional Start at Vila Euclides

President Lula chose the Estadio Municipal 1o de Maio in Sao Bernardo do Campo, where he led metalworkers’ assemblies in the 1970s, to open his re-election bid. He wore a hat and explained he had radiotherapy for skin cancer, saying: “I had radiotherapy on my head to treat a skin cancer, and I can’t get sun on my head, but I’m going to defy my health and take off the hat for you.”

He then removed the hat to cheers, a symbolic gesture at a site steeped in labor history. The venue recalls the ABC strikes that helped launch his political career, underscoring his working-class roots.

The event targeted women and evangelicals, with Women’s Minister Cida Gonçalves, Senate candidates Benedita da Silva, Simone Tebet, and Marina Silva, and First Lady Janja on stage or cited. Singer-pastor Kleber Lucas performed “Deus Cuida de Mim,” a gospel hit that resonated with the crowd.

Lula emphasized gender respect, stating that men must respect women “not as servants.” He also urged support for allied congressional candidates to build a majority for a possible fourth term.

In his speech, he defended domestic industrialization of minerals and rare earths, framing it against the US-China dispute. This policy push aims to boost Brazil’s strategic autonomy and economic resilience, according to Folha, Poder360, O Globo, and R7.

Flavio Bolsonaro’s Security-Focused Launch

Senator Flavio Bolsonaro opened his campaign at Praia de Copacabana, a traditional bolsonarista stage, wearing a bulletproof vest and broadcasting live. He said he had received more than 1,800 death threats and that Senate police on Saturday detained a person planning an attack on him in Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais.

The choice of Copacabana is rich in political symbolism, often hosting massive rallies for the Bolsonaro family. The bulletproof vest was a stark visual reminder of the security threats he claims to face.

He promised to classify the PCC, Comando Vermelho, and militias as terrorist organizations if elected, putting security at the center of his campaign. This hardline stance aims to appeal to voters concerned about rising crime in Brazilian cities.

Present with him were his wife Fernanda, PL figures Douglas Ruas and Daniella Marques, and running mate Alfredo Gaspar. Their presence signaled party unity, as reported by Valor, Estadao, UOL, and G1.

The launch leaned heavily on public safety, a contrast with Lula’s stress on industrial policy and social themes the same day. His platform, as presented in Copacabana, did not dwell on the economy or state oil giant Petrobras.

Caiado and Zema: Opposition Launches

Governor Ronaldo Caiado of Goias launched with a Mass and a car caravan through municipalities ending in Luziania, positioning himself as opposition to Lula. The religious opening aimed to shore up conservative support, a key base for the opposition.

The caravan passed through towns in the region bordering the federal district before wrapping up in Luziania, according to Folha. Caiado framed himself squarely against the Lula government as he opened his run.

Romeu Zema (Novo) also began his campaign on August 16, in Montes Claros, Minas Gerais, where he serves as governor. He launched at the Mercado Municipal in the city.

Both governors began their runs in the states they lead, a common tactic for building on local support. Their entries add more names to a crowded field of challengers to the incumbent.

Pablo Marcal’s Sub Judice Candidacy

Pablo Marcal registered his candidacy with the TSE on Saturday, despite being ineligible until 2032 under TRE-SP rulings, with his status marked “awaiting judgment.” He declared assets of about R$7.418 billion (~US$1.42 billion), mostly fixed-income, including a plot worth R$490 million (~US$94 million) at the current exchange rate of R$5.21 per dollar.

The declared fortune sits mostly in fixed-income holdings, with a large land parcel in Santana de Parnaiba making up part of the rest, according to G1. The figure is far larger than what he reported in his 2024 mayoral run.

His ineligibility stems from TRE-SP rulings tied to his 2024 São Paulo mayoral campaign, with an appeal rejected on August 5 by a 7-0 vote. Whether he can actually campaign now rests with the TSE, which must still judge the registration.

Because the candidacy is sub judice, it remains open to challenge and could be struck down before voting begins. For now, his name is on the list but his status is unsettled.

Why This Matters for Investors in Brazil 2026 Election Campaign

As an investor or expat in Latin America, you should watch this race closely because the outcome could reshape Brazil’s economic policy, especially around Petrobras and oil. Political risk is real: a shift in government might alter energy pricing, regulatory stability, and fiscal discipline, all of which move markets.

Lula’s push for mineral industrialization could increase state involvement in strategic sectors, potentially raising costs for private investors. In contrast, Bolsonaro’s security agenda might divert funds from social programs, impacting consumer demand.

Marcal’s contested candidacy is a reminder that Brazil’s courts can reshape the field even after registration closes, adding legal uncertainty to the mix. Watching how the TSE rules will tell you how settled the ballot really is.

The election’s outcome will also influence Brazil’s international relations, affecting trade and investment flows. Keep an eye on Petrobras-related news and congressional dynamics, as these are key indicators of policy direction.

With the campaign now officially underway, expect volatility tied to polls and policy promises. Diversification and risk assessment will be crucial for those with exposure to Brazilian assets.

Frequently Asked Questions

When did Brazil’s 2026 election campaign officially start? The campaign officially opened on Sunday, August 16, 2026, the first day candidates could legally ask for votes. This followed Saturday’s registration deadline at the TSE. What was notable about Lula’s campaign launch? Lula held his launch at Vila Euclides stadium in Sao Bernardo do Campo, where he once led strikes. He removed his hat despite skin cancer treatment, courting women and evangelicals with a gospel performance. Why did Flavio Bolsonaro wear a bulletproof vest? Bolsonaro wore the vest at his Copacabana rally, citing over 1,800 death threats and a recent planned attack. This underscored his security-focused platform. Is Pablo Marcal eligible to run? Marcal registered but is ineligible until 2032 under court rulings. His candidacy is sub judice, pending a final TSE decision, despite declaring R$7.4 billion (~US$1.42 billion) in assets.

World.title: Colombia earthquake death toll reaches 289
World.content:
Colombia · Emergency

Key Facts Magnitude: 7.4 earthquake struck near San José del Palmar, Chocó, at 07:34 local time on 10 August.

7.4 earthquake struck near San José del Palmar, Chocó, at 07:34 local time on 10 August. Death toll: 289 confirmed dead as of 16 August, down from 294 after cross-checks.

289 confirmed dead as of 16 August, down from 294 after cross-checks. Missing: 143 people remain missing, with search teams winding down.

143 people remain missing, with search teams winding down. Affected: 185,016 people affected across 450 municipalities in 15 departments.

185,016 people affected across 450 municipalities in 15 departments. Homes: 26,945 destroyed and 127,557 damaged.

26,945 destroyed and 127,557 damaged. Private aid: Gilinski family donates COP 150 billion (~US$48 million) for rebuilding in Cali.

Rescuers wind down the search as Colombia’s 7.4-magnitude quake claims 289 lives — with 143 still missing and reconstruction efforts gaining momentum.

The Colombia earthquake death toll stands at 289, according to the latest UNGRD update on 16 August, a slight revision from earlier figures after cross-checks with the Fiscalía and Medicina Legal. Over 185,000 people are affected across 15 departments, with 143 still missing.

The 7.4-magnitude quake struck near San José del Palmar in Chocó on 10 August, devastating parts of Cali, Pereira, and the Eje Cafetero. Search-and-rescue operations are winding down as the country shifts focus to sheltering the displaced and rebuilding.

Rescue teams work at a collapsed building in Cali following the 7.4-magnitude earthquake. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The quake’s impact

The earthquake hit at 07:34 local time on Monday 10 August, with an epicenter 5 kilometers south of San José del Palmar at a depth of about 110 kilometers. The violent shaking caused buildings to collapse across several departments, with Cali and the Eje Cafetero suffering the worst damage.

According to UNGRD, 289 people have died, 4,187 are injured, and 143 are missing. Officials revised the death toll down from 294 after reconciling records with the Fiscalía, Medicina Legal, and rescue agencies, though some international reports still cite the earlier figure.

Infrastructure damage is staggering: 26,945 homes destroyed and 127,557 damaged, leaving thousands of families displaced. The quake also affected 285 health centers, 2,838 educational facilities, and 3,782 community centers, disrupting essential services for vulnerable communities.

Additionally, 66 buildings collapsed across the affected departments, adding to the structural toll. The damage disrupted essential services for vulnerable communities.

Rescue and relief efforts

Rescue teams are working around the clock, but operations are winding down as hopes of finding survivors fade. The government’s “Fondo Milagro” emergency fund, created under the Economic Emergency declaration, is channeling resources to the hardest-hit areas, including rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

By the latest official tally, rescuers had pulled hundreds of people alive from the debris — 354 in the days after the quake. Teams from across the country converged on Cali, Pereira and the Eje Cafetero, where the collapses were most severe.

On 15 August, Medellín hosted a benefit concert, “Colombia, Medellín Te Quiere,” at the Centro de Eventos La Macarena, raising COP 6 billion (~US$1.9 million) and 31 tonnes of food and hygiene aid. The event featured 25 artists and was backed by Mayor Federico Gutiérrez.

Officials are now focusing on providing shelter and psychosocial support for displaced families. The UNGRD is coordinating with local governments to ensure aid reaches remote villages in Chocó and Valle del Cauca.

Remarkably, a 3-year-old girl was pulled alive from the rubble in Cali well beyond the critical 72-hour survival window. Her rescue offered a rare moment of hope amid the devastation, even as Reuters reported the broader aid effort expanding nearly a week on.

The death toll may still change as debris removal progresses and more bodies are recovered.

Private sector response

The business community has mobilized quickly to support reconstruction. The Gilinski family, led by one of Colombia’s richest men, Jaime Gilinski, announced a COP 150 billion (~US$48 million) donation on 16 August to rebuild hospitals and schools in Cali, his hometown.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the pledge, which underscores the private sector’s commitment to recovery. Overall, businesses have raised more than COP 150 billion (~US$48 million) for reconstruction efforts, providing critical capital for rebuilding.

This private funding will complement government programs, including the Fondo Milagro and rent subsidies. The scale of donations signals confidence in the country’s resilience and long-term recovery prospects.

In addition to the Gilinski donation, small and medium enterprises are contributing through in-kind aid and volunteer efforts. The collective response highlights a national solidarity that could accelerate rebuilding.

What it means for investors

For investors and expats in Latin America, this earthquake underscores the region’s seismic risk, but also its resilience. Colombia’s government has declared an economic emergency, creating a framework to manage reconstruction and stabilize affected regions.

Crucially, Colombia has asked the US to suspend 12.5% tariffs to aid recovery, a move that could support trade relations. Washington’s response is pending, but such a suspension would ease financial pressures on the rebuilding process.

Ports reported no major damage, ensuring logistics remain operational—vital for exports and imports. This resilience protects supply chains and maintains investor confidence in Colombia’s economic stability.

Cali, a major economic hub, is set for significant rebuilding, which could create opportunities in construction, engineering, and related sectors. The influx of private donations signals confidence in the country’s recovery trajectory.

Looking ahead

The UNGRD continues to update its figures as search-and-rescue operations conclude. The death toll may still change as teams reach more collapsed structures, but recovery is now the priority.

The earlier Saturday 15 August balance had cited 14,493 homes destroyed and 81,506 damaged, before the Sunday reconciliation revised those numbers upward. Authorities are focused on providing shelter and medical care for the 185,000 affected people, while planning for long-term reconstruction.

The path to recovery will be challenging, but unified public and private efforts offer hope for a swifter comeback.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the magnitude of the Colombia earthquake? The earthquake had a magnitude of 7.4, according to the USGS, striking near San José del Palmar in Chocó department on 10 August 2026. How many people died in the Colombia earthquake? As of 16 August, the UNGRD reports 289 deaths, though earlier international reports cited up to 294. The toll may change as rescue efforts continue. How can I help the victims of the Colombia earthquake? Donations can be made through the government’s Fondo Milagro or to recognized NGOs. The business sector has also raised significant funds, with the Gilinski family donating COP 150 billion (~US$48 million). Was there any damage to Colombia’s ports? No major damage was reported at key port facilities, according to authorities, allowing logistics to continue without major disruptions.
