World.title: Ukraine launches large-scale drone attack on Russian military and energy infrastructure
World.content:
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones across Russia targeting military industries and energy facilities on Sunday, killing at least six people in one of Kyiv’s largest aerial attacks since Russia's full-scale invasion of the country began in early 2022.

 

Kyiv has stepped up its attacks on Russia this year with long-range missiles and drones. Aside from hitting military and energy targets, it has also increasingly targeted Wildberries depots, burning billions of dollars’ worth of merchandise belonging to the Russian online retail giant.

Ukraine also came under attack overnight into Sunday, with two people were killed at a steel plant in Kryvyi Rih, one of the country's largest steel factories.

Strikes also killed two people in the Zaporizhzhia region and one in Sumy.

Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelenskyy took to social media to give an update on the response to the damage caused by Russian strikes.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gives an update on the damage caused by overnight strikes

Zelenskyy reiterated that Russia has been using North Korean ballistic missiles on Ukraine, and urged that European missile interceptors should be mobilised to help Ukraine rather than "be allowed to sit in storage".

In total, the Ukrainian president said more than 1,500 drones have been launched into Ukraine by Russia over the past week.

In Russia, authorities said five people died in the southern region of Rostov.

Two were killed in Belgorod and Moscow, where the Ukrainian military said it was targeting military factories and energy facilities.

Russia's military said it had destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones, 600 of which it claimed were heading for the capital.

World.title: Europe continues to battle wildfires as Belgium sees biggest blaze in recorded history
World.content:
Wildfires are continuing to burn across several parts of Europe, with firefighters battling major blazes in Belgium, Germany, France, Croatia, Spain and Greece amid persistent heat and dry conditions.

 

A fire in Belgium's High Fens nature reserve has more than doubled in size in 24 hours, to around 3,000 hectares. The fire, which started two days ago, is now the largest wildfire in Belgium's recorded history.

Authorities in the country's Wallonia region said more than 250 firefighters and other emergency service workers were deployed on Saturday night. The reserve is particularly vulnerable to wildfires because of its extensive peatlands and pine forests, which have been dried out by prolonged hot weather

In a post on social media, Belgium's unified defence force said it had sent personnel and vehicles to support firefighters.

Belgian defence forces have assisted firefighters to combat the spread of the fires

Firefighters from neighbouring Germany and Luxembourg have also been sent to help contain the fire, which is heading towards the border with Germany. Local farmers have also been assisting with the blaze.

Belgium activated the EU Civil Protection Mechanism on Saturday, which brought in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from Sweden, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic.

The EU's Civil Protection & Humanitarian Aid has deployed firefighting aircraft from across the continent to support Belgian fire crews

On Saturday afternoon, some residents in Belgium’s Liège province were asked to evacuate their homes. Local media reports that 600 people had been asked to leave, and that a rest shelter had been set up in a gymnasium in the neighbouring Malmedy municipality.

Across the border inside Germany, emergency services made significant progress in fighting a fire in the Hürtgen forest that forced evacuations on Friday. Around 2,000 people who had to leave the village of Gey were able to return home on Saturday evening, German news agency dpa reported.

In France, authorities say there were no major flare-ups overnight as they continue to tackle large-scale fires in the southwestern Landes region. More than 1,700 hectares have been scorched since Thursday, mostly pine forests. French media reports that 550 firefighters, assisted by military personnel and six water-bombing aircraft are in attendance. The fire remains out of control.

Another fire in the northeast of the country has begun to improve. 100 hectares have burned in the Ardennes region. The situation had been described as "unprecedented in the recent history", according to the deputy director of the Ardennes fire service, David Gouzou.

In Croatia, four people have been arrested on suspicion of starting wildfires on the coastline. Fires ripped through pine forests and olive groves amid high temperatures and droughts.

In Greece, fire crews have spent a second day fighting an outbreak in a forest on the island of Skyros. The local mayor told media he believed the fire would be fully extinguished within a day.

Authorities in Spain's Aragon deployed what they called the largest firefighting arsenal in the region's history as French reinforcements were due to help contain a wildfire that has threatened a 1,000-year-old monastery.

The fire, which broke out just over a week ago in its Huesca municipality of Las Peñas de Riglos continued to spread, affecting an area of ​​up to 16,600 hectares. Windy conditions have caused the blaze to spread further, hindering efforts to contain it.

World.title: Taliban mark five-year anniversary of regaining power in Afghanistan
World.content:
On the fifth anniversary since regaining power in Afghanistan after US troops withdrew from the country, the Taliban celebrated what they call 'restored stability and an end to decades of conflict'.

 

Thousands of Afghans gathered on the streets of Kabul on Saturday in celebration, with cars draped in flags. Outside the former US embassy, a parade of athletes took place, featuring only men due to women being banned from participating in sport.

Celebrations were also held in other Afghan provinces, with Taliban flags and posters showing slogans that praise the Taliban’s return to power.

Celebrations in Kabul to mark five years of Taliban rule since the US withdrawal AP Photo/Nava Jamshidi. Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Five years on, some countries hold unofficial relations with the Taliban administration, though only Russia has formally recognised it as Afghanistan's legitimate government.

On Saturday's anniversary, Zia Ahmad Takal, a Taliban foreign ministry spokesman, invited more countries to "invest, and make extensive use of the available economic opportunities" in Afghanistan.

A worsening humanitarian crisis

In a video message posted to social media, the United Nations's special rapporteur on the human rights situation in Afghanistan, Richard Bennett, said the country was undergoing a deep human rights crisis.

UN Special Rapporteur Richard Bennett on the human rights situation in Afghanistan

UNESCO, the UN’s education and culture agency, estimates that some 2.4 million girls have been excluded from secondary education. The UN World Food Program said child malnutrition has reached critical levels in a third of Afghanistan’s provinces and is expected to worsen due to funding shortfalls.

Almost immediately after taking power in 2021, the Taliban defied promises to allow women to access education and employment, imposing a ban on girls’ education beyond the sixth grade and later banning higher education for women altogether

Now, women are severely restricted from public spaces, and are banned from areas including like parks and gyms. They are outright banned from taking part in sports and travelling to other locations without a male present.

The Taliban’s treatment of women and girls remains one of the main barriers to wider international recognition of its government.

The withdrawal of US troops

The Taliban took power in 2021, after US and allies withdrew following a war lasting two decades and costing an estimated $1 trillion, according to then-US President Joe Biden that year.

The withdrawal led to chaotic scenes at Kabul airport as crowds of people tried to flee the country in desperation.

Hundreds gather near a US military transport plane at the international airport in Kabul as the US withdraws in 2021 (AP Photo/Shekib Rahmani) Copyright 2021 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

In a statement over the weekend, the French Foreign Ministry reaffirmed its solidarity with Afghan citizens, insisting there would be no normalisation of the Taliban rule as long as they do not respect their international obligations for the upholding of human rights, the fight against terrorism and inclusive governance.

In a statement of its own earlier in the week, the European Union reiterated its position that it "does not recognise or legitimise the Taliban-run de facto authorities but it maintains operational contact with them on its core values and interests, including women’s and girls’ rights."

Nevertheless, EU officials and Taliban representatives met in Brussels in June to discuss speeding up the deportation of Afghan migrants to the country, in a move that was criticised as "normalisation" of ties with the regime.

World.title: In Turkey, one of the world's longest conflicts reaches a turning point
World.content:
Turkey stands on the threshold of closing a conflict spanning almost 50 years, after the Turkish parliament this week passed a law allowing exiled Kurdish militants to return home and rejoin society. The legislation aims to end the war with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), which has battled the Turkish state for independence since 1984.

Advertising

On Monday, legislators voted 468-88 in favour of a law detailing how the PKK will lay down arms, disband and guide most members back into civilian life.

Many see this legislation as a turning point after decades of bloodshed.

“This law in question is going to make a giant contribution,” predicts sociologist Mesut Yegen of the Diyarbakir-based Kurdish Studies Center.

“If the PKK militants are convinced that they can be safe in Turkey, it's estimated that some 15,000 people in Europe, in Syria, in Iraq and in the prisons in Turkey are going to be either released or are going to be able to come back home.”

The PKK leadership, based primarily in Iraq, is not covered by the legislation. Nor is the group's founder and leader Abdullah Ocalan, imprisoned since 1999 in a Turkish jail.

He initiated the peace process and last year called for the disarmament and dissolution of the PKK.

People hold a photograph of Abdullah Ocalan, the jailed leader of the militant Kurdish group PKK, in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Hope, caution

Istanbul, now the city's with the world’s largest Kurdish population, became a sanctuary in the 1990s as hundreds of thousands fled the violence raging in Turkey's southeast. At the conflict’s peak, the Turkish army destroyed villages in relentless scorched-earth campaigns.

In Istanbul's Bagcilar district, home to a vibrant Kurdish community, conversations reveal a fragile mix of hope and caution.

“This law seems good for the honour of the Kurds and to stop bloodshed,” said 31-year-old Ahmet, who only wanted to be identified by his first name. “Mothers should not shed tears anymore.”

But others were more wary. “The state has been delaying our rights for decades; I do not believe this process will be different,” said Kava, who also preferred not to give his full name. “I do not trust an arrangement in which Kurds do not have legal status.”

Kurds make up around a fifth of Turkey’s population, but are not legally recognised as a minority.

Emotions appear equally divided among Turks. “If they’re agreeing to live under the Turkish flag and love our country, that’s fine – let them,” said 51-year-old Mehmet Tas.

But 40-year-old Ertugral Zengin is unconvinced. “They committed a crime – and now they are to be pardoned? Do I want something like that? No, I won’t accept it.”

PKK ends 40-year fight but doubts remain about the next steps

Political momentum

The decades-long conflict has claimed 40,000 lives and forced more than 3 million people from their homes.

While major political parties support the peace process, hardline nationalist groups remain staunchly opposed, insisting it rewards a PKK they see as already defeated.

The process hinges on the laborious task of disarming the PKK and verifying its weapons are gone.

Maintaining the current political momentum is vital, warns Asli Aydintasbas, a Turkey expert at the Brookings Institution, a think tank in Washington DC.

“If this drags on, political support for the legislation and for the return of former PKK members, seen by many Turks as terrorists, would become politically problematic for the government. Timing and moving fast is very important to achieve reconciliation,” she says.

The government is expected to face growing pressure to address Kurdish rights, including Kurdish-language education in schools and local autonomy, along with broader democratic reforms.

Social media buzzes with questions: how can PKK members walk free while critics of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan remain behind bars?

Kurdish demonstrators in Diyarbakir, Turkey, on 27 February 2025. © AP - Metin Yoksu

Peace or politics? Turkey’s fragile path to ending a decades-long conflict

Yegen warns that since the new legislation fails to address Kurdish rights and democratisation reforms, the government needs to move swiftly.

“The fact that these two issues are not touched upon by the law has created many doubts on both Kurdish and Turkish sides about whether disarmament will be the government's only agenda,” he says.

For Erdogan, steering the peace process to success could secure the vital Kurdish vote in the 2028 elections. Yet extending Kurdish cultural rights risks alienating Turkish nationalists, and relaxing pressure on the opposition brings its own perils as their electoral strength grows.

For now, the negotiations present a rare window for reconciliation and lasting peace.

World.title: Italy: Thieves steal key Renaissance paintings in Sicily
World.content:
Four Renaissance paintings by Antonello da Messina were stolen from his Sicilian hometown on Saturday after surviving earthquakes and centuries of history. Crooks took them while locals celebrated a religious holiday.

Criminals have once again targeted a small regional museum to steal priceless artworks on public display, this time in Messina, Sicily.

Local authorities say robbers bypassed alarm and security systems at the Regional Museum of Messina (MuMe), Italy, around 10:00 p.m. (2000 GMT) on Saturday evening as the city celebrated the high point of its "Ferragosto" summer holiday, the Catholic Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Thieves were able to make off with several panels painted by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina, the most important artist ever born on the island of Sicily.

Three of the five surviving panels from Antonello's 1473 "San Gregorio Polyptych" were taken in the robbery as well as a smaller, double-sided panel locked in an armored display case.

"We are devastated by what happened. They were some of Antonello da Messina's most important and best-known works. It is a tremendous loss for the museum, the city, the community and the art world," MuMe Director Marisa Mercurio told Italy's ANSA news agency.

Messina Mayor Federico Basile called the theft "deeply reprehensible," saying it was "even more painful" for having taken place as the city celebrated the Assumption of the Virgin.

The museum remained closed Sunday as investigators searched for evidence.

Saturday's theft followed a Friday announcement that three paintings stolen in northern Italy this March and worth some $10 million had been recovered by authorities Image: Italian Carabinieri Press Office/AFP

Works of 'enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance'

"It is an extremely serious and significant loss," said Mercurio, "They have stolen works of enormous cultural, artistic and symbolic importance, not only for Messina but for Sicily as a whole. All we can do now is hope they are recovered as soon as possible."

Though the sum financial loss has not been made public — initial estimates range from €70-€80 million ($81-$92 million) — Antonello's market value increased considerably in March of this year when the Italian state laid out $14.9 million (€13 million) for the purchase of another panel that he painted around 1460.

A moving two-sided panel in oil with an "Ecce Homo" portrayal of Christ (recto) and "Saint Jerome in the Desert" (verso), the purchase and news that the painting would soon return to Italy was greeted with enthusiasm.

Messina was among the cities hoping to display the newly returned work.

Antonello was born around 1430 and trained first in Naples before studying Provencal and Flemish painting and ultimately returning to Messina in 1457, where he would work until his death in 1474.

Seen as a key figure in what was an early example of technology transfer, Antonello is largely credited with bringing revolutionary new Flemish oil painting techniques to southern Europe while at the same time spreading knowledge of Italian perspective drawing among his colleagues north of the Alps.

The return of Antonello's painting to his hometown, went the argument, would have huge symbolic value for a city that lost most of its cultural heritage, including what remained of Antonello's life and work, on December 28, 1908 — when an earthquake flattened Messina and killed nearly 60% of its population in a matter of seconds.

Antonello's market value and reputation were given a boost when the Italian government laid out $14.9 million (€13 million) this March for the purchase of a panel he painted in 1460 Image: Mauro Scrobogna/LaPresse/picture alliance

What paintings were stolen in Sicily?

The paintings stolen on Saturday belonged to an altarpiece installed at Messina's Monastero San Gregorio until it was destroyed in the 1908 quake.

Referred to as the "San Gregorio Polyptych" in its post-quake state, it consisted of six tempera paintings on wooden panels.

The five pieces in the museum portrayed the "Annunciation of the Virgin" in two upper panels, and the larger "Madonna of the Rosary Enthroned" flanked by full-length portraits of Saints Gregory and Benedict below.

The works were the only by Antonello never to have left Messina.

Authorities say the thieves left two panels leaning against the exterior of the museum despite having removed them from the wall and gotten them outside.

Another work, the small, two-sided oil painting on wood taken from the armored case, bore the image of Christ on one side and a Franciscan monk with the Virgin and Child on the other.

Art detective lauds police after Louvre jewel heist arrests To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What will happen to the paintings now?

Saturday's robbery comes just days after Italian authorities announced the recovery of three stolen artworks by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cezanne and Henri Matisse worth about €10 million.

Those works were stolen from a regional museum, too, the Magnani Rocca Foundation in Parma, on March 22.

Five people — allegedly Moldavan gangsters — have been detained in connection with the theft.

Despite having (often outdated) alarm systems, museums present soft targets for criminals.

Brazen thefts at museums around the world have highlighted this problem — most dramatically in Paris, where gangsters stole priceless historic jewels from the famous Louvre in broad daylight on October 19, 2025.

Experts say the fact that stolen artworks are often instantly recognizable makes them impossible to sell via reputable channels. Instead, such objects are used as collateral among crime bosses.

In Germany, members of Berlin's infamous Remmo crime family were convicted and put in prison in connection with the 2019 theft of historic jewels from the Green Vault at Dresden's Royal Palace.

Most of the jewels from the heist were recovered, albeit damaged, but the cost to taxpayers was enormous. The jewels from the Louvre heist have yet to be recovered.

Sicily's most famous art theft happened more than half a century ago, when unknown perpetrators broke into the church of the Oratorio di San Lorenzo in Palermo to cut Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio's "Nativity with Saint Francis and Saint Lawrence" from its frame and spirit it away in the dead of night, never to be seen again, after having hung there for more than three centuries.

World.title: UAE, Saudi Arabia, others condemn Israel's rejection of Trump Gaza plan
World.content:
The statement came as US envoy Jared Kushner and Gaza peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov held ceasefire and implementation talks with regional mediators in Egypt.

The United Arab Emirates and seven other countries on Sunday condemned Israel's rejection of President Donald Trump's plan to end the war in the Gaza Strip.

It comes a week after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pullout will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

Trump's Board of Peace said last month that it had reached a deal for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.

The foreign ministers of the UAE, Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Egypt issued their joint statement as Trump's envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and Nickolay Mladenov, Trump's Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, were in Egypt for Gaza ceasefire-related talks.

Countries back Trump Gaza peace road map

Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point road map aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.

The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An international stabilization force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.

"Rejecting the Road Map constitutes an explicit refusal to proceed with the implementation of the Comprehensive Plan, and directly threatens to derail the extensive efforts exerted by US President Trump to bring an end to the war in Gaza and establish the conditions for lasting peace," the foreign ministers said in their Sunday statement.

"Such rejection confirms that Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza and the rest of the Occupied Palestinian Territory," they added.

Hamas delegation joins ceasefire talks in Cairo

Hamas on July 30 avoided using the term "disarmament," but said it would hand over its weapons to a new Palestinian governing body that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

Khalil al-Hayya, the leader of the group, which is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries and the EU, was in Cairo on Sunday for Gaza ceasefire-related talks.

Kushner met with Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi Image: Egyptian President Office/APAimages/IMAGO

US envoys Kushner and Mladenov were also in Egypt and met with mediators from Egypt, Qatar and Turkey to discuss implementation of the deal.

Netanyahu said last Sunday that Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections to the peace plan.

"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," said the Israeli prime minister.

Israel says it won't withdraw from Gaza until Hamas disarmed To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite this, the foreign ministers called on the Board of Peace and the US "to take immediate and concrete measures within its mandate to uphold the integrity of the Comprehensive Plan and prevent any party from obstructing its implementation."

World.title: Ukraine attacks Wildberries, Russia's biggest online market
World.content:
Since mid-July, Ukraine has been targeting warehouses of Russia's largest online retailer Wildberries almost every day. Ukraine says it's disrupting front-line shipments. But experts say it's disrupting Russia's economy.

Early Sunday, a fire broke out in a warehouse belonging to Russia's largest online marketplace, Wildberries, in the town of Podolsk, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) south of Moscow. The fire was the result of a large-scale overnight attack by Ukrainian drones, most of which were intercepted by Russian air defenses.

On Friday, Ukraine struck a different Wildberries warehouse, in Tver, north of Moscow. The day before, it had set fire to another warehouse in Salavat, further east.

About 20 Wildberries logistics hubs have been under near-daily attack in the past few weeks. At least nine employees have been confirmed dead, and scores injured, while a handful of the storehouses have halted operations.

The Moscow-based e-commerce consultancy Data Insight estimates Wildberries has lost as much as 480 billion rubles worth of goods ($5.7 billion/€4.9 billion) and about a third of its warehouse space. Combined damaged to the company and its sellers are estimated as high as 800 billion rubles ($9.5 billion).

Putin admits Ukraine's drones are hurting Russia's economy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While Kyiv argues the retailer helps supply Russia's military, Moscow maintains it serves only civilian purposes. Either way, the attacks have been placing an increased strain on Russia's economy.

"I think [Ukraine is] going after a choke point," Fabrice Pothier, CEO of the geopolitical consultancy firm Rasmussen Global, told DW. "Wildberries is, in a way, a choke point of Russian society and the Russian economy."

Wildberries: Russia's Amazon

Wildberries is often described as Russia's answer to the Amazon marketplace.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the ensuing sanctions on Russian trade, many online e-commerce platforms such as Amazon withdrew from the region. In response, Russian authorities permitted so-called parallel imports, essentially allowing Russian companies to sidestep sanctions by importing goods without the consent of the original rights holders.

These companies drastically undercut conventional prices, allowing their sales volume to skyrocket. In the case of Wildberries, for example, revenue increased sevenfold between 2021 and 2025. Its competitor, Ozon, offers similarly staggering numbers, with a reported $49.3 million revenue and 59% growth in 2025.

Today, Wildberries is the largest e-commerce platform in the country, controlling about half of the respective market. Ozon dominates about 30% of the market. Together, they handle goods and services equivalent to about 8.5% of the Russia's gross domestic product (GDP).

Why is Ukraine targeting warehouses?

Following the initial attacks in mid-July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy argued that the warehouses struck were "elements of Russian logistics [...] used to distribute equipment for the war: navigation systems, components for drone production, and other supplies for the Russian army."

The Kremlin has consistently rejected this claim. But an analysis by the independent outlet Verska identified "tens of thousands of military and dual-use goods" on the platform between May and August this year, amounting in sales worth hundred of millions of rubles.

Why Ukraine is targeting Russia's biggest online retailer To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Zelenskyy's office, said interrupting the flow of military goods to the front lines was just one reason for attacking the company's storage space. Disrupting a business with around 6 trillion rubels in turnover, he told DW, would also affect its creditors, including Sverbank and VTB, both of which are majority state-owned.

Not only could this drain state coffers, "if [the company] were to go bankrupt, it will probably have a domino-effect on the economy," as Pothier explained.

And "there is a bigger objective at play," the consultant added, "which is to bring back war to its sender" by disrupting civilian life. As many as 400,000 sellers have been affected by the attacks, the Russian Association of Electronic Trading Platforms reported. As a result, civilians are losing sources of income, access to goods and services, and, increasingly, a sense of normality.

Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce platform, a part of life for millions of people Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

The platform hosts over 1 million sellers — most of them small- and medium-sized — and reaches some 80 million users each month.

But targeting Wildberries was also meant to send a message to Russian elites, according to Podolyak. These include the billionaire Suleiman Kerimov, the diplomat Anton Vaino or politician Alexey Gromov, all of whom are counted in Putin's inner circle, and possibly have varying degrees of involvement with the Wildberries company.

What makes Wildberries a target?

Wildberries has been investing in massive logistics hubs. The largest span the size of several dozen soccer fields, making them fairly easy — and highly flammable — targets.

With hundreds of thousands of retailers affected in the attacks, Wildberries head and co-founder Tatyana Kim has now turned to the government for financial support Image: Evgeniy Razumniy/Kommersant Photo/Sipa USA/picture alliance

The company is also said to have incurred substantial debt, with some questioning whether it is still able to service them. According to financial reporting of its main operating entity, RWB LLC, short-term borrowing spiked nearly eightfold between 2024 and 2025. Along with long-term liabilities, Wildberries' debt may be as high as $14 billion, with VTB as the single-largest creditor.

Now, the other state-backed creditor, Sberbank, has signaled it is preparing to absorb losses. In response to attack on Wildberries' warehouses, Chief Financial Officer Taras Skvortsov said: "Regarding [Wildberries'] credit quality, there is indeed damage. [...] Their financial condition and potential future cash flow have decreased."

Billionaire Tatyana Kim, CEO and co-founder of Wildberries, has now reportedly turned to the government for support. While the government has confirmed talks, no details on a potential decision have emerged. It is expected, however, that VTB will play a key role in rescue efforts.

This article was originally written in Russian. It was updated on August 15 to reflect the latest developments.

World.title: Hundreds flee as Belgium battles wildfire at German border
World.content:
A rapidly spreading wildfire has scorched about 2,700 hectares in the High Fens nature reserve near Belgium's border with Germany. The German town of Monschau has also warned residents of possible evacuation orders.

Belgium is battling its largest wildfire on record which has burned around 2,700 hectares (6,700 acres) in the eastern High Fens nature reserve near the German border.

The fire has approached to within 3 kilometers (2 miles) of the German border, causing authorities in Germany to warn of smoke danger.

On Saturday, the European Union deployed three helicopters and two water bombers as Belgium deployed additional firefighters in a bid to bring the massive blaze under control.

The blaze is described as by officials as the largest in Belgium's modern history Image: Laurent Cavenati/Belga/AFP

Authorities ordered around 600 residents in parts of Waimes, Sourbrodt and Buetgenbach to evacuate as shifting winds and heavy smoke raised concerns that the fire could reach homes. Tourists were also advised to leave the area.

"You can't see a thing anymore, there's smoke everywhere," David Rodolfs, a restaurant owner in Waimes, told the AFP news agency.

A gymnasium in a neighboring municipality was opened up to offer shelter.

Reinforcements were pulled from across the country to fight the blaze Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

How have firefighting efforts fared?

The blaze, which broke out on Friday, has spread rapidly across peatlands and pine forests. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin told AFP he was "shocked" at the fire's speed and extent of the destruction.

"There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said.

Difficult terrain has hampered firefighting efforts, with operations relying heavily on aerial resources and forcing firefighters to allow difficult-to-access areas to burn, according to Yernaux.

Meanwhile, Belgium activated the EU's civil protection mechanism, bringing in three helicopters and two water-bombing aircraft from the Czech Republic, Sweden and the Netherlands.

Firefighters from Germany and Luxembourg have also joined the response, while farmers have helped emergency crews by wetting down the area.

Residents in parts of the nearby villages were ordered to evacuate on Saturday afternoon as a precautionary measure Image: Dimitri Korczak/AFP

Residents in Germany's Monschau warned of possible evacuation

Authorities in the German town of Monschau in the Eifel region, which is located just 2 kilometers from the border, have warned residents to prepare for possible evacuation.

They also warned of health dangers from smoke and have advised people living in three districts of the town to temporarily seek accommodation elsewhere if possible.

However, the local fire brigade has said it does not expect the fire to enter German territory any time soon.

"We are continuing to monitor the situation," Philipp Krüger, the operations manager of the Monschau fire brigade, told the DPA news agency.

Local farmers have headed to the fire zone to support emergency crews Image: Dha/Photo News/IMAGO

Monschau, a major tourist attraction in the Eifel region, has some 12,000 residents. It is particularly known for its picturesque Old Town with its half-timbered houses.

It is located just some 23 km from the site of another major blaze in Germany's Eifel region that forced some 2,000 people from their homes on Friday.

Climate change making wildfires spread faster

Belgium has experienced another spell of extreme heat this week, with temperatures reaching 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country.

Scientists say human-caused climate change is increasing the likelihood of hot and dry conditions that allow wildfires to spread faster and burn longer.

European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib called the blaze the latest sign of the "climate upheaval" affecting the continent.

"Never before has the wildfire season started so early in the year and reached such northern latitudes," she said.

Edited by: Karl Sexton, Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Ukraine launches one of its largest attacks of war
World.content:
Russia says hundreds of drones targeted Moscow overnight, with six fatalities in the capital and southern Rostov region. Five people were killed in strikes across Ukraine.

Hundreds of drones targeted the Moscow region in a sustained overnight assault that killed at least six people, according to the Russian capital's mayor, as Ukraine steps up long-range attacks deep inside Russia.

Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 600 drones had been flying toward the Moscow region between Saturday evening and 6:30 a.m. local time (0330 UTC) on Sunday, adding that 201 were destroyed over the region.

What happened in Moscow drone attack?

Russia said five people had been killed in Ukraine's attacks, five in the southwestern city of Rostov and one in the Moscow region.

Sobyanin said three people were wounded in the area inside Moscow's MKAD ring road and were receiving medical treatment.

Ukraine has intensified long-range strikes inside Russia in recent weeks, targeting military and industrial facilities as well as warehouses far from the front line.

Ukraine's Kyiv Independent newspaper reported that Ukrainian forces had targeted a warehouse belonging to Russian online retail giant Wildberries as well as industrial facilities in several cities across the Moscow region.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of the scale of the attack.

Where did Russia attack in Ukraine?

Russian attacks have killed at least five people and wounded dozens more across Ukraine, according to Ukrainian officials.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a missile strike on his hometown of Kryvyi Rih killed two people and injured 14 others, while another person was killed in the northeastern city of Sumy.

How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure," Zelenskyy said.

Zelenskyy said the Russian missile attack on Kryvyi Rih caused multiple casualties, with emergency services responding at the scene. The city, a major industrial center in central Ukraine, has repeatedly been targeted during the war.

In the southern Zaporizhzhia region, a man and a woman were killed when a Russian strike hit their home, regional military administration head Ivan Fedorov said.

Spanish fighter jet shoots down drone over Romania

The attack came as NATO countries on Ukraine's borders faced fresh drone incursions of their own.

Romania's Defense Ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone early Sunday after it entered Romanian airspace from Moldova near the border with Ukraine.

The aircraft was operating on NATO duties and intercepted the drone at 5:01 a.m. local time (0201 UTC).

Debris fell in an unpopulated area of Galati county, close to the Ukrainian border.

Romanian authorities did not immediately identify the drone's origin or say who launched it.

Romania has repeatedly reported drone debris on its territory since 2023 following Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube.

On Friday, an Italian Eurofighter operating under NATO command also shot down a foreign drone that entered Latvian airspace.

World.title: Bus crash in Hungary kills at least 12
World.content:
Police say they have arrested the driver of a bus that crashed in Hungary, killing at least 12 people. The bus was carrying Polish pilgrims, media report.

At least 12 people have died after a Polish coach crashed into a ditch and overturned in eastern Hungary, police said on Sunday.

According to emergency services, 47 people were injured in the incident, 10 seriously.

The bus overturned after crashing into a ditch, police said Image: Zoltan Mathe/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

What do we know about the accident?

The accident occurred on the M3 motorway near Mezokeresztes, around 140 kilometers (87 miles) east of Budapest, according to police in the district capital, Miskolc.

Police said they believe the driver fell asleep at the wheel during the overnight journey into Sunday. He was subsequently arrested.

Poland's PAP news agency reported that the bus had been carrying a group of pilgrims from Podkarpackie province in the far southeast of Poland.

The group, said to number 59 people, including two drivers, had been returning from Bosnia-Herzegovina, PAP said.

Fourteen ambulances were deployed to the scene of the crash, reports said.

Hungary's National Directorate for Disaster Management said that several of the passengers had been trapped under the vehicle when it overturned.

Several passengers were said to have been trapped under the bus when it tipped over Image: Balazs Toth/Mezokovesd Kepekben/REUTERS

Condolences from Hungary, Poland

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has voiced his condolences to the families of the crash victims in a Facebook message and thanked emergency and rescue services.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki said he was deeply shaken. "In the face of this unimaginable tragedy, which affects us all, my thoughts and prayers go out to the families and loved ones of the victims," the 43-year-old wrote on X.

World.title: Troops from North Korea to boost Russia's Ukraine forces
World.content:
Intelligence agencies report that North Korea is preparing to send up to 50,000 troops to Russia. But military experts doubt this will make a fundamental difference in the course of Russia's war with Ukraine.

In late 2024, North Korea sent troops to help defend the Kursk region of Russia from Ukraine. International officials estimate that 14,000-15,000 North Korean troops were initially deployed to assist Russia in its war in Ukraine.

Now, Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies suspect that North Korea is planning to send an additional 30,000-50,000 troops to Russia. Ukrainian officials have also stated that North Korean ballistic missiles are being fired from Russia.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has raised concerns that North Korea's improved combat and weapons experience could pose a security threat to Ukraine, as well as the Asia-Pacific region.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

N. Korean troops could bolster Russia's defenses

Observers have had mixed responses to Zelenskyy's remarks. Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military and political expert at the Ukrainian Center for Security Studies, told DW that new troops from North Korea would likely be used to secure Russia's border territories. Aside from remaining in Kursk, North Korean soldiers could also help secure southwestern Vornezh.

"These forces could free up Russian occupational forces," Kovalenko said. "Russia would then be able to deploy around 15,000 troops to battles along front lines in Vovchansk, Kharkiv, Sumy or even Chernihiv."

Kovalenko does not expect North Korean troops to fight on Ukrainian territory.

The Russian military analyst Ruslan Leviev agrees. "It's one thing to recapture Russian territory," he told DW, "and an entirely different thing to be present on internationally recognized Ukrainian territory, taking part in a war of aggression."

"Diplomatically speaking," he said, "those are two entirely different concepts."

Russia not outgunned, experts believe

Leviev said he had not seen concrete evidence of a noteworthy North Korean presence in Russia. He said Moscow had enough troops available without having to draw foreign soldiers into the fight.

"If you look at the front line, you can see that Russia's forces have been fairly active since mid-July," Leviev said. "That's a clear sign they still have enough forces."

Russia has spread terror in Ukraine with rocket attacks on civilian targets Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

Estimates by the economist Janis Kluge, of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, back this up. "While Russia's recruitment campaign has shown signs of strain this year, regional spending figures indicate that Russia is still recruiting around 1,000 contract soldiers each day," he recently wrote in a report .

Intelligence on North Korea's short- and medium-range ballistic systems, the KN-23 and KN-24, is far less speculative. Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) states that North Korea has delivered 148 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles since 2025.

In July, Zelenskyy said one such missile had struck a home near Ukraine's Kryvyi Rih, killing two adults and three children.

The HUR recently reported that a North Korean missile unit was deploying to Russia's Voronezh region, where it could be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy has taken this as indication that Russia's strategic reserve is depleted.

Kovalenko has come to a different conclusion. Instead of having run out of reserves, he said, he believes that Russia is looking to launch a higher number of missiles "to spread more terror."

'Instruments of terror'

Ukrainian military sources have said North Korean missiles are similar to Russia's Iskander missiles, but with a greater payload, longer range and lower accuracy.

The military expert Yuri Fyodorov calls North Korea's missiles "instruments of terror." He told DW that "it is very difficult to hit a small target with North Korean weapons." He said he believed that Russia had deliberately targeted residential areas with these missiles.

Like the Russian Iskander 9M723, KN-23 and KN-24 missiles can only be stopped by US-made Patriot air-defense systems, which Ukraine has run critically low on.

Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Leviev said ballistic missiles would play a key role in this phase of the war. As Ukraine's stockpiles run low, he said, it will become a growing priority to Russia to keep a steady supply.

This summer, Leviev said, he has seen Russia launch far more ballistic missiles than in previous years. Should Russia's missile supply run low by winter, he said, "there will still be North Korea reserves, to make sure Ukraine cannot catch its breath."

No turning point in war

None of the experts DW spoke with believes North Korea's involvement will bring about a turning point in Russia's war with Ukraine.

Jenny Town, of the US-based Foreign Policy Research Institute, said the time had passed for North Korea's involvement to make a significant difference. Instead, she said, Russia and North Korea have established a mutually beneficial partnership that is only likely to deepen through the course of the war with Ukraine.

Kovalenko also doesn't expect Russia to make substantial territorial gains along the front lines, but he is concerned about the upcoming winter. "October, November and December could become very trying for Ukraine," he said.

Russian forces could benefit from a possible new military call-up, from freeing up fighters it replaces with North Korean troops and from a further stream of ballistic missiles. "That would be no good for the course of the war, and for Ukraine's war interests," said Fyodorov .

This article was originally written in Russian.

World.title: US: Hurricane Lala brings Hawaii heavy rain, strong winds
World.content:
The Category 1 storm passed over Hawaii's Big Island without making landfall and is gradually weakening. However, the hurricane caused roads to flood and turned rivers into raging torrents.

Hurricane Lala passed over Hawaii's Big Island on Saturday without making landfall and began moving away on Sunday as a tropical storm, while still bringing strong winds and heavy rain to the region.

The hurricane had earlier strengthened to Category 1 as its eye approached the southern part of Big Island.

It was expected be the Big Island's first possible direct hit from a hurricane in 155 years but that was not to be as the storm passed the island's southern tip.

What is the situation after Lala passed by?

Tropical storm conditions, with drenching rain and winds, have continued to spread toward the west on Sunday, from Maui to Oahu and then Kauai.

The National Hurricane Center warned that wind speeds on top of mountains and on the windward and leeward slopes could be up to 30% stronger than the winds near the surface that are used to calculate a storm's official strength.

Governor Josh Green said at least one person died in a car accident in the Big Island's South Point area and a number of roofs were blown off.

"There have been a lot of roads impacted, our crews have already been out to more than 30 sites," Green said.

Experts warn of flooding, mudslides

Earlier, Lala had maximum sustained winds of 75 miles per hour (120 kilometers per hour), with its center forecast to move over or near the southern end of the Big Island.

The National Hurricane Center warned the island could receive 10 to 20 inches (25 to 50 cm) of rain, with up to 25 inches possible in some areas.

"This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the US National Hurricane Center said.

The Big Island, also known as the island of Hawaii, is the archipelago's largest island by landmass — and with some 200,000 inhabitants, the second-most populous.

A hurricane warning was in effect for the Big Island, while tropical storm warnings covered Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau Image: NOAA/AP Photo/picture alliance

Hawaii declares state of emergency

More than 60,000 utility customers across Hawaii were without power, including over 31,000 on the Big Island, according to outage data.

The tropical storm warning covering Oahu — home to the state capital, Honolulu, and around 70% of the state's inhabitants— as well as the other major islands of Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Kauai and Niihau is still in place.

The hurricane damaged an electrical utility pole near Ocean View on the Big Island Image: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle/AP Photo/picture alliance

A storm surge of one to three feet was expected to be accompanied by "large and dangerous waves," according to officials.

Governor Green had declared a state of emergency and urged residents to shelter in place. "It's a serious storm," Green said.

Authorities also announced the closure of Hilo International Airport, adding that Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport would also be shut down.

Risk of wildfires rise

Authorities opened shelters and advised residents to clear drains and gutters, move valuables off the ground and prepare for possible extended power outages.

Lala was expected to dump 10 to 20 inches (25 to 50 centimeters) of rain on the Big Island Image: Taylor Cozloff/Civil Beat/dpa/picture alliance

Vanessa Almanza, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Honolulu, said dry and breezy conditions outside the storm would raise risk of wildfires.

In 2023, the Maui town of Lahaina burned during extreme winds as a hurricane passed far to the south.

Meteorologists said Lala's arrival coincides with a powerful El Nino event, which can increase hurricane activity in the Pacific.

Hawaii has not experienced a major hurricane landfall since Hurricane Iniki struck Kauai in 1992, causing six deaths and billions of dollars in damage.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: El Gobierno niega un “colapso” sanitario y reclama espacios en Ceuta para atender a los migrantes
World.content:
La sanidad en Ceuta está “tensionada”, pero no hay “colapso”. La ministra de Sanidad, Mónica García, ha repetido la frase en varias ocasiones ante los medios de comunicación. Lo ha hecho tras su reunión este domingo con el presidente de la ciudad autónoma y dirigente del PP, Juan Jesús Vivas. Y ha reclamado, también de forma reiterada, “espacios” en la localidad para alojar y atender en condiciones de salubridad a los migrantes que cruzaron de forma irregular la frontera con Marruecos los días 30 y 31 de julio. Según ha explicado, estos lugares son una prioridad para evitar que las personas que ahora se encuentran en situación irregular enfermen. Así, ha abogado por desmontar la tesis de que los migrantes son sinónimo de enfermedades, una asociación que considera “injusta y xenófoba”, ha recalcado. Enfrente, Vivas viene manifestando hasta ahora que no tiene recursos para cobijar a los extranjeros y ha demandado que los migrantes fuesen devueltos de inmediato. Este lunes responderá a lo dicho por la ministra en una comparecencia de prensa.

Una olla a presión esperaba en Ceuta este domingo la visita de la ministra. A las quejas de los médicos del único hospital de la ciudad autónoma, gestionado por el Gobierno central, se suma el hartazgo de muchos ceutíes. Algunos vecinos, como ya ha ocurrido con otros ministros en ocasiones anteriores, han esperado a la dirigente de Sumar para formalizar sus críticas a pie de calle y a gritos de “¡dimisión! ¡dimisión!” o “¡vete de aquí!“.

García ha tenido que escuchar las quejas tras llegar al puerto ceutí y después de días en los que las urgencias han tenido que asumir “un 50%” más de su capacidad, según explica el jefe de Medicina Preventiva, Julián Domínguez, que también es voluntario en el asentamiento de la playa de El Trampolín. “El diagnóstico es de sobrecarga asistencial, sumado a que estamos de vacaciones”, ha señalado Domínguez. El epidemiólogo ha confirmado un brote de gastroenteritis y casos puntuales de tuberculosis y sarna provocados por las condiciones de insalubridad en las que están las personas migrantes. También golpes de calor y heridas en la piel por el sol o provocadas en reyertas o caídas.

El presidente de la ciudad autónoma de Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, ha recibido a la ministra de Sanidad, Mónica García. Gabriela Sardá Núñez (Europa Press)

En estos 15 días, Ceuta ha atendido a 5.800 migrantes. Según los datos expuestos por García, 3.500 han sido asistidos en atención primaria y 2.300 en hospital. El primer día se atendió a 1.149 migrantes, pero la presión “ha ido disminuyendo un 70%”, con “una media en torno a 300 personas atendidas a lo largo de los diferentes días que ha ido variando entre 200 y 400”. Este domingo, 28 migrantes permanecen ingresados. “No es una situación de colapso”, ha subrayado.

En este sentido, la ministra ha incidido en que el sistema sanitario ceutí ha mantenido la atención a la población local. “Ninguna de las operaciones, consultas, asistencias sanitarias se ha suspendido. Ni esperamos que se suspendan”, ha apuntado. Así, ha afirmado que “la asistencia sanitaria a la población autóctona, a los ceutíes, no ha bajado”. Y ha asegurado que todos los que quieran hacer uso del sistema sanitario pueden hacerlo. “No hay colapso”, ha vuelto a decir.

En la misma línea, García ha precisado que la situación se ubica en el nivel 1 de la guía para la elaboración de planes de catástrofes en hospitales del Instituto Nacional de Gestión Sanitaria (INGESA), la entidad dependiente del Ministerio que gestiona la prestación del servicio en Ceuta y Melilla. La ministra ha reconocido que “el sobreesfuerzo” del personal sanitario en Ceuta en el marco de esta “situación excepcional” es lo que ha permitido que “no haya colapso”. No obstante, ha recordado que su ministerio no ha tenido que pedir apoyo a otras comunidades ni ha tenido que suspender vacaciones en Sanidad, como sí ha ocurrido con el personal del Ejército y de la Guardia Civil. “No hemos tenido que pedir más refuerzos”, ha señalado.

“La urgencia no está en el hospital, está fuera”

Además, ha recordado que en Ceuta hay “1.475 contratados” en el sistema sanitario y ha apuntado que se han sumado más manos desde la entrada masiva del pasado julio. “Tenemos 60 profesionales más trabajando para la crisis migratoria”. Con todo, ha reiterado que ahora mismo es necesario que se cedan y habiliten espacios salubres y seguros para atender a los migrantes en el territorio. “La urgencia no está en el hospital, está fuera, en el terreno”, ha remarcado, para luego incidir en que “es la prioridad de salud pública” para poder mantener la salubridad en la zona y realizar un estudio epidemiológico. Miles de personas continúan sin solución en las calles, en asentamientos como la playa de El Trampolín, el polígono de El Tarajal o en el barrio de El Príncipe.

García ha reconocido que se han detectado “dos casos de tuberculosis: uno que estaba en tratamiento en Marruecos y otro autóctono”. Sin embargo, ha reiterado que el hecho de que los inmigrantes tengan enfermedades, “como también tenemos nosotros”, en referencia a la población local, no puede servir de excusa para cargar de forma xenófoba contra las personas que cruzaron la frontera. Por último, al ser preguntada sobre el número de agresiones sexuales que se han producido, la ministra ha comunicado que los servicios de asistencia han atendido a cinco víctimas de violaciones, todas ellas migrantes.

Unos chicos desmayados y con fuertes dolores estomacales son atendidos por personas anónimas y por la Cruz Roja. Joaquín Sánchez

Este domingo, el Gobierno de Ceuta se ha negado a responder a García y se ha remitido a un comunicado publicado después del encuentro con la ministra, en el que le reclaman que “atienda las demandas del colectivo sanitario de Ceuta, médicos, enfermeros, auxiliares y otro personal, teniendo en cuenta que la sanidad es uno de los pilares del Estado” y le pide que no olvide que la ciudad está viviendo “el momento más crítico de su historia reciente”. Vivas comparecerá este lunes para dar más explicaciones.

Desde este viernes, el Gobierno de Ceuta ha empezado a derivar a niñas y adolescentes no acompañadas que estaban en un polideportivo del barrio de El Príncipe a dos naves con capacidad para unas 200 menores. “Hemos buscado algunos dispositivos, no hay muchas soluciones en Ceuta y hemos encontrado dos recursos que se han puesto a funcionar”, aseguró el consejero de Presidencia, Alberto Gaitán, por teléfono a este periódico. “Son dos naves con capacidades en torno a 200 y pico personas, que alivian, pero que no pueden acoger a todos los menores”, añadió el dirigente popular. Hasta ahora, 1.898 menores han sido filiados por la Policía Nacional. Al menos en una de las naves, el Gobierno ceutí ha acometido reformas para habilitar un espacio con literas en un polígono industrial.

World.title: El diario de Mohamed tras 15 días malviviendo en Ceuta, en busca de comida y lugar para dormir
World.content:
Mohamed, junto a otros jóvenes migrantes, frente a las pancartas que han pintado en el polígono de El Tarajal para reivindicar que tienen oficios y quieren trabajar.

El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

El joven de 26 años, que cruzó a nado desde Marruecos, relata en primera persona sus dos semanas en El Tarajal, entre el hambre, la incertidumbre y el miedo a ser devuelto

Mohamed tiene 26 años y nació en Castillejos, la ciudad marroquí que mira cada día hacia Ceuta. El pasado 30 de julio entró a nado en la ciudad autónoma. Desde entonces, lleva dos semanas sobreviviendo en una situación extrema: duerme en la calle, sin un lugar seguro donde refugiarse y dependiendo de la ayuda de la ONG Luna Blanca para comer una vez al día.

Este es su diario. En él cuenta, en primera persona, cómo tomó la decisión de irse, qué sintió mientras cruzaba el mar y qué ha ocurrido desde que puso los pies en Ceuta. Es el relato de un viaje que comenzó con la esperanza de encontrar una vida mejor y que, al otro lado de la frontera, se ha convertido en una lucha por sobrevivir.

30 de julio. Una frontera sin obstáculos

Me levanté el jueves a las ocho de la mañana. Había visto en El Faro de Ceuta que algunas personas estaban entrando a nado en la ciudad y pensé que quizá yo también tendría una oportunidad. Me vestí deprisa y salí.

No era la primera vez que intentaba llegar a España. Un año antes ya lo había intentado, pero la policía marroquí me expulsó. Esta vez fue diferente. No hubo obstáculos, así que entré.

No tuve miedo. Siempre había querido venir a España. Estudié Ingeniería Eléctrica y trabajaba en una fábrica en Tetuán 12 horas al día, seis días a la semana, por unos 300 euros al mes. No veía cómo podía construir mi vida así.

Llegué a Ceuta a las nueve de la mañana. Lo primero que hice fue caminar. Y seguir caminando. Había miles y miles de personas. Algunas habían llegado en camionetas desde ciudades tan lejanas como Casablanca.

Fui hacia el polígono de El Tarajal [en Ceuta] porque mis padres habían trabajado allí. Antes de la pandemia, las naves estaban llenas de negocios y el comercio transfronterizo daba trabajo a muchas familias de Castillejos. Cuando llegó el covid, cerraron la frontera y los vecinos de mi ciudad ya no pudieron entrar. Mis padres se quedaron sin trabajo y sin ingresos.

Ahora siento que soy la esperanza de mi familia.

El primer día empezó a hacerse difícil cuando llegó la hora de buscar comida. Pero la noche fue todavía peor. Tuve que dormir en el monte. Pensaba en mi familia, en todo lo que había dejado atrás. Lloré. No sabía dónde iba a dormir al día siguiente, ni siquiera si tendría algo que comer.

Mohamed durante su jornada de trabajo en Marruecos en una imagen cedida por él.

31 de julio. Mortadela y paciencia

Nada más levantarme, fui al arroyo para lavarme la cara, el cuerpo y la ropa. No tenía jabón, así que solo pude hacerlo con agua. Tampoco tenía nada que beber. Bebí del río y después me sentó mal al estómago.

Luego empecé a buscar comida. Mi familia me había dado algo de dinero, así que fui a una pequeña tienda de la barriada de El Príncipe y compré una barra de pan y un poco de mortadela. Me preparé un bocadillo y guardé el resto para la cena. Cuando volvía a tener sed, regresaba al río y bebía agua de allí.

Ese día conocí a Ismail y Munim, de 25 y 27 años. Empezamos a hablar y enseguida surgió la idea de juntar el poco dinero que teníamos para comprar comida y poder repartirla entre los tres durante varios días. Me cayeron bien. Los veo con ganas de trabajar y, sobre todo, sinceros. Desde entonces nos hemos hecho amigos. Nos cuidamos entre nosotros y eso, aquí, significa mucho.

Por la noche decidí que no quería volver a dormir en el monte. Me fui a las afueras de las naves de El Tarajal, donde duermen cientos de migrantes. Saqué la mortadela que había guardado por la mañana y me la comí para cenar.

Antes de dormir, me repetí lo mismo que llevo diciéndome desde que llegué: tengo que tener paciencia. Mucha paciencia.

Personas que entraron a nado en Ceuta y ahora están el en polígono de El Tarajal. joaquín Sánchez

El polígono de El Tarajal donde se refugia Mohamed se ha convertido en un laberinto de calles ocupadas por cientos o miles de migrantes llegados a Ceuta. Entre los garajes de los antiguos negocios se amontonan colchones, mantas y cuerpos que buscan un rincón donde pasar la noche. Algunos duermen directamente sobre el suelo. De día, el calor queda atrapado entre las naves y convierte el polígono en un horno. De noche, cuando baja la temperatura, muchos apenas tienen con qué cubrirse.

Una vez al día llega la comida. La reparte la ONG Luna Blanca bajo la escolta de ocho agentes de la Policía. Antes de que aparezcan las cajas, las personas empiezan a colocarse en fila. La cola crece hasta hacerse kilométrica. Para muchos, ese reparto es la única comida que tendrán ese día. Han pasado 15 días desde las llegadas a nado y el cansancio empieza a pesar sobre quienes viven aquí. También la tensión. No hay espacio suficiente, faltan recursos y nadie sabe cuánto tiempo tendrá que seguir durmiendo en el mismo lugar. Las discusiones y las peleas son frecuentes. También los robos.

En este espacio hay mujeres y niños. Algunos todavía llevan en el cuerpo las consecuencias del trayecto a nado. Las heridas que se hicieron al llegar no siempre han podido curarse en condiciones y, sin apenas acceso a higiene o medicamentos, algunas se han infectado. Otros sufren sarna u hongos y esperan un tratamiento que les permita curarse. El director de programas de Save the Children en España, Raúl Arnáiz, describe la situación en el polígono como “de una miseria extrema”.

A partir de aquí, vuelve el relato de Mohamed, que retomamos desde esta semana porque los días en El Tarajal empiezan a confundirse unos con otros: esperar para comer, buscar un lugar donde dormir y, sobre todo, esperar a que algo cambie.

Lunes 10 de agosto. Cada vez hay más tensión

Me levanté por la mañana y fui al arroyo para lavarme la cara y asearme un poco. Después salí a buscar algo de comida. Hay días en los que seguimos sin tener nada que comer.

Las pocas cosas que tengo las dejo en el polígono, al cuidado de una mujer que tiene tres hijos y pasa allí todo el día. Me las guarda para que no me las roben. Yo paso buena parte del día buscando algún sitio donde estar tranquilo.

No entramos en el centro de Ceuta porque hay mucha policía. Tampoco queremos molestar a nadie. Tenemos miedo de algunas personas. Nosotros solo queremos una solución, no queremos pelearnos con nadie. Sigo teniendo la esperanza de que algún día pueda ir a la Península.

Al móvil le queda un 5% de batería. Necesito cargarlo, así que voy a la casa de una mujer mayor que vive en la barriada de El Príncipe. Me deja enchufarlo un rato. Ese gesto, que en otro momento parecería insignificante, aquí es importante: sin batería, me quedo también sin una de las pocas formas que tengo de comunicarme.

Ese día conozco a Imane Khaddar, una chica de 23 años que vino desde Kenitra, en Marruecos. Me cuenta que la primera noche durmió en las calles de El Príncipe, pero se asustó al escuchar disparos. Desde entonces duerme en el polígono. Aquí la tensión empieza a notarse cada vez más. Algunos chicos discuten y terminan peleándose. Últimamente ocurre casi todos los días.

Por la noche busco un sitio en la zona donde duermen las mujeres y los niños. Allí me siento más seguro. Prefiero estar lejos de quienes consumen drogas y de quienes roban para comprarlas. Lo peor es que también hay niños que consumen drogas.

Intento dormir pensando que mañana será otro día.

Martes 11 de agosto. Pienso en volver. Y lloro

Me levanté temprano, como todos estos días, y fui al arroyo para lavarme la cara. Después salí a buscar algo de comer. A veces tenemos suerte y encontramos a alguien que nos ayuda y nos da algo de comida. Otras veces, no.

Me siento en un bordillo, frente al polígono, junto a un grupo de personas. Están preocupadas. Miran sus teléfonos y se enseñan unas a otras las noticias que circulan por las redes sociales en Marruecos. Hablan de que el ministro de Justicia ha dicho que mantiene su determinación de recuperar a los niños y menores que se encuentran en España. También vemos las declaraciones del ministro de Asuntos Exteriores español, que asegura que “hasta la última persona que ha entrado irregularmente en España volverá a Marruecos”.

Nos entra miedo.

Intentamos averiguar qué hay de cierto en esas noticias. Cada vez que aparece un periodista por el polígono, le preguntamos. Queremos saber qué va a pasar con nosotros. Las familias están especialmente preocupadas por sus hijos y por la posibilidad de que puedan separarlos.

Yo también tengo miedo. Y hambre.

Ese día, lo único que como son unos macarrones con tomate que reparte la ONG Luna Blanca. Caben en un pequeño recipiente de plástico redondo. A veces también nos dan agua o leche.

Intento no pensar demasiado. Pero es difícil cuando escuchas que puedes ser devuelto. Cuando llevas días durmiendo en la calle y sin saber qué va a pasar mañana, una noticia así lo cambia todo.

Por las noches, cuando me tumbo, pienso en la posibilidad de tener que volver. Y lloro.

Estoy sufriendo mucho.

La ONG Luna Blanca, ha repartido el viernes 7 de agosto, unas 4.500 raciones de comida a los jóvenes Marroquíes en el polígono de El Tarajal. PACO PUENTES

Miércoles 12 de agosto. Hacemos pancartas: solo queremos una oportunidad

Hoy tuvimos suerte. Una chica vino hasta el polígono con dos bolsas de comida que había comprado en un supermercado. Había manzanas, pan, queso, cereales, zumos… Decidí repartirlo entre los niños. Los mayores podemos aguantar un poco más. A los pequeños les hace más falta.

Después llegó una mujer canadiense que trabaja con una ONG. Traía un botiquín para atender las heridas de quienes estamos aquí. Nos dijo que algunos niños tenían infecciones que podían empeorar mucho si no los veía un médico.

Poco después, dos niños se desmayaron. Uno, según nos dijeron, por falta de comida. El otro apenas podía tragar por el dolor que tenía en la garganta. La mujer llamó a una ambulancia. Llegaron dos sanitarios, les tomaron la tensión y les hicieron varias pruebas antes de llevárselos al hospital.

Hoy hemos cogido varias sábanas blancas para hacer pancartas. Con pintura roja que nos han dejado, hemos escrito lo que queremos que se escuche fuera de estas naves: que tenemos oficios, que sabemos trabajar y que solo queremos una oportunidad para hacerlo.

En otras sábanas hemos escrito “gracias a la Policía” y “viva España”.

Las hemos colgado para que puedan verse desde fuera. Es nuestra manera de decir que queremos que se nos dé una oportunidad.

Dos migrantes desplomados en el suelo por la falta de comida y agua son atendidos por sanitarios. joaquín Sánchez

Jueves 13 de agosto. La policía pasa

Me desperté por la mañana y repetí la rutina de estos días. Fui al arroyo para lavarme y después salí a buscar algo que comer. Llevo varios días con la misma camiseta. Me la dio una voluntaria italiana durante los primeros días. En ella hay una frase: “Nadie es ilegal”. La sigo llevando porque es de las pocas cosas que tengo y porque, de alguna manera, siento que también habla de nosotros.

Por la noche estoy cansado y solo quiero dormir, pero aquí es difícil. Hay mucho ruido y duermo directamente sobre el suelo. Por suerte, tengo amigos que están pendientes de mí y me protegen de los robos. De madrugada empieza a hacer frío. Me despierto y vuelvo a pensar en lo mismo: en lo que puede pasar conmigo. Lloro cuando pienso en mi futuro. Durante la noche, a veces aparece la Policía para comprobar cómo está la situación.

Y así termina otro día.

Viernes, 14 de agosto. No me dejéis aquí

Algunas mañanas, varios coches entran en el polígono, dan vueltas entre las naves y nos pitan para despertarnos.

Hoy salí con mis tres amigos a buscar comida y conseguimos lo de casi siempre: un poco de pan y mortadela. Tengo hambre y sed casi todo el tiempo.

Hay mujeres que necesitan medicamentos y que pasan los días con dolor, esperando que alguien pueda ayudarlas. Muchas sufren en silencio.

A pesar de todo, seguimos aquí. Seguimos esperando que algo cambie, aunque algunos días sea difícil imaginar cuándo.

Varios chicos en el polígono del Tarajal de Ceuta. Joaquín Sánchez

Cuando llega el momento de despedirnos, Mohamed apenas encuentra palabras. Está cansado. También angustiado. Mira alrededor, hacia las naves en las que ha pasado estos últimos días, como quien ya no sabe cuánto más puede aguantar.

Nos despedimos y, justo antes pide ayuda. “Por favor, no me dejéis aquí”. Esa es la última frase de su diario.

World.title: La crisis de Ceuta aviva el debate sobre las vacaciones de los políticos: demagogia y problemas reales de gestión
World.content:
—“Si un presidente autonómico de mi partido estuviera de farra mientras el pueblo se ahoga, o mientras su territorio se quema, sería cesado de manera automática”.

—“España se quema. Feijóo, a pie de fuego. Sánchez, a pie de playa. No hay más preguntas, señoría”.

Son dos tuits del año pasado: el primero, del ministro socialista Óscar Puente atacando al presidente de Castilla y León, Alfonso Fernández Mañueco (PP); y el segundo, del senador popular Francisco Bernabé criticando al jefe del Ejecutivo. Pero se han reproducido de manera muy similar este verano, como los propios incendios. El debate sobre las vacaciones de los políticos es un clásico al que juegan todos los partidos y suele incluir grandes dosis de demagogia, aunque en algunos casos, como el momento actual, aludan a problemas reales tanto de gestión como de comunicación.

“El presidente del Gobierno, como cualquier líder político de primera línea”, afirma el politólogo Pablo Simón, “no tiene vacaciones de verdad”. “Nunca desconectan, están permanentemente pendientes de lo que ocurre”, añade. Para este analista, en este debate se mezclan varios elementos: por un lado, “la deriva populista clásica de que los políticos disfrutan a costa del erario público, el cuestionamiento de las élites que irrumpe con fuerza a raíz del 15-M”; y por otro, “el mundo de la hipercomunicación en la que vivimos, donde no importa tanto lo que haces como lo que parece que haces, lo que origina esas fotografías de presidentes autonómicos sujetando una manguera en un incendio, por ejemplo”.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, entonces líder del PP gallego, posa con una manguera tras un incendio en Meis (Pontevedra) en 2006. SALVADOR SAS (EFE)

La demagogia...

En el cómputo de las dosis de demagogia entran los náuticos y la camisa clara de Alberto Núñez Feijóo sujetando una manguera en los incendios de 2006 —él mismo reconoció años después que la imagen había sido “una metedura de pata”—; las alusiones al “palacete pagado por todos” mientras “para millones de españoles irse de vacaciones es un lujo” que ha repetido recientemente el popular Elías Bendodo, en alusión a los días de descanso de Sánchez en la residencia oficial de La Mareta; o las referencias al presidente autonómico que se va “de farra” que utilizó Puente contra Mañueco el pasado verano. Para gestionar la lucha contra el fuego no hace falta estar “al pie de las llamas”; sí asegurarse de que se despliegan sobre el terreno los medios necesarios. Y lo mismo ocurre con otro tipo de crisis.

Los argumentos demagógicos multiplican, además, las posibilidades de que se vuelvan en contra, como le ocurrió a la presidenta madrileña. Tras criticar Isabel Díaz Ayuso en numerosas ocasiones que Sánchez vive “en cuatro palacios pagados por todos los españoles”—refiriéndose a La Moncloa y a las residencias oficiales de verano o descanso de las que pueden disfrutar todos los presidentes del Gobierno: Las Marismillas, en el Parque Nacional de Doñana (Huelva); Quintos de Mora, en Los Yébenes (Toledo) y La Mareta, en Lanzarote— EL PAÍS reveló en julio del año pasado que la dirigente popular había pasado unos días de asueto en un chalé con piscina en la sierra de Madrid comprado por 4,3 millones de euros en 2023 por el Gobierno de la Comunidad, es decir, con dinero público. En aquella ocasión, fue este periódico y no el Ejecutivo madrileño el que informó de que Ayuso estaba disfrutando de ese chalé, como ocurrió recientemente con la compra del ático de Chamberí por 6,3 millones de euros de la que tampoco informó en su momento (abril) la Comunidad de Madrid.

Algo similar le ha ocurrido a Díaz Ayuso esta misma semana. “Estos ministros se van de fiesta a cuerpo de rey y dicen que han gastado 72.000 euros. Mientras, España invadida por Marruecos, la cesta de la compra, por las nubes; los ministros peleados entre ellos buscando un puestazo internacional; el presidente y su familia dándose la gran vida con los impuestos y los recursos de todos, incluidos los agentes que a Ceuta nunca llegaron”, tuiteó la presidenta madrileña junto a la foto del acto organizado por el Ministerio de Ciencia en el Observatorio de Yebes (Guadalajara) para seguir el eclipse.

El alcalde de la localidad, Enrique Quintana, del PP, discrepó en Cuatro de las declaraciones de Ayuso pese a formar parte de su “propio partido” y destacó que el evento acogió a 500 personas, entre ellas los trabajadores del Observatorio y sus familias, así como concejales de distintos partidos políticos. El Gobierno eligió Yebes para emitir la señal institucional de vídeo del eclipse por su radiotelescopio de 40 metros de diámetro y por estar allí ubicada “una de las mayores instalaciones científicas del mundo”, según el Ministerio de Ciencia. Fueron invitados astronautas españoles de la Agencia Espacial Europea y otros expertos con el objetivo de convertir el evento, en palabras de la ministra Diana Morant, “en un acto para divulgar la ciencia”. Algunos medios aseguraron que el Gobierno había montado el acto para tapar la crisis de Ceuta, pero el mismo se anunció el pasado mayo, casi tres meses antes. También se publicó que Sánchez iba a acudir a Yebes a ver el eclipse, pero eso, según aseguran fuentes de La Moncloa, “nunca estuvo sobre la mesa”.

La ministra de Ciencia, Diana Morant (en el centro de la imagen) el pasado miércoles desde el Observatorio de Yebes (Guadalajara) Alberto Ortega (Europa Press)

También Miguel Ángel Rodríguez, jefe de gabinete de Ayuso, ha tratado de minimizar la polémica generada por la compra del ático de Chamberí calificando de “despilfarro” el acto del Gobierno en Yebes.

El año pasado, a su vez, se viralizaron en redes unas declaraciones de Feijóo: “Las vacaciones están sobrevaloradas”. Tras el revuelo generado, el propio líder del PP aclaró que había sido “una broma”.

... y los problemas reales de gestión

No obstante, e independientemente de los días de descanso de los miembros del Gobierno, sí ha habido fallos de gestión y de comunicación en la crisis de Ceuta que han alimentado el viejo debate sobre las vacaciones de los políticos. Para la politóloga Cristina Monge, “no se trata de si deben tenerlas o no, que por supuesto que sí, siempre coordinándose entre ellos, sino de saber reaccionar”. A su juicio, lo sucedido en Ceuta “demandaba un operativo especial que no se ha dado ante una de las mayores crisis geopolíticas de las últimas décadas”. “En la manifestación del pasado domingo los ceutíes gritaban que se sentían abandonados y, si se sienten así, es porque algo no se ha hecho bien”, sostiene.

La reacción del Gobierno ante la crisis, intentando adelantar el regreso a “la normalidad”, ha contribuido a generar la idea de que la situación actual obedece al descanso vacacional del Ejecutivo y, principalmente, de su presidente. Sánchez interrumpió sus días de descanso para desplazarse a Ceuta el pasado 31 de julio y describir lo ocurrido como una “violación de la integridad territorial de España”.

“Evidentemente”, explica Pablo Simón, “el presidente ha estado pendiente, pero lo que espera la gente es que lo proyecte”. “Por eso el propio Gobierno ha tratado de generar una contranarrativa con la famosa foto de la videoconferencia con los ministros desde La Mareta”, días después de la entrada de miles de inmigrantes irregulares en la ciudad autónoma. En una de las imágenes difundidas no se ven las piernas del presidente bajo la mesa del despacho, lo que ha provocado una catarata de especulaciones y de burlas. Fuentes de La Moncloa aseguran que se trata de “un efecto óptico” y que no editaron la fotografía. También añaden que hubo otras videoconferencias parecidas, antes y después, de las que no se tomaron imágenes.

Miles de ceutíes participan en una protesta el pasado domingo para reclamar una respuesta a la crisis desatada en la ciudad autónoma. Reduan Dris (EFE)

Es probable, como ha ocurrido otros veranos, que el debate sobre las vacaciones del presidente no hubiera muerto aunque la crisis de Ceuta se hubiera resuelto de manera adecuada. Pero en este caso, como señalan los expertos consultados, el Gobierno ha cometido varios errores. “Es un ejemplo típico de Ciencia Política que damos en la facultad”, explica Monge. “Lo primero es definir bien el problema; lo segundo, dimensionarlo, y lo tercero, poner los recursos necesarios para solucionarlo. Si haces mal lo primero y lo segundo, es imposible acertar en lo tercero”. Para esta politóloga, “el Gobierno definió mal el problema: porque no es una crisis migratoria, sino geopolítica”. “A las 24 horas habló de la entrada de 49.000 personas y han sido cerca de 80.000″, apunta. Y recalca: “No puedes equivocarte en un 100% porque el operativo necesario es distinto, del mismo modo que no es lo mismo tener 2.000 menores no acompañados que 4.000. Por eso ha habido familias acogiéndolos, niños durmiendo en la calle y personas que han estado varios días sin comer”.

La gestión ha fallado y el Defensor del Pueblo ha iniciado una actuación de oficio para saber por qué. Ha requerido información a la Secretaría de Estado de Migraciones, a la Delegación del Gobierno, a la Fiscalía General y a las autoridades de Ceuta. Pero, además, ha habido fallos en la comunicación.
