World.title: Southwest monsoon seen to strengthen again in third week of August
World.content:
WEATHER SYSTEMS. Satellite image of the two low pressure areas outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of August 16, 2026, 3 pm.

Four provinces in Northern Luzon and one in Central Luzon are seeing moderate to heavy rain from Sunday afternoon, August 16, to Monday afternoon, August 17

MANILA, Philippines – While the southwest monsoon or habagat eased during the weekend, it could strengthen again in the third week of August, the weather bureau warned the public on Sunday afternoon, August 16.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in a briefing at around 5 pm on Sunday that the southwest monsoon will still affect Luzon and the Visayas, especially areas on the western side, in the coming days.

PAGASA’s latest rainfall outlook shows these provinces may be most affected over the next 72 hours:

Sunday afternoon, August 16, to Monday afternoon, August 17

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Zambales

Monday afternoon, August 17, to Tuesday afternoon, August 18

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Zambales, Bataan, Cavite, Batangas, Occidental Mindoro, Antique

Tuesday afternoon, August 18, to Wednesday afternoon, August 19

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas, Occidental Mindoro, Antique

For Sunday evening, aside from the provinces mentioned above, Metro Manila, the Cordillera Administrative Region, Ilocos Norte, Batanes, Cagayan, Nueva Vizcaya, Nueva Ecija, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, and Occidental Mindoro are also seeing scattered rain and thunderstorms due to the southwest monsoon.

The Visayas and the rest of Luzon may just have isolated rain showers or thunderstorms on Sunday evening, still because of the southwest monsoon.

In areas with significant rainfall, floods and landslides remain likely.

PAGASA is also monitoring two low pressure areas (LPAs) outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

The first LPA, which formed last Thursday, August 13, was located 2,395 kilometers east northeast of extreme Northern Luzon as of 3 pm on Sunday.

It initially had a high chance of developing into a tropical depression, but this likelihood gradually decreased. It is currently unlikely to become a tropical depression in the next 24 hours.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Grace Castañeda-Carpio also said the first LPA is moving away from PAR.

Meanwhile, the second LPA formed just on Sunday. It was last spotted 1,385 kilometers east of Central Luzon at 3 pm, and could enter PAR in the evening, according to Carpio.

So far, the second LPA has a low chance of developing into a tropical depression within 24 hours. Beyond that period, the likelihood of tropical cyclone development may increase.

Carpio also said another LPA or potential tropical cyclone may form west of Northern Luzon in the coming days.

These weather disturbances could eventually pull or enhance the southwest monsoon.

PAGASA expects up to four tropical cyclones to develop within or enter PAR in August. There have already been two during the month — Tropical Depression Luis and Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira).

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) reported on Sunday morning that the death toll from the southwest monsoon, Luis, and Maymay combined stands at 23. Seventeen others were injured, while one remains missing.

The bad weather in August has affected at least 4.87 million people or 1.4 million families across 10 regions, based on NDRRMC data.

So far, the estimated cost of damage to infrastructure is already at P3.4 billion, while the estimated cost of damage to agriculture has risen to over P689 million. – Rappler.com

World.title: Gilas Pilipinas counting on Kai Sotto’s return, but ‘no word’ yet from star big man
World.content:
ALL SMILES. Justin Brownlee (32) and Kai Sotto (11) in action for Gilas Pilipinas in the 2024 FIBA Asia Cup Qualifiers.

It remains uncertain whether Kai Sotto, who has not suited up for Gilas Pilipinas in over a year, will return to action as the Philippines fights to keep its FIBA World Cup bid alive

MANILA, Philippines – Gilas Pilipinas needs Kai Sotto now more than ever as its FIBA World Cup aspirations hinge on its upcoming games in the Asian Qualifiers.

But it remains uncertain whether the 7-foot-3 big man, who has not suited up for the national team in over a year, will return to action anytime soon.

“No word,” said head coach Tim Cone when asked about Sotto’s participation in the fourth window of the Asian Qualifiers, where the Philippines will host Jordan and Iran on August 28 and 30, respectively, at the Mall of Asia Arena.

Sotto last donned the national colors in 2024, when he powered the Philippines to a superb 4-0 start in the FIBA Asia Cup Qualifiers that included a breakthrough victory over New Zealand.

He suffered a knee injury in January 2025 and has not played for Gilas Pilipinas since then.

Without Sotto, the Nationals have lost nine of their last 13 games in FIBA play, with their only victories coming against teams ranked outside the world top 60: No. 65 Saudi Arabia, No. 77 Guam, and No. 81 Iraq.

Most of their losses came against world No. 7 Australia and No. 25 New Zealand, with No. 39 Philippines falling to the Boomers three times and the Tall Blacks four times over that stretch.

Ending the first round of the Asian Qualifiers with a 2-4 record, the Filipinos need to win as many games as possible against Iran, Jordan, and Syria in the second round to have a chance at earning a World Cup slot.

Iran and Jordan carry identical 5-1 records, while Syria is tied with Gilas Pilipinas at 2-4.

That is where it gets more complicated.

Already dealing with Sotto’s absence, the Nationals face more manpower issues as they also miss the big men Quentin Millora-Brown, who continues to recover from a back surgery, and Mike Phillips, who begged off from the fourth window to attend his brother’s wedding.

“We certainly have our issues. It’s really on me to make sure we get all the best players and we haven’t been able to do that. I’ve been failing at my job because I just haven’t been able to get all the best players,” Cone said.

That makes Sotto’s return all the more important for the team.

However, Cone said the 24-year-old Sotto is still pursuing an NCAA opportunity in the United States, which is a potential pathway to the NBA.

“Even for the Asian Games, no word. From my understanding, he’s still working on the NCAA, trying to get there to the NCAA,” said Cone.

While the odds are stacked against them, Cone is determined to work with the resources at his disposal, confident that the core of Dwight Ramos, Kevin Quiambao, Carl Tamayo, Justin Brownlee, and AJ Edu is capable of getting the job done.

“The margin of error is really dissipated for us. Like I’ve been saying, over the last few weeks, this is all-hands-on-deck kind of thing,” said Cone.

“We’re going to put up a fight here,” he added. “We’d like a little bit more size but it is what it is.” – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Exposing the Revilla flood control contracts — the easy part
World.content:
For more than 20 years, it had been the talk not just in Cavite but in national political circles that the company of Princess Revilla (Rebecca Bautista-Ocampo) was getting contracts either from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) or from contractors who were bagging projects from the agency.

Her company, Graia Construction Corporation, was formed in 2003. That year, her father, Ramon Revilla Sr., was nearing the end of his final term as senator. He had been the longtime chairperson of the Senate committee on public works — a body that had a hand in shaping the budget of the DPWH. The following year, her brother Ramon “Bong” Revilla Jr. would be elected senator and “inherit” — yes, like a family property — the chairmanship.

As I said, however, these things were only talked about in frustrated or disgusted whispers. (I’ll spare you the Tagalog expressions we had heard, but you can use your imagination.)

Until the flood control scandal broke.

Until the public realized how this newest form of corruption, difficult to detect before now, was perfected during the Duterte administration.

Until Rappler called on citizens to help us verify the leads we had gotten or to give us new ones from their localities.

Until Rappler started a series on “policontractors” and their relatives cornering projects in their fiefdoms, and Caviteños started asking: “Kelan ‘nyo iimbestigahan ang mga Revilla? (Followed by unpublishable words…)”

Until a curious and courageous campus journalist from the University of the Philippines Manila named Axel Cainglet took on the challenge, and once and for all looked for solid proof of what, for the longest time, was only “common knowledge” of conflict of interest (which is a crime), if not alleged full-blown corruption.

Axel, news editor of The Manila Collegian, is under my mentorship in the current cycle of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship. Quick to absorb instructions and understand contexts and relationships, he extracted from the DPWH portal almost a decade’s worth of contracts that Graia Construction got from the agency. He cross-tabulated them per city and town.

Together, we plotted the contracts against a timeline of political events involving members of the Revilla clan who were in the legislature. And the result was this story, which was our most-read one, with impressive numbers, for a full day — from morning until late night: Bong Revilla’s sister bags almost P5-billion DPWH contract in family’s Cavite bailiwick.

Instantly, Rappler got thank you messages from Caviteños, and most readers were commenting with variations of “What have we been talking about?” and “This has been going on for so long.”

Thankfully, sources privy to the projects are offering us more information. Like they knew we will see this issue through.

Providentially, when an ABS-CBN reporter asked the Ombudsman about Rappler’s findings (start at 6:09 mark), he revealed that a team of prosecutors too had already been gathering evidence for months.

If you’d ask me, though, all this was the easy part. We expose, anti-corruption advocates are encouraged, citizens appreciate the work, government prosecutors start the arduous process of building a case…

And then the election comes. And voters still reelect the contractors or their relatives. And the national budget stays as “unsexy” news that most people choose not to follow. And contractors like Graia, even if projects are proven to be substandard or unfinished, continue getting DPWH projects unless they are banned.



I am not being pessimistic. I’m just trying to say, we — journalists, watchdogs, and every citizen who cares enough for clean and honest governance — need to continue the work, and work harder at what we do.

If you believe in Rappler’s work and the part that independent journalism plays in building a better nation, I hope you can support us by becoming a Rappler+ member or by contributing to our investigative journalism fund. – Rappler.com

Inside the Newsroom is a newsletter delivered straight to your inbox every week. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to manage your newsletter subscriptions.

World.title: How Janine Berdin learned to trust in her own artistry
World.content:
The breakout Bisaya artist shows why her voice, lyrics, and overall craft are here to stay

Cebuana singer-songwriter Janine Berdin has always been known for her iconic voice. From being the champion of Tawag ng Tanghalan in 2017 and a regular on ASAP Natin ‘To, her distinctive tone and vocal power has made her one of the most unique singers in OPM right now.

But with her first self-written album, LAB SONGS NG MGA TANGA, and her viral worldwide hit, “What if I miss you for the rest of my life?” she is growing into an artist with a masterful command of not only her vocals, but also her own sound and lyricism.

Her debut album is a sleeper hit full of grunge, pop punk, emo, and shoegaze influences, with the grit and intensity of the instrumentals perfectly matching Janine’s iconic vocals. However, it is the narratives contained in her album that make her an artist worth watching.

Vulnerable, relatable, raw, witty, and weirdly specific, Janine’s biggest strength as a songwriter is her generosity and ability to share her rich inner world with her audience.

Turning heartache into material

“I think everything we experience is the same with other people, just dressed differently or in a different font,” she said. “I just like to write about the stuff that I don’t hear being talked about yet. I needed something that could relate to my feelings. So I make it my responsibility to write a song that makes me feel like this.”

This is how she described the writing process for fan-favorite track “Friendship Over” on her deluxe album, MORE LAB SONGS NG MGA TANGA. It’s a riff-heavy pop confessional that captures so specifically the universal pain of growing apart and mourning a lost connection.

Janine’s songwriting is sincere and honest, as she usually gets material from her own personal experiences. But even if her lyrics come from very specific parts of her life (the line, “Di ka man lang nag-hi sa akin” was a real experience she had with an ex), her listeners can still deeply relate and connect with her songs.

When asked, though, if she finds it difficult or embarrassing to go back to her painful experiences to make art, she readily answered that she doesn’t.

“It’s okay, I got through it, that’s why I get to talk about it, and it might help someone out there who is going through the same things,” she said. “I am really okay with tapping into stuff I have moved on from, I’ve grown from, and it’s good writing material.”

One beautiful song of hers borne from a painful experience is “PROMISE..!!!” a track that has solidified itself in Janine’s discography as one of her most emotionally vulnerable, fragile, and, in her own words, “pathetic.” It carries in both its lyrics and instrumentation the desperation and denial of trying to hold on to someone who no longer wants to stay.

She shared that her painful past experiences have led her towards the life and identity she is grateful for today. “I learned how to respect myself. I love myself, I also met someone who takes good care of me. So thank you to the people who treated me like shit, I am now a grown woman.”

Make what we like, everything else will follow

This unapologetic sincerity and authenticity is what Janine and her team anchor themselves on as artists.

“I wanted to be the number one fan of my own songs,” Janine shared. “When it came to making this record, me and my bandmates were like, we have to make this honest and make stuff we like and not think of anything else. If we like it, then someone else will have to like it as well.”

A track that encapsulates this attitude perfectly is “Mirisi,” a standout trilingual track with lyrics in English, Filipino, and Bisaya. The word mirisi is a Bisaya term that captures the expression, “serves you right.”

“I built the song around the chorus, and for some reason I heard Bisaya in my head,” she said.

Born and raised in Cebu, the word mirisi sparked Janine’s imagination, as she has never encountered a direct translation in any other language she speaks. “’Mirisi’ is something I’m super proud of. It’s the only track I have produced.”

She shared that “Mirisi” is one of the songs that represents her growth as an artist who is now more confident in her choices, takes risks, and trusts her own vision. “I feel like I am most honest with my music, because I did grow up as a people pleaser.”

From other people’s expectations to voices that planted doubts in her heart, Janine has had to overcome loneliness and uncertainty in order to commit to her vision and believe in her own art, especially when success felt slow or out of reach.

“I was saying to people, ‘Okay lang naman talaga kung walang streams (it’s okay if there are no streams), cause what’s important is there are people who listen to me.’ But it came to a point where I thought, ‘What is my art for if no one else hears it?’ So I became very lonely for a time.”

There is no song that represents this triumph better than her breakout hit, “What if I miss you for the rest of my life?” Many people’s first encounter with this song was by stumbling upon it on social media, when Janine posted a performance snippet with the simple caption, “I wrote this song while shitting on the toilet.”

No one could scroll away, however, when they were attacked by Janine’s powerful vocals, her band going all out on the instrumentals, and, most of all, the heartwrenching lyrics of someone refusing to move on from a past relationship.

The song went viral all over the country and beyond, with international superstars like Demi Lovato, Lauren Jauregui, Doechii, and SZA praising Janine’s work.

As the song that pushed her voice further than it has gone before, Janine has always had faith in this track. “I really worked hard for this song and when no one believed in it, I believed in it the most, so I am grateful that it got to where it is now.”

All worth the wait

From shooting her own videos to promote the song with her friends and bandmates, Janine always knew this song was special. Watching the flood of streams and reactions to her song in real time kept driving her to tears.

“When I saw the streams, when I saw real people making edits to the song, it was a super emotional experience. And I knew people would connect to this song! I never stopped believing in it.”

Throughout the ups and downs of life, and the uncertainties that come with being a rising young artist in the Philippines, Janine’s greatest strength is her faith in her team and her vision.

“I told my band all the time, ‘Someday, someone will get it.’ So again, I knew it was going to come, because I was a fan of my music. But when it came, I wasn’t prepared for how big it was going to get.”

Her very first headline concert, “Concert ni Janine Berdin,” live at the New Frontier Theater on October 7, is a testament to just how much her music has finally reached the people who she knew would love it as much as she does.

By being brave enough to be honest, strong enough to have faith in her artistry, and possessing the power of both her words and her voice, Janine Berdin is on her way to becoming one of OPM’s most exciting rising stars. The day she had been waiting for, the day that people would finally “get” her music, looks like it’s finally arrived. – Rappler.com

Elise Suarez is a Rappler intern from Puerto Princesa City and a Humanities student of the University of Asia & the Pacific.

World.title: [Finterest] Concentrix rolls out matched PERA for employees. Is it time to start yours?
World.content:
In case you haven't heard of the hottest retirement savings program, PERA offers you a way to start investing for your retirement while getting tax advantages

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ biggest private employer is putting an increasingly used retirement product in front of tens of thousands of its workers.

Concentrix Philippines is rolling out an employer-matched Personal Equity and Retirement Account (PERA) for its employees nationwide through investment platform DragonFi, potentially giving the government’s tax-advantaged retirement program one of its biggest corporate pushes yet.

DragonFi and Concentrix described the initiative as the largest employer-matched PERA program offered to Filipino IT-BPM workers. Concentrix describes itself as the largest private employer in the Philippines across all industries, with over 100,000 employees in the country.

Bringing PERA into a workforce this large could be a big boost for a retirement program that has yet to gain mass adoption but is quickly growing. By June 30, 2026, the number of PERA contributors had surged to 30,055, nearly five times the 6,193 recorded a year earlier, with combined investments reaching P755.6 million, according to Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas data shared with Rappler.

So what exactly is PERA?

In a sense, PERA is the Philippine’s counterpart to tax-advantaged individual retirement accounts in other countries, like the 401(k) system in the US.

Created under the PERA Act of 2008, it is a voluntary retirement savings program meant to supplement SSS, GSIS, company retirement plans, and a worker’s other investments. Money placed in a PERA can be invested in qualified products, including money market, bond, and equity funds. Note, however, you can’t pick individual stocks and bonds to be included in your PERA.

One of its main attraction is the tax treatment.

An employee or self-employed Filipino may contribute up to P200,000 a year, while overseas Filipinos may contribute as much as P400,000. Qualified contributions earn a 5% tax credit, meaning someone contributing the full P200,000 may receive up to P10,000 in tax credits. Investment income earned by qualified PERA investments is also tax-exempt, as are qualified retirement withdrawals.

For those interested to open a PERA, just remember that it’s designed for retirement, not as a savings account that you can freely dip into.

To make a qualified tax-free withdrawal, a contributor generally has to be at least 55 years old and have contributed for at least five years. Early withdrawals can trigger penalties and the repayment of tax incentives, with limited exceptions such as prolonged hospitalization or permanent total disability. – Rappler.com

Finterest is Rappler’s series that demystifies the world of money and gives practical advice on managing your personal finances.

World.title: Scholars Call for Broader View of Golden Horde’s Legacy
World.content:
ASTANA – Three historians from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the Republic of Tatarstan in Russia explored how the Golden Horde continues to shape the historical narratives and identities of their countries during a podcast organized by Kazakh historian and Golden Horde researcher Zhaksylyk Sabitov.

The discussion highlighted both the shared historical legacy of the medieval empire and the distinct national perspectives that have emerged across Central Asia and the Volga Region.

According to Damir Iskhakov, an ethnologist and researcher of Tatar ethnogenesis at the Marjani Institute of History in Kazan, perceptions of the Golden Horde have changed significantly in recent decades.

“There was a time when many Kazakhs believed their origins lay primarily with the Kipchaks or other earlier peoples rather than the Golden Horde. Today, historical evidence and the composition of Kazakh clans clearly demonstrate a direct connection with the Golden Horde,” he said.

He added that growing scholarly interest has strengthened understanding of the Golden Horde’s contribution to the formation of the Kazakh nation.

Gaibulla Babayarov, a specialist in ancient Turkic epigraphy and numismatics at the Institute of Oriental Studies in Tashkent, noted that bringing together experts from different countries enriches understanding of the Golden Horde.

“Each country has its own unique perspective, which makes discussions like this especially valuable,” Babayarov said.

Babayarov highlighted that the Golden Horde is often mistakenly viewed as unrelated to Uzbekistan’s history.

“In reality, the Golden Horde period played an important role in the ethnogenesis of the Uzbek people,” he said.

While most of present-day Uzbekistan belonged to the Chagatai Ulus, the country’s northwestern territories, particularly Northern Khorezm, were part of the Golden Horde. Many Uzbek clans originated in the Dasht-i Kipchak, with Babayarov estimating that nearly half of traditional Uzbek tribal groups trace their roots to that region.

“For this reason, the histories of the Golden Horde and the Chagatai Ulus should be studied together rather than separately. They share common roots and represent a shared historical heritage,” he said.

Clan system united Turkic peoples

The discussion also focused on the Golden Horde’s clan structure.

Iskhakov described the subject as one of the least studied areas of medieval history because of the limited number of surviving historical sources.

“One of our main tasks today is to trace how a relatively small number of original clans, perhaps 12 or 14, eventually evolved into the much larger clan system described in the Edige epic, which refers to the ‘Ninety-Clan Horde.’ What is remarkable is that many of these clans can still be traced among various Turkic peoples,” Iskhakov said.

He also noted that the Golden Horde was organized through a strict hierarchy of clans. The ruling dynasty was closely connected through marriage alliances with the leading emir families that helped govern the state.

Babayarov added that Soviet-era scholarship often overlooked clan history in Uzbekistan because Uzbeks were portrayed primarily as a settled people rather than a society with strong tribal traditions.

He noted that ethnonyms and clan names remain preserved in village names across much of Uzbekistan, particularly in the Samarkand, Kashkadarya and Surkhandarya regions.

Balancing genetics and history

Sabitov urged caution when interpreting genetic research in historical studies.

“Genetics is an important research tool, but it should not be used to determine who is or is not a ‘real’ representative of an ethnic group,” he said.

He noted that genetic studies often produce various conclusions depending on the questions researchers ask.

“If you search for similarities among Turkic peoples, you will find similarities. If you search for differences, you will find differences. Ethnicity cannot be reduced to DNA,” he said.

Iskhakov agreed, saying genetics is useful for tracing family relationships over several centuries but becomes much less reliable when applied to medieval populations.

“Ethnic identity is shaped primarily by shared historical memory, language and culture. Genetics represents only one small part of that much larger picture,” Iskhakov said.

Revisiting Tatar history

Iskhakov also recalled how Soviet historiography largely excluded the Golden Horde from the history of the Tatars.

He said that during the Stalin era, official scholarship promoted the theory that modern Tatars descended exclusively from the Volga Bulgars. While the Golden Horde was portrayed as unrelated to Tatar history.

Only after the collapse of the Soviet Union did historians begin integrating the Golden Horde into mainstream interpretations of Tatar ethnogenesis.

“Today, the Golden Horde occupies its rightful place in the multi-volume history of the Tatar people. We now recognize the contributions of the ancient Turks, the Bulgar period, the Kipchaks and the Golden Horde as equally important stages in our shared history,” Iskhakov said.

World.title: Archaeological Discoveries Across Kazakhstan Shed New Light on Medieval Life
World.content:
ASTANA – A series of recent archaeological discoveries across Kazakhstan is offering new insights into the history, culture and everyday life of communities that lived on the Great Steppe centuries ago.

Findings from archaeological sites in the Zhambyl, Turkistan and Pavlodar regions include medieval buildings, a mosque and paved streets, valuable artefacts and a remarkably preserved mobile dwelling associated with the Kimak-Kipchak period (9th-10th centuries). Together, the discoveries highlight the diversity of life in the medieval steppe and the region’s links with neighbouring civilisations.

Archaeologists working at the Akzhar settlement in Zhambyl Region have uncovered remains of structures dating to the 11th–12th centuries. The medieval settlement is located west of the Kurenbel village in the Zhualy district, between tributaries of the Akzhar River.

The excavations revealed structures made of mud brick, along with fragments of ceramics, iron and glass objects, stone tools and bones of domestic animals, reported the region’s Culture and Language Development Department. Researchers say the findings can help reconstruct the daily life of the people who inhabited the settlement during different periods.

The animal remains are of particular interest to researchers, as their study could provide information about the diet, economy and lifestyle of the settlement’s residents.

The excavations are being carried out as part of a scientific program studying the Syr Darya and Karatau regions in antiquity and the Middle Ages. Researchers expect the findings to help clarify Akzhar’s role in the development of medieval urban culture in the Karatau region.

Further south, archaeological work at the Otyrar settlement in the Turkistan Region has revealed several layers of historical development dating 13th-18th centuries.

Researchers identified five construction horizons containing residential and household areas, brick-paved streets and kilns used for firing bricks. One of the most notable discoveries was a collective burial site, known as a dakhma, identified for the first time at Otyrar.

At the lowest, fifth construction horizon, archaeologists uncovered the remains of a mosque dating to the Golden Horde period. A street paved with large stones led to the building and connected to a staircase made of fired bricks. According to the researchers, a paved street of this scale had not previously been documented at Otyrar.

The excavations also revealed painted window grilles, parts of inkpots, door or gate fittings, Chinese-style ceramic fragments, Chinese coins and coins minted in the names of rulers of the Golden Horde, a powerful state that dominated much of the Eurasian steppe from the 13th to 15th centuries.

One particularly notable discovery was a ring bearing an inscription, which researchers believe may have served as a seal in the medieval period.

The archaeological evidence points to Otyrar’s extensive connections with other parts of the region. Similar materials have been found at sites associated with Sogdiana, Tashkent, Fergana and Zhetysu, while imported objects and coins indicate the city’s participation in wider trade and cultural networks.

Researchers also believe the newly uncovered street could help reconstruct the layout of medieval Otyrar and identify commercial and public spaces that once stood along it. The excavations at the Otyrar settlement were conducted by a team led by Mukhtar Kozha, a professor and chief researcher at the Institute of Archaeology of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi International Kazakh-Turkish University.

In the Pavlodar Region, archaeologists have uncovered what researchers describe as an exceptionally rare example of a mobile dwelling from the Kimak-Kipchak period, reported the region’s press office.

The discovery was made at the Baidala burial ground in the Kenzhekol rural district of Pavlodar. The site is considered one of the significant archaeological monuments associated with the era of the Kimak Khaganate. According to researchers, the area may correspond to Imakia, described as a political center of the Kimak Khaganate, a medieval state or tribal confederation that existed roughly from the 9th to the early 11th century in what is now northeastern and central Kazakhstan and parts of western Siberia.

The most significant discovery is a fully preserved mobile dwelling consisting of a wooden wheeled structure with a tent-like covering. Archaeologists said its construction is similar to that of the traditional Kazakh yurt and that the discovery appears to be unprecedented in the archaeological record of the Eurasian steppe.

The dwelling was accompanied by a wooden saddle, stirrups, a bit, weapons, jewellery, silk textiles and other artefacts. These objects provide additional evidence about the material culture and everyday life of medieval nomadic communities. Before the discovery, knowledge about similar mobile dwellings largely came from written sources and schematic depictions.

Archaeological research at Baidala has been conducted for more than two decades led by archaeologist Timur Smagulov. Further excavations, conservation and restoration of the finds are planned, along with proposals to turn the complex into a museum site and develop it as an important historical and cultural heritage attraction.

The remains of buildings and streets reveal the organization of settled communities and their urban infrastructure, while the mobile dwelling offers a rare physical representation of nomadic life. Artefacts from Otyrar, meanwhile, point to the movement of goods, technologies and cultural influences across Central Asia and beyond.

For archaeologists, such discoveries are more than isolated objects or structures. They provide pieces of evidence that can be combined to reconstruct how people lived, travelled, traded and interacted across the Great Steppe.

While excavations and conservation work continue, researchers expect further discoveries to contribute to a more detailed understanding of Kazakhstan’s medieval heritage and its place in the broader history of Eurasia.

World.title: Preparing for Economy That Doesn’t Yet Exist: Why Kazakhstan’s Experiment Is Worth Watching
World.content:
One of the things that has surprised me most over the past year is how rarely my conversations with futurists actually stay focused on artificial intelligence. We usually begin there. We talk about generative models, autonomous agents, the next version of ChatGPT, the speed at which these systems are evolving. Yet after twenty or thirty minutes, AI almost disappears from the conversation. We find ourselves talking instead about labor markets, education, political institutions, governance and, eventually, something much larger than technology itself: the possibility that we are approaching the end of an economic model that has shaped modern societies for generations.

AI isn’t the story

That shift in perspective has been difficult to ignore. We often compare AI to the internet or smartphones because it makes the transformation easier to understand. Those technologies undoubtedly changed our lives. But they never challenged one of the central assumptions underpinning modern economies: that human labor is the primary engine through which value is created and wealth is distributed. Artificial intelligence might.

During one of our interviews, futurist Brett King made an observation that has stayed with me ever since. The more automation we introduce into the economy, he said, the less the traditional mechanics of capitalism function in the way they were originally designed. As he put it, it will be the end of capitalism as we know it. Whether or not one agrees with his conclusion is almost secondary.

The more interesting question is what governments should do if he is even partially right. Because history suggests that institutions rarely have the luxury of waiting until structural change is complete before deciding how to respond. By then, the transition is usually far more painful than it needed to be.

Perhaps this is why I have gradually become less interested in AI itself and more interested in leadership. Not political leadership in the conventional sense, but the ability of governments to think beyond immediate political cycles and prepare societies for an economy that does not yet fully exist.

Brett challenged another assumption that many of us have taken for granted over the last four decades: that markets, left largely to themselves, will eventually solve most problems.

“The free market hasn’t solved climate change. The free market hasn’t solved poverty. It hasn’t solved homelessness. This is not something that the free market is going to solve. This is a function of coordinated governance,” he told me.

It is a provocative argument, particularly at a time when governments around the world are still trying to determine how much they should regulate artificial intelligence and how much they should simply allow innovation to unfold. Yet there is something compelling about the distinction he makes.

Artificial intelligence is not disrupting a single industry. It is beginning to influence healthcare, transportation, logistics, finance, manufacturing, education and public administration simultaneously. Unlike previous technological revolutions, it does not fit neatly within the responsibility of one ministry or one regulator. It cuts across virtually every institution that modern states have spent decades building.

If that is true, then leadership acquires a different meaning. It becomes less about managing today’s economy efficiently and more about preparing citizens for tomorrow’s economy before it fully arrives. This is perhaps why Kazakhstan has become an unexpectedly interesting case study.

Preparing before the future arrives

For years, discussions about Kazakhstan’s future largely revolved around energy, critical minerals, connectivity and its geopolitical position between major powers. Increasingly, however, another narrative has begun to emerge, one that places artificial intelligence at the center of the country’s long-term development strategy rather than treating it as another digital policy initiative.

Over the past two years, the government has launched the International AI Center Alem.ai, expanded the AI-Sana education initiative, invested in computing infrastructure and accelerated efforts to integrate artificial intelligence into public administration.

That shift is also evident in Kazakhstan’s official discourse. Speaking at the second meeting of the Council for the Development of Artificial Intelligence, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said that “traditional growth models based on resources and labour are losing effectiveness” and warned that unless Kazakhstan rapidly transitions to a fully integrated, AI-powered, data-driven economy, it risks falling behind in the global technological race.

Whether every initiative succeeds is, in some ways, beside the point. History offers very few examples of governments navigating technological revolutions perfectly. But there is a meaningful difference between preparing too early and preparing too late. One risks investing in ideas that will inevitably evolve. The other risks discovering that the rules of the global economy have already changed. This is precisely what Brett was referring to when he spoke not about technology, but about time.

Modern societies, he told me, have become trapped inside quarterly earnings reports, annual budgets and electoral cycles. Yet transformative projects have never been built that way. Cathedrals took generations. The Panama Canal took decades. The Apollo program demanded sustained political commitment that extended far beyond a single administration. AI, he believes, belongs in that same category of civilizational change.

Listening to him, I found myself wondering whether our biggest challenge is not AI at all. Perhaps it is our shrinking political imagination. Can democratic governments still think thirty years ahead? Can they justify investments whose returns may only become obvious long after today’s leaders leave office? Those questions feel increasingly relevant when looking at Kazakhstan.

President Tokayev has repeatedly noted that digital transformation is no longer optional but essential for maintaining competitiveness in a rapidly changing world. Speaking at the AI conference this July in Shanghai, he stressed that no country should remain merely a consumer of AI technologies and that every nation must develop its own human capital so technological progress serves society rather than deepening inequality.

“No country should remain merely a consumer of artificial intelligence. Every nation must have the opportunity to develop its own human capital, digital infrastructure and institutional capacity. At its core, this is a matter of fairness and equity,” he said.

The human side of an AI economy

What I find interesting is not the ambition itself. Many governments now speak enthusiastically about AI. What stands out is the attempt to connect AI with education, state capacity and long-term economic planning rather than viewing it simply as another technology sector. That connection surfaced repeatedly during my conversations with both futurists Brett King and Ron Immink.

Ron approached the issue from an entirely different direction. He was less concerned with algorithms than with culture. Most leading AI systems, he pointed out, continue to think primarily in English. Yet languages carry different ways of understanding the world, different historical experiences and different cultural contexts. If artificial intelligence is to become genuinely intelligent, it cannot simply translate languages; it must learn to understand them.

That observation gave me a different perspective on a seemingly minor piece of news: Kazakh has become one of the fastest-growing languages on ChatGPT. It is easy to dismiss that as an interesting statistic. But perhaps it represents something larger. In the age of AI, language is no longer only a question of identity. It increasingly becomes a question of participation. Cultures that exist inside AI systems will inevitably have a stronger voice in shaping how those systems understand humanity itself.

Education raises a similar challenge. Ron believes our schools are still largely organized around the needs of an industrial economy, preparing students for stable careers inside systems that may not exist in their current form within a generation. Brett goes even further. He says that philosophy, psychology, ethics and lifelong learning may become just as important as engineering because the defining skill of the AI era will not simply be coding. It will be adaptation.

After months of interviewing futurists, I have come to think that AI is asking governments a surprisingly old question. Not whether they can innovate faster than everyone else, but whether they are capable of imagining a future that does not yet exist and preparing for it anyway. No one knows what the AI economy will ultimately look like. Predictions differ, technologies evolve faster than policies, and history has a habit of humbling even the most confident forecasts. There is no guarantee that every initiative launched today will produce the intended outcome. But perhaps that is not the point. The point is that waiting for certainty may no longer be an option.

Looking at Kazakhstan today, what I find noteworthy is less the technology itself than the shift in thinking behind it. AI is no longer being discussed simply as another digital industry or another innovation agenda. Increasingly, it has become part of a broader conversation about education, institutions, public administration and the country’s long-term economic direction. Whether through AI-Sana, investments in computing infrastructure, the development of Alem.ai, or recent efforts to integrate AI across government, the common thread is an attempt to prepare before the transition becomes unavoidable.

Perhaps that is what leadership will increasingly mean in the age of AI: not the ability to predict every technological breakthrough, but the willingness to create the conditions for a country to adapt to profound uncertainty. Kazakhstan appears to be making that bet today, investing in institutions, education and digital capacity before anyone can say with confidence what the AI economy will ultimately look like.

World.title: Data Center Valley Is More Than AI: It’s Kazakhstan’s Economic Diversification Bet
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is advancing construction of the Data Center Valley in the Pavlodar Region, a large-scale computing infrastructure project intended to support artificial intelligence development, attract international technology companies and create a new export-oriented segment of the digital economy, as Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov reviewed progress on Aug. 13.

The first facility, with a planned capacity of 50 megawatts, is now under construction. Excavation work for the energy center and AI factory buildings is 90% complete, while foundation work and construction of administrative facilities are underway. Officials said the main buildings of the data center and power units are expected to be completed by the end of December 2026. Commissioning work is scheduled to finish in May 2027, with the facility expected to begin operations in June 2027.

Kazakhstan has also acquired a 215-megawatt substation to supply the site, and is developing water and telecommunications infrastructure. In the longer term, Data Center Valley is designed to expand in stages to a total capacity of up to 1 gigawatt. That would turn the project from a single data center into a large computing campus capable of hosting data centers, AI factories, GPU clusters and cloud platforms for international hyperscalers.

Why computing capacity is becoming strategic

As artificial intelligence requires large amounts of computing power, data centers are becoming an essential part of the infrastructure supporting the digital economy. For Kazakhstan, the potential opportunity is to move beyond being primarily a consumer of foreign digital services and develop the infrastructure needed to host computing capacity within the country.

“Data Center Valley is creating a new export potential for Kazakhstan. By locating computing capacity within the country, we are creating conditions for developing domestic AI solutions, attracting global companies and entering the international market for digital services,” Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said.

According to Kazakhtelecom Board Chairman Bagdat Mussin, the project’s expansion will depend on confirmed client demand.

“Our first priority is to complete construction of the first facility in June 2027. At the same time, we are creating the engineering foundation that will allow us to gradually increase the campus capacity in line with confirmed customer demand,” he said.

The project will therefore need to solve two parallel challenges: building enough infrastructure to attract major technology companies while avoiding capacity that significantly exceeds demand.

From infrastructure to a digital ecosystem

The project is also being developed with international partners. Firebird AI and NVIDIA are involved in building an ecosystem around artificial intelligence, cloud technologies and next-generation digital services.

Another proposal discussed during the meeting, the Cloud First Policy, or Data Embassy project, illustrates this ambition. The initiative could allow foreign states to store data in Kazakhstan while retaining full legal sovereignty over it.

Data Center Valley is being developed as countries across the region seek to position themselves in the rapidly expanding market for artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. The first 50-megawatt facility, expected to open in June 2027, will therefore be an early test of a much larger strategy.

World.title: Kazakh Voters Increasingly Seek Concrete Policy Solutions, Experts Say
World.content:
ASTANA — Healthcare, education and social protection are emerging as key areas of competition in Kazakhstan’s election campaign, with experts saying voters are increasingly looking beyond broad promises to how seven political parties intend to deliver measurable improvements in quality of life.

Those issues were at the center of an Aug. 14 meeting of the Sarap Expert Club in Astana, where researchers, healthcare and education specialists and human-capital experts examined how social concerns are shaping party platforms and voter expectations ahead of the election.

The election to the Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral Parliament, is scheduled for Aug. 23. Seven political parties are set to compete, with 545 candidates registered for the race. Campaigning will end at midnight on Aug. 21, followed by a campaign silence day on Aug. 22. More than 12.6 million people are eligible to vote on Aug. 23. As of Aug. 13, the Central Election Commission had accredited 656 observers representing foreign states and international organizations.

Experts said the parties largely agree on the problems across healthcare, education, employment and social protection but increasingly differ over who should provide the solutions, how they should be financed and how their effectiveness should be measured.

Zhuldyzai Iskakova, head of the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development, which organized the Sarap meeting, said the televised debates helped make those differences more visible to voters. Three nationally televised debates have already aired live on Qazaqstan TV, Channel 7 and Jibek Joly, while the final debate is scheduled for Aug. 19 on 24KZ.

The first two debates drew a combined audience of around two million viewers, according to experts at the meeting.

“They examined their programs in detail and challenged one another,” Iskakova said. “There is a common perception that the parties are broadly similar and that it is difficult to understand what distinguishes them. In reality, there are fundamental differences between them.”

From social promises to competing solutions

Zhanar Sankhayeva, head of the Department of Political Research at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, said political parties are placing greater emphasis on social protection, healthcare and education in their election programs.

“Healthcare is among the top three issues of greatest concern to citizens, while education ranks among the top six priorities affecting people’s everyday lives,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the substance of party platforms could play an important role in voters’ decisions. She cited a survey by the Institute of Public Policy in which 44.4% of respondents identified parties’ initiatives, policy proposals and campaign promises as one of the important factors influencing their choice.

The expert said public expectations in the social sphere are also evolving. While earlier demands focused largely on expanding access to education and healthcare, voters are increasingly concerned with the quality of the services they receive.

“I would describe the current competition between parties in the social sphere as a transition from a competition of social promises to a competition of concrete models for solving social problems,” she said.

Sankhayeva said the election campaign is now entering a “more mature phase.”

“Voters are also moving from a general interest in the election toward forming specific political preferences,” she said.

Long-term priorities

According to Nazarbayev University Vice President Gulmira Qanay, the quality of people’s lives is a clear indicator of how effective or ineffective state policies are. Health, education, safety, professional opportunities and confidence in the future are among the main factors shaping quality of life.

She highlighted the constitutional emphasis on developing human capital, science and education, which should be an important part of the agenda for the future members of the Kurultai.

“We can see major transformations taking place around the world. If we look at the achievements of leading countries over the past 50 years and examine how they reached their current level of development, much of what we see today is the result of investments made in science, education, medicine and the social sphere,” said Qanay.

However, she also stressed that improvements in quality of life require long-term investment rather than measures tied only to an election cycle.

“These are not achievements that appear in a day or two. (…) That is something future members of the Kurultai should also keep in mind,” she added.

After saying that government policy should ultimately be judged by whether it improves people’s quality of life, Qanay said the same principle should apply to higher education, with universities assessed less by formal credentials and more by what graduates are able to do afterward.

Qanay said Kazakhstan should place greater emphasis on developing intellectual capital and designing education policy around research, evidence and measurable outcomes, particularly as digitalization and artificial intelligence transform the skills and standards expected of universities and the wider education system.

Healthcare challenges

Healthcare illustrates the gap that can emerge between policy ambitions and the everyday delivery of public services. Bakytzhan Tazhibay, chair of the AQNIET Kazakhstan Sectoral Trade Union of Healthcare and Public Service Workers and a pediatric urologist, said his review of all seven party platforms showed broad agreement on the sector’s principal challenges.

These include unequal access to quality care between major cities and remote villages, a lack of transparency in the mandatory social health insurance system, shortages of medical personnel and the bureaucratic burden placed on healthcare workers.

“Any reform will remain on paper if we forget about the people responsible for putting it into practice,” Tazhibay said. “At the center of the healthcare system are doctors, nurses, paramedics and other medical workers.”

He identified staff shortages and professional burnout as direct threats to the quality and safety of patient care. Although healthcare salaries have increased, he said, many doctors and nurses still work more than one full-time position to provide an adequate income for their families. This problem is particularly acute outside major cities.

He described elections as a “moment of truth for society.”

“This is the time when the country’s course of development is set, determining what our social policies, labor laws, family support, and healthcare system will look like for years to come,” he added.

Tazhibay called for healthcare expenditure equivalent to at least 5%–6% of gross domestic product, more stable base salaries, workloads consistent with professional standards and greater public and trade-union oversight of the social health insurance system.

World.title: From Grain to Value Chains: Kazakhstan Seeks to Transform Its Agricultural Export Model
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has nearly doubled its agricultural exports over the past five years, reaching $7 billion in 2025 from $3.8 billion, according to an analysis published by the World Financial Review. The growth has strengthened Kazakhstan’s role as a food supplier to Central Asia and beyond. Still, it raises a broader question about the country’s agricultural future: can rising export volumes translate into a higher-value agri-food economy?

According to the World Financial Review, Kazakhstan’s growing agricultural capacity and location between major Eurasian markets are creating new opportunities for the country to play a larger role in regional food security. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the UN Food and Agriculture Organization project that international trade will become increasingly important to global food systems, with around 22% of calories consumed worldwide expected to cross international borders by 2034.

For Kazakhstan, which borders or has close transport links to rapidly growing markets in Central Asia, China, the Caucasus and beyond, this creates an economic advantage. The country can supply regions with growing food demand while using its agricultural surplus to expand exports.

Kazakhstan’s agricultural products are already exported to more than 72 countries. Grain and flour remain among its most important exports, particularly to neighboring markets. Over the first 11 months of the latest marketing season, exports of grain and flour reached 13.5 million tons, according to figures cited in the World Financial Review.

Shipments increased particularly sharply to regional markets. Exports to Afghanistan rose by 59% to 2.2 million tons, while supplies to Uzbekistan increased by 37% to 5.6 million tons. Exports to the Kyrgyz Republic reached 504,000 tons, up around 40%, while shipments to Turkmenistan rose 34% to 210,000 tons.

These figures underline Kazakhstan’s importance as a regional supplier. But they also reveal the limits of an export model based primarily on increasing volumes of agricultural commodities.

From exporting more to creating more value

The more significant shift may now be taking place in food processing. According to official data, agricultural exports reached $7 billion in 2025, up 37% year-on-year. More than half of this amount, around $3.6 billion, came from processed agricultural products, whose exports grew by 35% compared with the previous year. The figures suggest that Kazakhstan is beginning to capture a larger share of the value generated from its agricultural production.

Vice Minister of Agriculture Yerbol Taszhurekov said processing is becoming one of the main drivers of growth in Kazakhstan’s agro-industrial complex. Speaking at a March 5 briefing at the Central Communications Service, he said the country’s strategy is not simply to increase agricultural output but to retain more of the economic value generated by it within Kazakhstan.

“Our strategic task is not only to increase the production of agricultural raw materials but also to ensure their processing within the country, including deep processing that creates products with high added value. Processing forms new production chains, creates jobs in the regions and strengthens Kazakhstan’s export potential,” Taszhurekov said.

But not all processing represents the same level of economic transformation. Turning wheat into flour is already a step beyond exporting raw grain. Deep processing, however, can create products such as starch, gluten, amino acids, syrups, vitamins and bioethanol, connecting agriculture to more complex industrial supply chains.

This distinction may become increasingly important for Kazakhstan. The country’s long-term agricultural strategy is therefore not simply about producing more grain, but about moving further along the value chain. The government aims to increase the share of processed agricultural products to 70%. New deep-processing facilities planned by 2028 are expected to have a combined capacity of 5.8 million tons per year and attract around 1.9 trillion tenge (US$3.9 billion) in investment.

Changing the fields to change the export model

The transformation is also evident in what Kazakhstan produces. In recent years, the area under wheat cultivation has declined by nearly 900,000 hectares. In comparison, oilseed acreage has increased by more than one million hectares and land used for pulse crops has expanded by 275,000 hectares, according to the World Financial Review.

This is more than a change in crop statistics. A broader crop mix creates a wider raw-material base for domestic processing industries. Oilseeds, for example, can support vegetable oil production, while pulses and grain can feed into increasingly sophisticated food and industrial processing. Kazakhstan produced a record 4.8 million tons of oilseeds in 2025, while food production rose 8.1% to 3.9 trillion tenge (US$8 billion).

The shift suggests that Kazakhstan’s agricultural diversification is becoming increasingly connected to its industrial policy. Diversification in the fields is intended to support diversification in factories, which in turn could change the composition of exports.
