World.title: In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare?
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPay In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare? Matt Wade and Craig Butt August 17, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The top 1 per cent of income earners in 83 Sydney suburbs take home over $1 million a year on average, while in a cluster of harbourside neighbourhoods, to make the 1 per cent bracket, you need to earn more than $3 million. Analysis of official personal income data by this masthead casts fresh light on how ultra-high pay packets are distributed across the city. In Bellevue Hill, about five kilometres east of Sydney’s central business district, the average income for the highest paid 1 per cent of taxpayers was $6.3 million in 2022-23. That was $1.2 million lower than the previous year but it was still the highest average for the 1 per cent in any city suburb. The top 1 per cent of Sydney earners takes home over $1 million a year. Nine



The adjacent neighbourhood of Rose Bay-Vaucluse-Watsons Bay had the city’s second-highest average earnings for the top 1 per cent at $6.12 million (down from $6.37 million the previous year). Third was Woollahra, where the top 1 per cent took home an average of $5.05 million (up from $4.99 million). There were eight Sydney neighbourhoods where the top 1 per cent had average earnings between $3 million and $5 million (all of them waterfront suburbs) and 72 where average earnings were between $1 million and $3 million. You can search how suburbs and localities across NSW compare here: While suburbs with the highest average incomes for the top 1 per cent were mostly in the eastern suburbs and on the north shore, several were located in the city’s north-west, including Dural-Kenthurst ($1.66 million) and Glenhaven ($1.58 million).



In two outer western Sydney neighbourhoods – Horsley Park-Kemps Creek and Mulgoa-Luddenham-Orchard Hills – the top 1 per cent took home just over $1 million a year. Demographer and social researcher Mark McCrindle said the high average earnings for the top 1 per cent in parts of western and north-western Sydney showed how patterns of income and wealth have shifted. “It tells a story of a changing Sydney,” he said. “Yes, we’ve got very high incomes in those harbourside suburbs which has been the case for 100 years, but we’ve got new locations with high incomes as well. The dynamics of wealth have spread geographically.” McCrindle said income distribution patterns across Sydney showed not all high-income earners wanted to live on the waterfront.



“Some choose to invest their money in a large property, perhaps in bushland, rather than in the harbour area. Places like Dural, Kenthurst and Glenhaven in Sydney’s north-west have really changed economically.” However, in some western suburbs, the earnings of the top 1 per cent was well below the citywide average. Lowest was Auburn North, about 20 kilometres west of the CBD, where the average income of the best paid 1 per cent was $200,656. Suburbs where the top 1 per cent have especially high incomes correlate closely with house prices. Bellevue Hill, which had Sydney’s best paid 1 per cent of earners, also had the city’s highest median house price of $10.4 million, according to Domain’s June quarter House Price Report. In neighbouring Vaucluse, the median house price was $9.5 million and in Rose Bay it was $6.5 million. In Bellevue Hill, the best paid 1 per cent earned an average of $6.3 million a year in 2022-23. It also has a median house price over $10 million. Renee Nowytarger The top 1 per cent of earners across the whole of Greater Sydney had an average income of $1,027,863 in 2022-23.



That was about 12 times more than the average annual personal income for all Greater Sydney taxpayers of $84,947 and 16 times the city’s median income (the middle value of all earners) of $62,180. Sydney was the only Australian capital where the average earnings for the top 1 per cent was a seven-figure total. Next highest was Perth, with average earnings of $928,762 a year for the top 1 per cent, followed by Melbourne with $792,491. The earnings figures show Sydney is Australia’s most unequal capital city for income: the top 1 per cent of earners received 12.1 per cent of the city’s income in 2022-23. That compares with 11.1 per cent in Perth, 10.2 per cent in Melbourne and 8.7 per cent in Brisbane. Nationally, the top 1 per cent earned 9.9 per cent of all personal income. Outside of Sydney there were some localities where the top 1 per cent had extremely high earnings. In the Upper Hunter town of Scone, the average income of the top 1 per cent of earners was just under $5 million, the fourth highest in NSW.



In Bangalow, near Byron Bay, the average income for the top 1 per cent was $1.9 million while in Robertson-Fitzroy Falls in the Southern Highlands, that average was $1.87 million. The suburb with the highest 1 per cent average income of anywhere in Australia was Cottesloe in Perth, where you need to be bringing in $36 million a year on average to be in that suburb’s top 1 per cent. In many neighbourhoods, including Cottesloe, the average income among the top 1 per cent is skewed by a few earners with extremely high earners – the top 0.1 per cent – who drive up the average. The analysis used Australian Bureau of Statistics personal income data, which draws on Tax Office records for the 2022-23 financial year, the most recent available. It includes figures for “Statistical Area Level 2” (SA2) localities that are similar to suburbs.



The data covers only individual pre-tax income; it does not include assets owned by individuals such as housing and shares. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Is Greek yoghurt really the miracle protein fix it’s made out to be?
World.content:
Tips & adviceHealthy eating Is Greek yoghurt really the miracle protein fix it’s made out to be? Is Greek yoghurt better for you than Greek-style yoghurt? We whey up the facts from the social media spin about the protein-powered staples still flying off the shelves. Caterina Hrysomallis August 17, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

No, you’re not imagining it. There’s been lots of buzz around Greek yoghurt recently, probably spurred by the collision of two TikTok trends. The first is still trending: “protein-maxxing”, which simply means maximising protein intake, with Greek yoghurt commonly identified, alongside chicken breasts, as top-tier healthy protein sources. The second? Placing Biscoff biscuits into a small tub of Greek yoghurt, leaving it for a few hours or overnight to create a mini dessert. Ironically, this combo is called a “Japanese cheesecake”. One claim that’s gained traction is that “Greek-style” yoghurt is not as good for you as “Greek”. Another is that other kinds of yoghurt, like natural yoghurt, are inferior. Meanwhile, yoghurts with long ingredient lists are also copping criticism. So, what’s real and what’s just social media speculation? Let’s break it down.



Chobani is among the better-for-you Greek yoghurt brands. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up What is Greek yoghurt? “To keep it really simple, Greek yoghurt is strained not stirred. That’s the key differentiating factor,” says dietitian Helena McDonald. The production process gives Greek yoghurt its superpower: high protein. “The straining process removes the whey and makes it a whole lot thicker. In doing so, it concentrates the protein content of the yoghurt.” Traditional Greek yoghurt is strained three times.



For Greek people, Greek yoghurt is the heart of a good tzatziki. It’s used in marinades, sometimes in filo pastry cheese pies, and is the key to yiaourtopita (yoghurt cake with lemon). Adam Liaw’s dill and mint tzatziki: a delicious way to eat Greek yoghurt. William Meppem How do you pick a good Greek yoghurt? Let’s rule one criterion out: if you’re looking for Greek-produced yoghurt in Australia, you won’t find any due to biosecurity restrictions. The term “Greek yoghurt” is not actually protected. Brands can call something Greek yoghurt even if it’s not from Greece or contains non-traditional additives. This makes things a little tricky.



If you’re after authenticity, traditional Greek yoghurt is plain, leans on milk, live cultures and sometimes cream – while avoiding thickeners. “There’s a really big misconception that ‘Greek-style’ yoghurts are worse for you and full of rubbish, which isn’t necessarily true.” Helena McDonald, dietitian “Many yoghurts here do call themselves ‘Greek-style’, even though they might not have other non-traditional additives in them.” Why? Simply, those brands are being cautious. “There’s a really big misconception that ‘Greek-style’ yoghurts are worse for you and full of rubbish, which isn’t necessarily true,” says McDonald. It all comes down to the ingredients list.



“The best thing you can do is always get familiar with flipping over packaging and looking at the ingredients label and the nutritional profile. A minimal ingredients list is always a good thing”. Two standout, authentic options are Chobani and Evia – both contain minimal ingredients and very high amounts of protein. Adam Liaw’s breakfast crumble with cherries and yoghurt. William Meppem Are longer ingredient lists ‘bad’? Not necessarily, despite their vilification on parts of social media. McDonald says it’s more about interrogating what the ingredients are. “There could be multiple types of natural fruit; that’s not inherently problematic.”



Be sure to compare products using the “per 100 gram”, not “per serving”, column, given that sizing can vary so much across the yoghurt category. McDonald says look out for number codes which refer to artificial sweeteners, emulsifiers and thickeners. “The jury’s still out around how much they impact our health and our gut microbiome. There is some evidence around emulsifiers being harmful for people with irritable bowel disease, ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s, but again, it’s all emerging.” Other yoghurts still deserve your attention. Getty Images Should we default to Greek yoghurt for nutritional purposes?



McDonald says it really depends on your goals and dietary requirements. “There’s no doubt it’s one of the best types of yoghurt that you can get.” It’s great for those with high-protein requirements. “For example, if you’re wanting to build muscle and optimise your body composition goals.” It’s also lower in carbohydrates, which means it’s lower in sugar and lactose. McDonald says that natural yoghurts are also a solid choice, as they generally lean towards a wholefood-based ingredient list. These are, however, lower in protein, as they’re typically stirred, not strained.



Greek yoghurts are lower in calcium, as so much of this is in the removed whey. Most yoghurts help add probiotics to the digestive system, but there are times when McDonald recommends very specific yoghurts. “Some brands offer specific strains and quantities of probiotics, which can be useful for certain digestive concerns. Some have evidence to support them in being helpful for things like constipation and other gastric concerns.” Related Article Natural, Greek, coconut, high-protein: The nutritional pros and cons of your favourite yoghurt What’s the go with fat content?



Where fat isn’t a concern, it can be helpful to keep the fat content in dairy products “as it may make you more satisfied from your meal and therefore less likely to go looking for other things later”, says McDonald. Dietary fat also helps with the absorption of fat-soluble nutrients, including vitamins A, D, E and K.



At the end of the day, this is just one food, so you if you don’t have specific dietary concerns, it’s not worth stressing over fat content too much. “It’s better to focus on a balanced diet that isn’t reliant on overly processed foods”, says McDonald. Raise your yoghurt pouch to that. Related Article Aussies are suckers for yoghurt pouches. We put them to the taste test – with mixed results Related Recipe collection 70 sweet and savoury yoghurt recipes

World.title: Brisbane’s most expensive homes are in our suburb, but we still love underdogs and outsiders
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion Brisbane’s most expensive homes are in our suburb, but we still love underdogs and outsiders Stephen Vagg Contributor August 17, 2026 — 5:00am

August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the late 1990s I lived in a top-floor apartment on New Farm’s Moray Street, aka Brisbane’s Most Liveable Street in 1993. I had a view of the Story Bridge, and lived just across the road from Wilson Outlook Reserve, while only paying $150 a week in rent. Mind you, the grass of that reserve was routinely covered in discarded syringes from local junkies, so it’s swings and roundabouts. All Brisbane suburbs change over time, but some change more rapidly than others, and nowhere is that truer than in New Farm. An area originally known as “Binkin-ba” (meaning “place of the land tortoises”), it was converted into a literal new farm in 1827 by notorious flog-happy British officer Captain Patrick Logan, later killed by Aboriginal people for doing some non-consensual exploring in their backyard.



The farm didn’t last that long, and neither did other features of the suburb over the years: the horse-drawn tram, for instance, which personally I’d love to see make a comeback; or the racecourse which later turned into New Farm Park; or the power station, which still exists in the form of Brisbane Powerhouse; or the deserted quarry at the bottom of New Farm cliffs, which is now the site of the Howard Smith Wharves. New Farm is always evolving. At one stage it was predominantly a low-rent area, providing accommodation for those who worked in the factories, wharves and submarine bases (no kidding) of Teneriffe. It was also a long-standing sanctuary for underdogs, oddballs and outsiders, such as immigrants, artists, drunks, derelicts and the LGBTIQ+ community. Now it’s very much a high-rent area, infested with botox clinics, $8 soy lattes, real estate agents and nepo babies, while many of the old inhabitants can no longer afford to live here. A house sold for $25 million in November, and New Farm topped the list of most expensive Brisbane homes last time I looked. Yet for all New Farm’s flaws, the suburb retains a magic about it, for me at least. Hemmed in on three sides by the “much prettier at night” Brisbane River, it’s close to the CBD, but feels far away.



It’s one of the best suburbs to walk or jog around, being full of different mini-neighbourhoods: the raffish charms of Brunswick Street with its vape stores and e-scooters; the Noosa-esque chic of James Street, with its designer brands and Range Rovers; the view of the city skyline and Story Bridge from the Riverwalk; the jacaranda-clad New Farm Park, the “lungs” of the suburb; the cocktails and pirate-ship playground of Howard Smith Wharves; the laurel trees of Abbott Street; the zen calm of New Farm Library, with its endlessly patient librarians; the bustle of Merthyr Village, particularly on pension day. It’s one of the best suburbs to jog around. Morgan Roberts The suburb always feels humming and alive, even on sleepy afternoons, and every time we lose something of the past (RIP Gertie’s Bar), something else seems to pop up instead (hello, Junk Bar). New Farm also has a genuine sense of community. For instance, in 2024 a French restaurant, À la Bonne Franquette, started up on Brunswick Street, run by a young married couple with a cute baby. They worked so hard (even the baby) and the food was so great, the whole neighbourhood was willing them to succeed – I certainly bought more of their beef bourguignon than I could afford at the time. And eventually they did succeed, and all of New Farm (well, the bit near me) cheered, because it’s nice to see a business that’s not a real estate agency do well. Co-owner Hugo Wintzer outside his restaurant. “A la bonne franquette” means “fuss free”. Morgan Roberts



The New Farm spirit is demonstrated in other ways, such as the Neighbourhood Centre, The Village Voice, and the way most locals stick up for the homeless whenever some bigot bags them on the New Farm Community Facebook page. This spirit is constantly under attack from things like the cost-of-living crisis and the real estate/botox/pearl-clutching brigade determined to turn us into a Queensland outpost of Sydney’s Mosman, but it’s still hanging in there, and as long as New Farm retains some sort of sympathy for the outsider and the underdog it will always be special. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs Yes, the cliches about my suburb are all true. Roll your eyes if you must Lucinda Kent Contributor My director wife Louise Alston and I recently made a feature film, All My Friends Are Back in Brisbane, about a woman who returns home from overseas and moves to New Farm, as we did during COVID. More than half the picture was set and shot in New Farm. We filmed in our apartment and other places I love in the suburb, such as Death Before Decaf, Hey Mr. Cafe, Wilson Outlook, Merthyr Park and near the sign on Moray Street that still proudly declares it was Brisbane’s most liveable street in 1993. The cash budget was $13,000, so we didn’t have an official production designer – but we had an unofficial one, and that was the suburb of New Farm. The movie made its Brisbane theatrical debut at Five Star Cinemas New Farm, across the road from our place, and had a 10-week run there. We tried to introduce every screening personally, and are constantly delighted at the love and passion New Farmians have for their suburb.



But then again why shouldn’t they? To us, it’s the best place in Brisbane, warts and all (botox and all, rather – the warts here tend to be surgically removed).

World.title: Developer hopes to cut out council for golf course resort, housing approval
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandDevelopment Developer hopes to cut out council for golf course resort, housing approval Julius Dennis August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The developer behind the proposal for a five-star hotel, industrial park and housing on rural land south-east of Brisbane has laid out plans that could bypass council and see a state-sanctioned development area established. Stephen Williams, best known for Riverlink in Ipswich and West Village in inner-Brisbane’s West End, says he is confident the state will add the land in Mount Cotton to the urban footprint and declare it a priority development area, paving the way for major changes. The land, largely comprising chicken farms and a winery, is in the Redland City Council area, which voted to support an investigation to include the area in the urban footprint earlier this year. Developer Stephen Williams is representing the Mount Cotton landholders. Julius Dennis Williams said he had initially been working with chicken farm owners Darwalla and Golden Cockerel, who were seeking a new use for their land as they planned to move their operations further away from the expanding Redlands population.



“The reason that opportunity came up is because of the avian flu risk for having chickens in the Redlands area, and the impact that could have on the activities of Golden Cockerel,” Williams said. Other landholders represented by Williams include local newspaperman and developer Warren Pryde and the Morris family, who own the nearby Sirromet Winery. Sirromet sits amid pristine land zoned rural. Sirromet Williams said he was confident applications currently with the state planner and Economic Development Queensland would result in the area being included in the urban footprint and deemed a PDA, which would enable the state to decide what happens on the land, not the council. The entire urban footprint of south-east Queensland is currently under review, with a draft plan expected by the end of the year.



Should he get his way, Williams said he hoped to move fast. “We have the ambition to meet some of the missing accommodation needs that are likely before the Olympic Games in 2032,” he said. The proposed development, including a five-star hotel, at Sirromet Winery in Mount Cotton. Under the plan, Sirromet would be transformed from a winery and events space with glamping facilities to a 250-room resort, complete with an 18-hole golf course, conference rooms and permanent villas. A masterplan seen by this masthead also includes a wellness centre, an expansion of the glamping facilities, horticultural gardens, a solar farm, and a wastewater treatment plant.



Related Article Exclusive

Development Council says development on farmland hinges on road with no timeframe Williams said it was business as usual at the winery for now, but that would be the first part of the plan to go ahead. The winery would connect the area to the already approved Southern Thornlands PDA. The southern end, made up of land owned by the chicken companies and pegged for a “technology park” and district centre that would include shops and condensed residential housing, would almost hug the already developed part of Mount Cotton. Between them is the land owned by Pryde and quarry owner Dick Karreman, who is on the project but represented by local developer Fiteni, Williams said. In Williams’ plan, this section, and part of a block owned by Golden Cockerel, would be residential blocks, roughly 20 per hectare.



But the council does not support more suburban development, and called for it to be excluded from the plan when it voted to support the area being investigated. Councillor Rowanne McKenzie, who brought the motion forward, said this was because the council already relied too heavily on household rates. “Approximately 90 per cent of council’s rate revenue is derived from residential properties, creating a heavy reliance on households to fund core services and infrastructure,” she said. In its letter to the government supporting the investigation of the land, the council said any urban development should be linked to the delivery of the Coomera Connector.



Referred to as the second M1, the Coomera Connector is an alternative route to the clogged motorway between the northern Gold Coast and Loganholme, just south of Brisbane, which has been in the works since 2016. Its final stage will swoop through the Redlands, near the proposed development. However, that section is only in the planning stage. “We note that that’s council’s decision, but we don’t agree with that. We agree it would be an ideal position, but it’s not based on any real traffic justification,” Williams said, arguing that upgrades to local infrastructure would be sufficient. While Williams said he was keen to work with the community and all levels of government, the council’s influence could be dashed by a PDA. Should that happen, it would be the fourth PDA in the Redlands, where infrastructure like sewerage and roads are contentious subjects.



Related Article Exclusive

Queensland councils In the red: Leaked report reveals council’s multimillion-dollar sewage problem A past Fiteni-linked development took more than a decade to connect to the wastewater network, while other projects have led to localised traffic problems. A council spokesperson said any work to core infrastructure would need to be covered by developers. In turn, Williams said he and the landowners would foot the bill for any infrastructure upgrades needed for the development, including a duplication of parts of Mount Cotton Road and an upgrade to the Mount Cotton water treatment plant. “We accept that we will have to pay 100 per cent of those costs,” he said.



“We have a strategy where we have sufficient land under our direct control that will allow us to discharge any treated effluent that we generate.” That would differ from the 8000-home Southern Thornlands PDA, where a core infrastructure agreement has been struck between the state and federal governments. The state said it was working through early feedback on the regional plan, and further public consultation would occur when a draft was released later this year. Fiteni’s director was contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Utterly petrified: I’ve tried more than once, but I’m done with skiing
World.content:
Reviews & adviceSki holidays Opinion Utterly petrified: I’ve tried more than once, but I’m done with skiing Catherine Marshall Travel writer August 17, 2026 — 5:00am

August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Let’s slice up the gnar,” bellows my instructor as I tackle the nursery run at the speed of an octogenarian sloth. “Don’t let your fear control you.” It’s my first time on skis, and I’m not just fearful, I’m utterly petrified. The landscape is magical – frozen lakes, snow-covered trees, icicles protruding like beautiful weapons from the eaves. But the cold is marrow deep, and my brain is playing tricks with the landscape; even gentle runs appear precipitous. Illustration: Jamie Brown “It’s mind over matter,” says the instructor as I trip over my skis while ploughing to a halt on a green run. “If you don’t master the slope, it will master you.” He has better luck with my 17-year-old daughter. It’s also her first ski trip, but she possesses the courage of the young – or the bravado of the foolhardy. I’m begging her not to fly off the mountainside when a child the height of a garden gnome speeds past us. My daughter looks embarrassed, but holds her counsel.



I’m exhausted by the time we pull out of Banff and head north along the Icefields Parkway. It’s minus-40 degrees and high winds have shuttered the ski lifts at Jasper’s Marmot Basin. Oh, what a pity. We sink into the heated outdoor pool at Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge and emerge to find our eyelashes frozen. 



“I can’t stop!” I wail, thunderbolting past him and tumbling just shy of a sheer drop. My fearless daughter has catapulted down the slope; she’s probably in the village drinking hot chocolate by now. As the instructor helps me to my feet, a blind skier and his sighted guide whizz by. Ice shimmers like a fairytale in their wake. It takes a few years to recover. Next time, I head to Colorado, where Vail’s Front Side runs sound tempting: Sourdough, Berries, Flap Jack, Cappuccino. Far better than the Back Bowls, which inspire terror with names like Seldom, Never, Rasputin’s Revenge and Outer Mongolia. My technique remains abysmal – I pitch, careen and nosedive downhill. “Don’t worry,” says my instructor. “It is through these falls that you learn.” Doesn’t he know I’m a slow learner? Moving on to Beaver Creek, a new instructor urges me not to fight the mountain. “Just fall down into it,” he says. “Just give your body permission to fall right down.”



Bad advice: I do fall, just as a man with a limb disability bullets past me on a mono-ski. Word about my ineptitude must’ve reached Breckenridge. Here I’m assigned an Australian ski instructor who dispenses pleasantries. He settles me into a chairlift, and we soar above slopes covered with fresh powder snow. Related Article Opinion

Ski holidays Think skiing in Australia is expensive? Here’s what it really costs Ben Groundwater Travel writer “We might have to do black runs just to get momentum,” the instructor says. “Otherwise I’ll need to push you.” I think he’s joking. Turns out he’s not. Heavy snowfall has closed the road from Denver, so there’s no one around to witness me stumbling from the chairlift to face my doom – a black diamond run named Adios which, on balance, sounds better than the neighbouring piste, Psychopath. “It’s going to be treacherous, challenging – and awesome!” the instructor says. It’s neither treacherous nor challenging; the gnar is so voluminous it holds me upright. Coddled waist-deep in powder, I glide in slow motion all the way down the mountain. I high-five the instructor and take my final bow. Adios, skiing.

World.title: The Soviets rebuilt this city. Now their work is receiving global attention
World.content:
Travel newsCentral Asia The Soviets rebuilt this city. Now their work is receiving global attention Julietta Jameson August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Soviet-era architecture is much maligned with its concrete, utilitarian forms often seen as representative of the rigid authoritarian regime that spawned it. But it is that very representation that has made the style valuable to the architectural canon. It tells its origin story loud and clear, and where it survives, its present-day use shows how communities build on history. Chorsu Bazaar with its shiny ceramic bowl-shaped roof. Now, there’s a new star of this design movement. Tashkent has just achieved UNESCO World Heritage status for its collection of 20th-century modernist architecture. But Tashkent’s buildings are outliers.



On April 26, 1966, a catastrophic earthquake destroyed much of the ancient capital of then-Soviet Uzbekistan. The disaster left hundreds of thousands homeless. 



“These buildings record how Tashkent imagined public life, collective identity and the future through architecture. The UNESCO recognition also carries a long-term responsibility: to conserve these buildings with rigour, keep them part of the life of the city and pass their knowledge to future generations.” The listed buildings include Chorsu Bazaar with its shiny ceramic bowl-shaped roof, Tashkent Circus, a flying saucer-like circular building topped by a blue dome and one of the city’s best-known modernist landmarks; and Kosmonavtlar metro station, whose shimmering blue interiors pay tribute to the Soviet space program and the cosmonauts of the Space Age. Inside Chorsu Bazaar. Tashkent Circus, one of the city’s best-known modernist landmarks. With Central Asia’s “Stans” having a travel moment, the listing gives visitors another reason to explore a capital some have perhaps rushed through. It is the gateway to Uzbekistan’s Silk Road jewels of Samarkand and Bukhara.



The listing is the latest development in a story of optimism. Since Uzbekistan began opening up to tourism under President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in 2016, investment has flowed into improved visitor infrastructure, making it increasingly a place to explore in its own right. Uzbekistan welcomed a record 11.7 million international visitors in 2025, the majority from neighbouring countries but with growing numbers arriving from further afield. Intrepid Travel says Central Asia is now one of its fastest-growing regions. Compared with pre-pandemic bookings, it says Kazakhstan bookings are up 1550 per cent and Uzbekistan 137 per cent. More broadly, Intrepid reports bookings across Central Asia have continued growing at about 30 per cent year-on-year. Inside the Tashkent Circus. Some might think of countries like Afghanistan, Iran or Pakistan in their perception of the broader region, but the main places tourists visit in Uzbekistan – Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva – are reasonably well-removed from all that.



Of course, it’s always a good idea to check the latest travel advice (Smartraveller currently recommends travellers “exercise a high degree of caution” for Uzbekistan) but the country has been working hard to make visitors feel welcome over the past 10 years. Related Article ★★★★

Train journeys On board the European high-speed train zooming through Central Asia’s desert Central Asia rewards travellers with a mix of experiences. Ancient Silk Road cities give way to mountainous wilderness, while metropolises such as Tashkent offer modern urban life. Each of the five “Stans” also offers their own unique culture and environment. With Uzbekistan now home to eight UNESCO World Heritage properties and the five Central Asian republics collectively home to nearly 30, the region’s emergence as a mainstream destination may simply be a matter of time. See intrepidtravel.com; acdf.uz

World.title: Record number of fraudsters booted from NDIS as Labor negotiates path for cuts
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDisability Record number of fraudsters booted from NDIS as Labor negotiates path for cuts Nick Newling August 17, 2026 — 5:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than 100 criminals and “dodgy consultants” operating within the National Disability Insurance Scheme have been banned as Labor seeks to crack down on fraudsters amid ongoing negotiations over the future of the $56 billion scheme. In the three months following the Albanese government’s April move to empower the scheme’s policing body, 111 individuals and providers have been issued banning orders, including one supplier who is alleged to have fraudulently claimed around $4 million in NDIS funds. A Sydney operator was banned in May after at least 70 NDIS participants told investigators from the scheme’s Quality and Standards Commission they were not aware of the firm and did not authorise claims on their behalf. The fraud crackdown comes as the federal government attempts to cut $36.2 billion out of the scheme by removing up to 300,000 participants. Shutterstock The record uptick in bans represented 70 per cent of the 158 bans handed down in 2026, and constituted the highest number of bans issued in a single quarter.



“Working in the NDIS is a great privilege, and if you abuse that privilege, you will be kicked out of the scheme,” NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister said. Related Article Disability Labor-led committee warns of human rights risks in NDIS reform “The new powers we’ve legislated have given the NDIS Commission the strong powers it needed to really take the fight to the shonks and grifters who thought they could take advantage of one of our society’s most important social programs.” The crackdown comes as the government attempts to cut $36.2 billion out of the system by removing up to 300,000 participants, returning the scheme to its foundational intention of only supporting people with permanent and significant impairment. Appearing on ABC TV’s Insiders on Sunday, McAllister said the government was confident of reaching an agreement on the legislation this week, and that attempts to curb fraud in the scheme were of “very strong” interest to both Labor and the Coalition.



“This scheme has to operate with integrity. When we see fraud, we very frequently see harm to people with disability, and I think there’s a shared view across ourselves and the Coalition,” McAllister said. The NDIS has suffered significant hits in public perception after years of reports of rorts within the scheme, and its ballooning bottom line. Health Minister Mark Butler, who announced changes to both youth participation in the scheme and its overall size in speeches over the past 12 months, is seeking to restrict eligibility to those who can prove permanent impairment from 2028. A Senate inquiry into Labor’s NDIS reforms released its final report green-lighting the laws on Friday despite weeks of testimony from disabled Australians, rights groups and legal services who said the changes could remove hundreds of thousands of people from the scheme within five years. “I remember what it was like when we didn’t have a scheme of this kind. It was really bad,” McAllister said. “We consider that changes to clarify who is eligible for the scheme and clarify what kinds of supports they should receive are absolutely essential if the community is to retain confidence in the scheme”. World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street slips after weak update on the US economy
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street slips after weak update on the US economy Stan Choe August 17, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market edged back from its all-time high following the latest report on the economy to come in surprisingly weak, this time about how much shoppers are spending at retailers. Such data could keep interest rates low, which is something Wall Street loves, but it also raises the risk of a slowing economy when inflation is still high. The S&P 500 slipped 0.2 per cent from its record set the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107 points, or 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.3 per cent. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures on Saturday pointing to a fall of 33 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The Australia dollar was trading at US70.79¢ at 5.16am AEST. US stocks gave up modest gains from early in the morning after oil prices swung higher. The price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 1.7 per cent to $US88.52 as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again.



Also raising uncertainty was a report showing shoppers spent less at US retailers last month than the month before. That surprised economists, who were forecasting another month of growth. On the bright side for financial markets, such a pullback in spending could take pressure off inflation. Inflation remains much higher than anyone would like, but reports earlier this week suggested the pace of increases in prices is decelerating. Related Article Big four Betting against the bank. ‘Widow-maker’ trades are making a comeback If inflation keeps trending that way, it could encourage the Federal Reserve to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. The downside of such data, including last week’s surprisingly weak report on the US job market, is that they raise the risk of a slowing economy. The Fed has no good tool to fix both a stagnating economy and high inflation at the same time, which is why what’s called “stagflation” is seen as a worst-case scenario.



Some on Wall Street cautioned against overreacting to the weak data on US retail sales, even if it was broad-based. It could simply be a snap back after retail sales in earlier months were boosted by unusual factors such as big tax refunds, the World Cup and even an earlier Prime Day event at Amazon, according to Jennifer Timmerman, senior investment strategy analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. US consumers nevertheless appear to be getting more discouraged about the economy. A preliminary survey by the University of Michigan suggested sentiment among them is weakening by more than economists expected. The survey said drops occurred across the political spectrum and showed up particularly among older, lower-income and other groups who can be hurt most by inflation. On Wall Street, Reddit jumped 12.6 per cent after learning its stock will join the S&P 500 index on Tuesday. Many professional investors and funds closely track the index, either mimicking it or at least measuring their performance against it. That can push many to buy a stock automatically when it enters the index. Applied Materials fell 5.1 per cent even though the company, whose technology helps make semiconductors, reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. CEO Gary Dickerson said global hunger for artificial-intelligence technology helped it deliver another record quarter.



But its stock had already more than doubled this year and built expectations very high, which helped pressure the stock on Friday. Related Article Energy Renewables are slashing power prices, but energy chiefs fear it may not last AI stocks in general have been swinging sharply on worries that their prices shot too high because of AI euphoria and that their strong growth in revenue may not be sustainable. All told, the S&P 500 fell 13.23 points to 7,785.76. Despite the loss, it nevertheless closed out a third straight winning week, its longest such streak since a nine-week run that ended in May. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 107.58 to 53,732.41, and the Nasdaq composite sank 73.86 to 26,729.16.



In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher and followed the price of oil. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.69 per cent from 4.63 per cent late Thursday. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe and Asia. London’s FTSE 100 slipped 0.2 per cent after Nigel Farage regained the seat in Parliament he quit a month ago, beating trash-can wearing comic candidate Count Binface in a special election. South Korea’s Kospi again had one of the world’s sharpest moves and jumped 2.4 per cent for its third straight gain of at least that much. Seoul has been at the centre of the world’s swings for AI stocks because its market is dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. World.title: In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare?
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPay In this Sydney suburb you need to earn $6.3m to be in the top 1%: How does your area compare? Matt Wade and Craig Butt August 17, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The top 1 per cent of income earners in 83 Sydney suburbs take home over $1 million a year on average, while in a cluster of harbourside neighbourhoods, to make the 1 per cent bracket, you need to earn more than $3 million. Analysis of official personal income data by this masthead casts fresh light on how ultra-high pay packets are distributed across the city. In Bellevue Hill, about five kilometres east of Sydney’s central business district, the average income for the highest paid 1 per cent of taxpayers was $6.3 million in 2022-23. That was $1.2 million lower than the previous year but it was still the highest average for the 1 per cent in any city suburb. The top 1 per cent of Sydney earners takes home over $1 million a year. Nine



The adjacent neighbourhood of Rose Bay-Vaucluse-Watsons Bay had the city’s second-highest average earnings for the top 1 per cent at $6.12 million (down from $6.37 million the previous year). Third was Woollahra, where the top 1 per cent took home an average of $5.05 million (up from $4.99 million). There were eight Sydney neighbourhoods where the top 1 per cent had average earnings between $3 million and $5 million (all of them waterfront suburbs) and 72 where average earnings were between $1 million and $3 million. You can search how suburbs and localities across NSW compare here: While suburbs with the highest average incomes for the top 1 per cent were mostly in the eastern suburbs and on the north shore, several were located in the city’s north-west, including Dural-Kenthurst ($1.66 million) and Glenhaven ($1.58 million).



In two outer western Sydney neighbourhoods – Horsley Park-Kemps Creek and Mulgoa-Luddenham-Orchard Hills – the top 1 per cent took home just over $1 million a year. Demographer and social researcher Mark McCrindle said the high average earnings for the top 1 per cent in parts of western and north-western Sydney showed how patterns of income and wealth have shifted. “It tells a story of a changing Sydney,” he said. “Yes, we’ve got very high incomes in those harbourside suburbs which has been the case for 100 years, but we’ve got new locations with high incomes as well. The dynamics of wealth have spread geographically.” McCrindle said income distribution patterns across Sydney showed not all high-income earners wanted to live on the waterfront.



“Some choose to invest their money in a large property, perhaps in bushland, rather than in the harbour area. Places like Dural, Kenthurst and Glenhaven in Sydney’s north-west have really changed economically.” However, in some western suburbs, the earnings of the top 1 per cent was well below the citywide average. Lowest was Auburn North, about 20 kilometres west of the CBD, where the average income of the best paid 1 per cent was $200,656. Suburbs where the top 1 per cent have especially high incomes correlate closely with house prices. Bellevue Hill, which had Sydney’s best paid 1 per cent of earners, also had the city’s highest median house price of $10.4 million, according to Domain’s June quarter House Price Report. In neighbouring Vaucluse, the median house price was $9.5 million and in Rose Bay it was $6.5 million. In Bellevue Hill, the best paid 1 per cent earned an average of $6.3 million a year in 2022-23. It also has a median house price over $10 million. Renee Nowytarger The top 1 per cent of earners across the whole of Greater Sydney had an average income of $1,027,863 in 2022-23.



That was about 12 times more than the average annual personal income for all Greater Sydney taxpayers of $84,947 and 16 times the city’s median income (the middle value of all earners) of $62,180. Sydney was the only Australian capital where the average earnings for the top 1 per cent was a seven-figure total. Next highest was Perth, with average earnings of $928,762 a year for the top 1 per cent, followed by Melbourne with $792,491. The earnings figures show Sydney is Australia’s most unequal capital city for income: the top 1 per cent of earners received 12.1 per cent of the city’s income in 2022-23. That compares with 11.1 per cent in Perth, 10.2 per cent in Melbourne and 8.7 per cent in Brisbane. Nationally, the top 1 per cent earned 9.9 per cent of all personal income. Outside of Sydney there were some localities where the top 1 per cent had extremely high earnings. In the Upper Hunter town of Scone, the average income of the top 1 per cent of earners was just under $5 million, the fourth highest in NSW.



In Bangalow, near Byron Bay, the average income for the top 1 per cent was $1.9 million while in Robertson-Fitzroy Falls in the Southern Highlands, that average was $1.87 million. The suburb with the highest 1 per cent average income of anywhere in Australia was Cottesloe in Perth, where you need to be bringing in $36 million a year on average to be in that suburb’s top 1 per cent. In many neighbourhoods, including Cottesloe, the average income among the top 1 per cent is skewed by a few earners with extremely high earners – the top 0.1 per cent – who drive up the average. The analysis used Australian Bureau of Statistics personal income data, which draws on Tax Office records for the 2022-23 financial year, the most recent available. It includes figures for “Statistical Area Level 2” (SA2) localities that are similar to suburbs.



The data covers only individual pre-tax income; it does not include assets owned by individuals such as housing and shares. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Is Greek yoghurt really the miracle protein fix it’s made out to be?
World.content:
Tips & adviceHealthy eating Is Greek yoghurt really the miracle protein fix it’s made out to be? Is Greek yoghurt better for you than Greek-style yoghurt? We whey up the facts from the social media spin about the protein-powered staples still flying off the shelves. Caterina Hrysomallis August 17, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

No, you’re not imagining it. There’s been lots of buzz around Greek yoghurt recently, probably spurred by the collision of two TikTok trends. The first is still trending: “protein-maxxing”, which simply means maximising protein intake, with Greek yoghurt commonly identified, alongside chicken breasts, as top-tier healthy protein sources. The second? Placing Biscoff biscuits into a small tub of Greek yoghurt, leaving it for a few hours or overnight to create a mini dessert. Ironically, this combo is called a “Japanese cheesecake”. One claim that’s gained traction is that “Greek-style” yoghurt is not as good for you as “Greek”. Another is that other kinds of yoghurt, like natural yoghurt, are inferior. Meanwhile, yoghurts with long ingredient lists are also copping criticism. So, what’s real and what’s just social media speculation? Let’s break it down.



Chobani is among the better-for-you Greek yoghurt brands. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up What is Greek yoghurt? “To keep it really simple, Greek yoghurt is strained not stirred. That’s the key differentiating factor,” says dietitian Helena McDonald. The production process gives Greek yoghurt its superpower: high protein. “The straining process removes the whey and makes it a whole lot thicker. In doing so, it concentrates the protein content of the yoghurt.” Traditional Greek yoghurt is strained three times.



For Greek people, Greek yoghurt is the heart of a good tzatziki. It’s used in marinades, sometimes in filo pastry cheese pies, and is the key to yiaourtopita (yoghurt cake with lemon). Adam Liaw’s dill and mint tzatziki: a delicious way to eat Greek yoghurt. William Meppem How do you pick a good Greek yoghurt? Let’s rule one criterion out: if you’re looking for Greek-produced yoghurt in Australia, you won’t find any due to biosecurity restrictions. The term “Greek yoghurt” is not actually protected. Brands can call something Greek yoghurt even if it’s not from Greece or contains non-traditional additives. This makes things a little tricky.



If you’re after authenticity, traditional Greek yoghurt is plain, leans on milk, live cultures and sometimes cream – while avoiding thickeners. “There’s a really big misconception that ‘Greek-style’ yoghurts are worse for you and full of rubbish, which isn’t necessarily true.” Helena McDonald, dietitian “Many yoghurts here do call themselves ‘Greek-style’, even though they might not have other non-traditional additives in them.” Why? Simply, those brands are being cautious. “There’s a really big misconception that ‘Greek-style’ yoghurts are worse for you and full of rubbish, which isn’t necessarily true,” says McDonald. It all comes down to the ingredients list.



“The best thing you can do is always get familiar with flipping over packaging and looking at the ingredients label and the nutritional profile. A minimal ingredients list is always a good thing”. Two standout, authentic options are Chobani and Evia – both contain minimal ingredients and very high amounts of protein. Adam Liaw’s breakfast crumble with cherries and yoghurt. William Meppem Are longer ingredient lists ‘bad’? Not necessarily, despite their vilification on parts of social media. McDonald says it’s more about interrogating what the ingredients are. “There could be multiple types of natural fruit; that’s not inherently problematic.”



Be sure to compare products using the “per 100 gram”, not “per serving”, column, given that sizing can vary so much across the yoghurt category. McDonald says look out for number codes which refer to artificial sweeteners, emulsifiers and thickeners. “The jury’s still out around how much they impact our health and our gut microbiome. There is some evidence around emulsifiers being harmful for people with irritable bowel disease, ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s, but again, it’s all emerging.” Other yoghurts still deserve your attention. Getty Images Should we default to Greek yoghurt for nutritional purposes?



McDonald says it really depends on your goals and dietary requirements. “There’s no doubt it’s one of the best types of yoghurt that you can get.” It’s great for those with high-protein requirements. “For example, if you’re wanting to build muscle and optimise your body composition goals.” It’s also lower in carbohydrates, which means it’s lower in sugar and lactose. McDonald says that natural yoghurts are also a solid choice, as they generally lean towards a wholefood-based ingredient list. These are, however, lower in protein, as they’re typically stirred, not strained.



Greek yoghurts are lower in calcium, as so much of this is in the removed whey. Most yoghurts help add probiotics to the digestive system, but there are times when McDonald recommends very specific yoghurts. “Some brands offer specific strains and quantities of probiotics, which can be useful for certain digestive concerns. Some have evidence to support them in being helpful for things like constipation and other gastric concerns.” Related Article Natural, Greek, coconut, high-protein: The nutritional pros and cons of your favourite yoghurt What’s the go with fat content?



Where fat isn’t a concern, it can be helpful to keep the fat content in dairy products “as it may make you more satisfied from your meal and therefore less likely to go looking for other things later”, says McDonald. Dietary fat also helps with the absorption of fat-soluble nutrients, including vitamins A, D, E and K.



At the end of the day, this is just one food, so you if you don’t have specific dietary concerns, it’s not worth stressing over fat content too much. “It’s better to focus on a balanced diet that isn’t reliant on overly processed foods”, says McDonald. Raise your yoghurt pouch to that. Related Article Aussies are suckers for yoghurt pouches. We put them to the taste test – with mixed results Related Recipe collection 70 sweet and savoury yoghurt recipes

World.title: Brisbane’s most expensive homes are in our suburb, but we still love underdogs and outsiders
World.content:
NationalQueenslandLife in the ’burbs Opinion Brisbane’s most expensive homes are in our suburb, but we still love underdogs and outsiders Stephen Vagg Contributor August 17, 2026 — 5:00am

August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the late 1990s I lived in a top-floor apartment on New Farm’s Moray Street, aka Brisbane’s Most Liveable Street in 1993. I had a view of the Story Bridge, and lived just across the road from Wilson Outlook Reserve, while only paying $150 a week in rent. Mind you, the grass of that reserve was routinely covered in discarded syringes from local junkies, so it’s swings and roundabouts. All Brisbane suburbs change over time, but some change more rapidly than others, and nowhere is that truer than in New Farm. An area originally known as “Binkin-ba” (meaning “place of the land tortoises”), it was converted into a literal new farm in 1827 by notorious flog-happy British officer Captain Patrick Logan, later killed by Aboriginal people for doing some non-consensual exploring in their backyard.



The farm didn’t last that long, and neither did other features of the suburb over the years: the horse-drawn tram, for instance, which personally I’d love to see make a comeback; or the racecourse which later turned into New Farm Park; or the power station, which still exists in the form of Brisbane Powerhouse; or the deserted quarry at the bottom of New Farm cliffs, which is now the site of the Howard Smith Wharves. New Farm is always evolving. At one stage it was predominantly a low-rent area, providing accommodation for those who worked in the factories, wharves and submarine bases (no kidding) of Teneriffe. It was also a long-standing sanctuary for underdogs, oddballs and outsiders, such as immigrants, artists, drunks, derelicts and the LGBTIQ+ community. Now it’s very much a high-rent area, infested with botox clinics, $8 soy lattes, real estate agents and nepo babies, while many of the old inhabitants can no longer afford to live here. A house sold for $25 million in November, and New Farm topped the list of most expensive Brisbane homes last time I looked. Yet for all New Farm’s flaws, the suburb retains a magic about it, for me at least. Hemmed in on three sides by the “much prettier at night” Brisbane River, it’s close to the CBD, but feels far away.



It’s one of the best suburbs to walk or jog around, being full of different mini-neighbourhoods: the raffish charms of Brunswick Street with its vape stores and e-scooters; the Noosa-esque chic of James Street, with its designer brands and Range Rovers; the view of the city skyline and Story Bridge from the Riverwalk; the jacaranda-clad New Farm Park, the “lungs” of the suburb; the cocktails and pirate-ship playground of Howard Smith Wharves; the laurel trees of Abbott Street; the zen calm of New Farm Library, with its endlessly patient librarians; the bustle of Merthyr Village, particularly on pension day. It’s one of the best suburbs to jog around. Morgan Roberts The suburb always feels humming and alive, even on sleepy afternoons, and every time we lose something of the past (RIP Gertie’s Bar), something else seems to pop up instead (hello, Junk Bar). New Farm also has a genuine sense of community. For instance, in 2024 a French restaurant, À la Bonne Franquette, started up on Brunswick Street, run by a young married couple with a cute baby. They worked so hard (even the baby) and the food was so great, the whole neighbourhood was willing them to succeed – I certainly bought more of their beef bourguignon than I could afford at the time. And eventually they did succeed, and all of New Farm (well, the bit near me) cheered, because it’s nice to see a business that’s not a real estate agency do well. Co-owner Hugo Wintzer outside his restaurant. “A la bonne franquette” means “fuss free”. Morgan Roberts



The New Farm spirit is demonstrated in other ways, such as the Neighbourhood Centre, The Village Voice, and the way most locals stick up for the homeless whenever some bigot bags them on the New Farm Community Facebook page. This spirit is constantly under attack from things like the cost-of-living crisis and the real estate/botox/pearl-clutching brigade determined to turn us into a Queensland outpost of Sydney’s Mosman, but it’s still hanging in there, and as long as New Farm retains some sort of sympathy for the outsider and the underdog it will always be special. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs Yes, the cliches about my suburb are all true. Roll your eyes if you must Lucinda Kent Contributor My director wife Louise Alston and I recently made a feature film, All My Friends Are Back in Brisbane, about a woman who returns home from overseas and moves to New Farm, as we did during COVID. More than half the picture was set and shot in New Farm. We filmed in our apartment and other places I love in the suburb, such as Death Before Decaf, Hey Mr. Cafe, Wilson Outlook, Merthyr Park and near the sign on Moray Street that still proudly declares it was Brisbane’s most liveable street in 1993. The cash budget was $13,000, so we didn’t have an official production designer – but we had an unofficial one, and that was the suburb of New Farm. The movie made its Brisbane theatrical debut at Five Star Cinemas New Farm, across the road from our place, and had a 10-week run there. We tried to introduce every screening personally, and are constantly delighted at the love and passion New Farmians have for their suburb.



But then again why shouldn’t they? To us, it’s the best place in Brisbane, warts and all (botox and all, rather – the warts here tend to be surgically removed).

World.title: Developer hopes to cut out council for golf course resort, housing approval
World.content:
Exclusive NationalQueenslandDevelopment Developer hopes to cut out council for golf course resort, housing approval Julius Dennis August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The developer behind the proposal for a five-star hotel, industrial park and housing on rural land south-east of Brisbane has laid out plans that could bypass council and see a state-sanctioned development area established. Stephen Williams, best known for Riverlink in Ipswich and West Village in inner-Brisbane’s West End, says he is confident the state will add the land in Mount Cotton to the urban footprint and declare it a priority development area, paving the way for major changes. The land, largely comprising chicken farms and a winery, is in the Redland City Council area, which voted to support an investigation to include the area in the urban footprint earlier this year. Developer Stephen Williams is representing the Mount Cotton landholders. Julius Dennis Williams said he had initially been working with chicken farm owners Darwalla and Golden Cockerel, who were seeking a new use for their land as they planned to move their operations further away from the expanding Redlands population.



“The reason that opportunity came up is because of the avian flu risk for having chickens in the Redlands area, and the impact that could have on the activities of Golden Cockerel,” Williams said. Other landholders represented by Williams include local newspaperman and developer Warren Pryde and the Morris family, who own the nearby Sirromet Winery. Sirromet sits amid pristine land zoned rural. Sirromet Williams said he was confident applications currently with the state planner and Economic Development Queensland would result in the area being included in the urban footprint and deemed a PDA, which would enable the state to decide what happens on the land, not the council. The entire urban footprint of south-east Queensland is currently under review, with a draft plan expected by the end of the year.



Should he get his way, Williams said he hoped to move fast. “We have the ambition to meet some of the missing accommodation needs that are likely before the Olympic Games in 2032,” he said. The proposed development, including a five-star hotel, at Sirromet Winery in Mount Cotton. Under the plan, Sirromet would be transformed from a winery and events space with glamping facilities to a 250-room resort, complete with an 18-hole golf course, conference rooms and permanent villas. A masterplan seen by this masthead also includes a wellness centre, an expansion of the glamping facilities, horticultural gardens, a solar farm, and a wastewater treatment plant.



Related Article Exclusive

Development Council says development on farmland hinges on road with no timeframe Williams said it was business as usual at the winery for now, but that would be the first part of the plan to go ahead. The winery would connect the area to the already approved Southern Thornlands PDA. The southern end, made up of land owned by the chicken companies and pegged for a “technology park” and district centre that would include shops and condensed residential housing, would almost hug the already developed part of Mount Cotton. Between them is the land owned by Pryde and quarry owner Dick Karreman, who is on the project but represented by local developer Fiteni, Williams said. In Williams’ plan, this section, and part of a block owned by Golden Cockerel, would be residential blocks, roughly 20 per hectare.



But the council does not support more suburban development, and called for it to be excluded from the plan when it voted to support the area being investigated. Councillor Rowanne McKenzie, who brought the motion forward, said this was because the council already relied too heavily on household rates. “Approximately 90 per cent of council’s rate revenue is derived from residential properties, creating a heavy reliance on households to fund core services and infrastructure,” she said. In its letter to the government supporting the investigation of the land, the council said any urban development should be linked to the delivery of the Coomera Connector.



Referred to as the second M1, the Coomera Connector is an alternative route to the clogged motorway between the northern Gold Coast and Loganholme, just south of Brisbane, which has been in the works since 2016. Its final stage will swoop through the Redlands, near the proposed development. However, that section is only in the planning stage. “We note that that’s council’s decision, but we don’t agree with that. We agree it would be an ideal position, but it’s not based on any real traffic justification,” Williams said, arguing that upgrades to local infrastructure would be sufficient. While Williams said he was keen to work with the community and all levels of government, the council’s influence could be dashed by a PDA. Should that happen, it would be the fourth PDA in the Redlands, where infrastructure like sewerage and roads are contentious subjects.



Related Article Exclusive

Queensland councils In the red: Leaked report reveals council’s multimillion-dollar sewage problem A past Fiteni-linked development took more than a decade to connect to the wastewater network, while other projects have led to localised traffic problems. A council spokesperson said any work to core infrastructure would need to be covered by developers. In turn, Williams said he and the landowners would foot the bill for any infrastructure upgrades needed for the development, including a duplication of parts of Mount Cotton Road and an upgrade to the Mount Cotton water treatment plant. “We accept that we will have to pay 100 per cent of those costs,” he said.



“We have a strategy where we have sufficient land under our direct control that will allow us to discharge any treated effluent that we generate.” That would differ from the 8000-home Southern Thornlands PDA, where a core infrastructure agreement has been struck between the state and federal governments. The state said it was working through early feedback on the regional plan, and further public consultation would occur when a draft was released later this year. Fiteni’s director was contacted for comment. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Utterly petrified: I’ve tried more than once, but I’m done with skiing
World.content:
Reviews & adviceSki holidays Opinion Utterly petrified: I’ve tried more than once, but I’m done with skiing Catherine Marshall Travel writer August 17, 2026 — 5:00am

August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“Let’s slice up the gnar,” bellows my instructor as I tackle the nursery run at the speed of an octogenarian sloth. “Don’t let your fear control you.” It’s my first time on skis, and I’m not just fearful, I’m utterly petrified. The landscape is magical – frozen lakes, snow-covered trees, icicles protruding like beautiful weapons from the eaves. But the cold is marrow deep, and my brain is playing tricks with the landscape; even gentle runs appear precipitous. Illustration: Jamie Brown “It’s mind over matter,” says the instructor as I trip over my skis while ploughing to a halt on a green run. “If you don’t master the slope, it will master you.” He has better luck with my 17-year-old daughter. It’s also her first ski trip, but she possesses the courage of the young – or the bravado of the foolhardy. I’m begging her not to fly off the mountainside when a child the height of a garden gnome speeds past us. My daughter looks embarrassed, but holds her counsel.



I’m exhausted by the time we pull out of Banff and head north along the Icefields Parkway. It’s minus-40 degrees and high winds have shuttered the ski lifts at Jasper’s Marmot Basin. Oh, what a pity. We sink into the heated outdoor pool at Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge and emerge to find our eyelashes frozen. 



“I can’t stop!” I wail, thunderbolting past him and tumbling just shy of a sheer drop. My fearless daughter has catapulted down the slope; she’s probably in the village drinking hot chocolate by now. As the instructor helps me to my feet, a blind skier and his sighted guide whizz by. Ice shimmers like a fairytale in their wake. It takes a few years to recover. Next time, I head to Colorado, where Vail’s Front Side runs sound tempting: Sourdough, Berries, Flap Jack, Cappuccino. Far better than the Back Bowls, which inspire terror with names like Seldom, Never, Rasputin’s Revenge and Outer Mongolia. My technique remains abysmal – I pitch, careen and nosedive downhill. “Don’t worry,” says my instructor. “It is through these falls that you learn.” Doesn’t he know I’m a slow learner? Moving on to Beaver Creek, a new instructor urges me not to fight the mountain. “Just fall down into it,” he says. “Just give your body permission to fall right down.”



Bad advice: I do fall, just as a man with a limb disability bullets past me on a mono-ski. Word about my ineptitude must’ve reached Breckenridge. Here I’m assigned an Australian ski instructor who dispenses pleasantries. He settles me into a chairlift, and we soar above slopes covered with fresh powder snow. Related Article Opinion

Ski holidays Think skiing in Australia is expensive? Here’s what it really costs Ben Groundwater Travel writer “We might have to do black runs just to get momentum,” the instructor says. “Otherwise I’ll need to push you.” I think he’s joking. Turns out he’s not. Heavy snowfall has closed the road from Denver, so there’s no one around to witness me stumbling from the chairlift to face my doom – a black diamond run named Adios which, on balance, sounds better than the neighbouring piste, Psychopath. “It’s going to be treacherous, challenging – and awesome!” the instructor says. It’s neither treacherous nor challenging; the gnar is so voluminous it holds me upright. Coddled waist-deep in powder, I glide in slow motion all the way down the mountain. I high-five the instructor and take my final bow. Adios, skiing.

World.title: The Soviets rebuilt this city. Now their work is receiving global attention
World.content:
Travel newsCentral Asia The Soviets rebuilt this city. Now their work is receiving global attention Julietta Jameson August 17, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Soviet-era architecture is much maligned with its concrete, utilitarian forms often seen as representative of the rigid authoritarian regime that spawned it. But it is that very representation that has made the style valuable to the architectural canon. It tells its origin story loud and clear, and where it survives, its present-day use shows how communities build on history. Chorsu Bazaar with its shiny ceramic bowl-shaped roof. Now, there’s a new star of this design movement. Tashkent has just achieved UNESCO World Heritage status for its collection of 20th-century modernist architecture. But Tashkent’s buildings are outliers.



On April 26, 1966, a catastrophic earthquake destroyed much of the ancient capital of then-Soviet Uzbekistan. The disaster left hundreds of thousands homeless. 



“These buildings record how Tashkent imagined public life, collective identity and the future through architecture. The UNESCO recognition also carries a long-term responsibility: to conserve these buildings with rigour, keep them part of the life of the city and pass their knowledge to future generations.” The listed buildings include Chorsu Bazaar with its shiny ceramic bowl-shaped roof, Tashkent Circus, a flying saucer-like circular building topped by a blue dome and one of the city’s best-known modernist landmarks; and Kosmonavtlar metro station, whose shimmering blue interiors pay tribute to the Soviet space program and the cosmonauts of the Space Age. Inside Chorsu Bazaar. Tashkent Circus, one of the city’s best-known modernist landmarks. With Central Asia’s “Stans” having a travel moment, the listing gives visitors another reason to explore a capital some have perhaps rushed through. It is the gateway to Uzbekistan’s Silk Road jewels of Samarkand and Bukhara.



The listing is the latest development in a story of optimism. Since Uzbekistan began opening up to tourism under President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in 2016, investment has flowed into improved visitor infrastructure, making it increasingly a place to explore in its own right. Uzbekistan welcomed a record 11.7 million international visitors in 2025, the majority from neighbouring countries but with growing numbers arriving from further afield. Intrepid Travel says Central Asia is now one of its fastest-growing regions. Compared with pre-pandemic bookings, it says Kazakhstan bookings are up 1550 per cent and Uzbekistan 137 per cent. More broadly, Intrepid reports bookings across Central Asia have continued growing at about 30 per cent year-on-year. Inside the Tashkent Circus. Some might think of countries like Afghanistan, Iran or Pakistan in their perception of the broader region, but the main places tourists visit in Uzbekistan – Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva – are reasonably well-removed from all that.



Of course, it’s always a good idea to check the latest travel advice (Smartraveller currently recommends travellers “exercise a high degree of caution” for Uzbekistan) but the country has been working hard to make visitors feel welcome over the past 10 years. Related Article ★★★★

Train journeys On board the European high-speed train zooming through Central Asia’s desert Central Asia rewards travellers with a mix of experiences. Ancient Silk Road cities give way to mountainous wilderness, while metropolises such as Tashkent offer modern urban life. Each of the five “Stans” also offers their own unique culture and environment. With Uzbekistan now home to eight UNESCO World Heritage properties and the five Central Asian republics collectively home to nearly 30, the region’s emergence as a mainstream destination may simply be a matter of time. See intrepidtravel.com; acdf.uz

World.title: People are going to 'lose hundreds of dollars a week' taking leave, union warns
World.content:
There is a risk that some people may not be able to afford to take leave when new rules take effect, unions and employment law experts say.

The Employment Leave Act has passed into law and will replace the Holidays Act in 2028.

It is designed to make leave rules clearer for employers and employees, and offer more certainty.

While much of the bill has been well received, including a change that will mean employees can take sick leave from their first day, and parents being able to access leave at their normal rate when they return from paid parental leave there are still concerns about some aspects.

Alison Maelzer, an employment law expert at Hesketh Henry, said people who worked a lot of overtime or whose pay included regular commission, could find their annual leave was paid at a much different rate to what they had been used to.

"Payments for annual leave will - unless parties agree otherwise - be at what amounts to the employee's lowest rate of pay.

"So at present, when you take annual leave, you are paid at the higher of your 'ordinary weekly pay' or your 'average weekly earnings'. Average weekly earnings is made up by calculating your gross earnings in the last 12 months, divided by 52. Your gross earnings will include any overtime you have been paid for, commission you've earned, and some bonus or incentive payments. These additional payments could amount to a significant portion of some employees' earnings in a year.

"Under the new system, the leave payment will be based on, for waged workers, the lowest hourly rate payable for the shift you're taking leave from, or for salaried workers, the salary that is attributable to one hour of work."

She said that would not usually include any incentives, overtime or bonuses that people might normally receive.

"For workers who work a lot of overtime, those who receive significant incentive payments, and/or those who receive a significant part of their pay through commissions, this will make a noticeable difference to the pay that they receive during annual leave. This may potentially discourage people from taking leave, which in turn can have flow-on effects for health, safety, and wellbeing, as well as productivity. It could also mean leave liability for employers increases. The same payment rates would apply when unused leave is paid out at the end of employment.

"For employees who are paid partly or wholly by way of commission, there is an ability to negotiate a 'leave payment rate'. If they are unable to reach agreement with their employer on a leave payment rate, they can be paid their leave at minimum wage."

Workers First Union national organiser Callum Francis said he shared that concern.

"Those that earn commission are going to find out quite shortly, if they haven't clicked, that they're going to be having less pay when they're on leave. It's potentially going to make it harder for them to take leave or want to take leave. This seems, at least from our point of view, like it isn't going to make life easier."

He said many people would be in a pattern where they relied in working overtime to have enough money coming into the household.

"People are going to take annual leave and suddenly realise that they're losing potentially hundreds of dollars in a week. They will suddenly find that taking annual leave is more difficult… our colleagues and the people we deal with in supermarket retail stores are regularly put on their minimum hour contracts and regularly work at least, if not another day, then a number of hours extra in a week to try to help ends meet…we are genuinely worried that people aren't going to be able to take leave, or they're going to cash it up because they're low on money, and they're not going to get that time out from work."

University of Otago associate professor Paula O'Kane said many people would not understand what had happened.

"What I think needs to be considered from an employer's point of view is really what contracts and what hours they're putting their people on as their base rate.

"So they might need to think more carefully about having more accurate contracts and more consistent contracts so that gets paid properly."

She said it would rely more on people being good employers and treating staff fairly.

"I'm not sure there was ever any easy solution to getting this right, at the moment it's quite complex [but] there's worrying things in [the bill] and I think a lot of it will come down to how an employer interprets and works with it.

"Sick pay not accruing for casual employees is a little bit problematic too because we could all say save that 4 percent you get extra into your pay packet for when you're sick [as a casual worker] but few people will be disciplined enough."

Employees would also need to think about which staff were truly casual and which were really permanent part-time.

She said it would have been better to consider an option where employees could accrue sick leave across jobs and take it from one to the next.
